Inflation rate
Real GDP
Money supply

Money demand

ECON-SP-EASY-62.q: In the short run, expansionary policy usually moves the economy toward:

Higher unemployment and lower inflation
No change in either variable

Lower inflation and higher unemployment
Higher inflation and higher unemployment
Lower unemployment and higher output

The inflation rate

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-153.q: The short-run Phillips curve slopes downward because higher AD tends to:
options: Raise output, lower unemployment, and raise inflation
Lower output, lower unemployment, and lower inflation
Raise unemployment while lowering inflation forever
Shift LRPC left immediately
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-153.feedback: Higher AD raises output and prices, which maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation.

options: Expectations adjust; unemployment returns to normal
Money demand becomes zero
AD stops affecting the short run
Inflation cannot change wages
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-154.commonError: Treating the short-run tradeoff as permanent.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-154.feedback: Once expectations adjust, unemployment returns to the natural rate.

An upward shift of the SRPC at every unemployment rate
A rightward shift of the vertical LRPC
A move down and right along the current SRPC
PM2A-SRPC-M-001.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.
PM2A-SRPC-M-001.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.

Lower expected inflation shifts the SRPC downward
The natural rate necessarily falls and shifts LRPC left
The adverse supply shock shifts the SRPC upward
PM2A-SRPC-M-002.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
PM2A-SRPC-M-002.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

Money demand is always zero
LRAS shifts right automatically
M1 excludes currency
ECON-SP-HARD-255.commonError: Believing in a permanent Phillips curve menu.
ECON-SP-HARD-255.feedback: Once expected inflation adjusts, unemployment returns to the natural rate.

options: Unexpected AD expansion
Higher expected inflation
Adverse oil shock
Rising natural unemployment
ECON-SP-HARD-258.commonError: Confusing movement along SRPC with shifts of SRPC.
ECON-SP-HARD-258.feedback: Unexpected AD expansion moves the economy along the existing SRPC in the short run.

ECON-SP-HARD-268.q: Which answer best separates short-run and long-run Phillips curve logic?

Policy cannot affect unemployment even briefly, because money is neutral in every period
Policy permanently lowers unemployment whenever inflation rises above zero
Policy shifts LRPC whenever actual inflation changes
ECON-SP-HARD-268.commonError: Confusing short-run effects with long-run neutrality.
ECON-SP-HARD-268.feedback: Demand policy can move unemployment in the short run, but expectations adjust and unemployment returns to natural.

Lower unemployment with higher inflation
Higher unemployment with higher inflation
No change in unemployment as inflation changes

The economy moves B to A because stronger demand reduces inflation and raises unemployment.
The economy moves A to B along SRPC0; unemployment is 2 percentage points below natural while inflation is 1 percentage point higher.

LRPC shifts right to 7 percent unemployment because weaker demand permanently worsens matching.
The economy moves B to A because weaker demand raises inflation and reduces unemployment.

Aggregate demand alone fixed both outcomes
The economy is on a higher SRPC
The economy moved up one unchanged SRPC

P52B-S2-SRPC-L-001.q: Two episodes produce the same increase in inflation. In one, unemployment falls after aggregate demand expands; in the other, unemployment rises after an adverse supply shock. What explains the difference?
options: Both episodes are movements along one SRPC, but they begin from different unemployment rates.
Both episodes shift the LRPC because inflation changes the natural rate in opposite directions.
The supply shock lowers expected inflation and moves the economy down an unchanged SRPC.
The demand expansion moves along an SRPC, while the supply shock shifts the curve.
P52B-S2-SRPC-L-001.commonError: Assuming every inflation change is a movement along one fixed Phillips curve.
P52B-S2-SRPC-L-001.feedback: Demand changes can move the economy along a given SRPC; supply shocks alter the inflation-unemployment relationship and shift the SRPC.

PG5-PC-L-012.q: Refer to the graph with A on SRPC0 and LRPC. Later observations show unemployment at A’s rate but persistently higher inflation. One analyst says the SRPC must have become vertical; another says the same vertical LRPC can coexist with a higher SRPC after contracts adjust. Which additional evidence would support the second interpretation?
options: Inflation rose once, which by itself proves that expectations already adjusted fully.
Current unemployment equals the natural rate, which requires every SRPC to be vertical.
The price level is higher, which proves that the natural unemployment rate permanently fell.
Wage-setting expectations have risen to match the sustained inflation while labor-market structure and supply conditions are unchanged.
PG5-PC-L-012.feedback: An unchanged natural rate locates the same LRPC. Evidence that expected inflation caught up, with other shifters held fixed, supports a higher SRPC crossing it. Equal unemployment and a higher inflation observation alone do not establish the expectations mechanism.
PG5-PC-L-012.imageAlt: Phillips graph with downward SRPC0, vertical LRPC, and their intersection A.
PG5-PC-L-012.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from −2.5 to 10. Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6.5), A at (5,2.5), and (10,−1.5). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5. Dashed guides from A mark 5 on the horizontal axis and 2.5 on the vertical axis.

PM2A-SRPC-L-004.q: A demand expansion moves the economy to lower unemployment and higher inflation. A year later unemployment returns to its original rate while inflation remains higher. Which sequence fits?
options: A supply improvement followed by movement down the SRPC
Movement along an SRPC followed by an upward SRPC shift
Two movements along one permanently fixed SRPC
An LRPC shift left followed by falling expectations
PM2A-SRPC-L-004.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
PM2A-SRPC-L-004.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

PM2A-SRPC-L-005.q: An adverse supply shock raises inflation while output falls. How should the AD-AS result transfer to the Phillips model?
options: Higher inflation and unemployment indicate an upward SRPC shift
Higher inflation and lower unemployment indicate movement along SRPC
Lower inflation and unemployment indicate a downward SRPC shift
Unchanged inflation with lower unemployment indicates an LRPC shift
PM2A-SRPC-L-005.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
PM2A-SRPC-L-005.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

PM2A-SRPC-L-006.q: A policymaker cites the downward-sloping SRPC as proof that permanently higher inflation will secure permanently lower unemployment. What is the decisive flaw?
options: The SRPC actually slopes upward for every demand change
Inflation cannot respond to aggregate demand in the short run
The natural rate is always zero after an expansion
Expected inflation adjusts, so the short-run unemployment gain is not permanent
PM2A-SRPC-L-006.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
PM2A-SRPC-L-006.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3000.commonError: Confusing the Phillips curve with the AD-AS model.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3000.q: What does the short-run Phillips curve show?
options: A short-run tradeoff between inflation and unemployment
A long-run tradeoff between inflation and output
A fixed relationship between money supply and GDP
A direct measure of government spending
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3000.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows that lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation, and higher unemployment is associated with lower inflation.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3001.q: Expansionary policy raises aggregate demand. In the short run, what Phillips curve movement should follow?
options: Lower inflation and higher unemployment
Higher inflation and lower unemployment
Higher inflation and higher unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3001.feedback: Expansionary policy raises AD, which can lower unemployment but raises inflation in the short run.

P52B-S2-SRPC-B2-001.q: Aggregate demand contracts unexpectedly while expected inflation is initially fixed. What short-run Phillips-curve movement is most likely?
options: Toward lower inflation and higher unemployment.
Toward higher inflation and lower unemployment.
The entire SRPC shifts up-right immediately.
Unemployment stays fixed at the natural rate in the short run.
P52B-S2-SRPC-B2-001.commonError: Confusing a demand-driven movement along the SRPC with a shift of the curve.
P52B-S2-SRPC-B2-001.feedback: An unexpected demand contraction moves the economy down and right along the current SRPC.

PM2A-SRPC-EB-007.q: On a given SRPC, which combination lies farther up and left?
options: Higher inflation and higher unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment
Higher inflation and lower unemployment
Lower inflation and higher unemployment
PM2A-SRPC-EB-007.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
PM2A-SRPC-EB-007.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

PM2A-SRPC-EB-008.q: Expected inflation is unchanged and aggregate demand falls. What happens first?
options: The economy moves up and left along its SRPC
The economy moves down and right along its SRPC
The SRPC shifts upward at every unemployment rate
The LRPC shifts left of the natural rate
PM2A-SRPC-EB-008.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.
PM2A-SRPC-EB-008.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.

PM2A-SRPC-EB-009.q: Which event most directly shifts rather than moves along the SRPC?
options: A change in expected inflation
An unexpected change in aggregate demand
A temporary change in real spending
A movement between two points on one curve
PM2A-SRPC-EB-009.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
PM2A-SRPC-EB-009.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

PM2A-SRPC-FB-010.q: A demand boom first lowers unemployment, then wage expectations catch up. Which complete Phillips sequence is most defensible?
options: Shift LRPC left, then move down the same SRPC as expectations rise
Shift SRPC downward, then keep unemployment permanently below natural
Move down-right along SRPC, then shift LRPC right after wages adjust
Move up-left along SRPC, then shift SRPC upward toward the natural rate
PM2A-SRPC-FB-010.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
PM2A-SRPC-FB-010.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

PM2A-SRPC-FB-011.q: A supply disruption raises inflation and unemployment together. Which interpretation survives both the graph and mechanism tests?
options: The LRPC shifts left because inflation increased
The SRPC shifts downward because output fell
The SRPC shifts upward because the tradeoff worsens
The economy moves up-left along a fixed SRPC
PM2A-SRPC-FB-011.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
PM2A-SRPC-FB-011.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

PM2A-SRPC-FB-012.q: A central bank unexpectedly expands demand. Which claim correctly separates the short run from the long run?
options: Inflation falls temporarily and remains lower after all contracts adjust
Unemployment may fall temporarily, but expectations adjustment removes the permanent tradeoff
Unemployment falls permanently because the SRPC stays downward sloping after expectations adjust
The SRPC immediately becomes vertical before output or nominal wages can change
PM2A-SRPC-FB-012.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
PM2A-SRPC-FB-012.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

PM2A-SRPC-LB-013.q: A demand expansion moves unemployment below natural. Wage contracts later incorporate the higher inflation. What is the next Phillips-curve development?
options: The SRPC shifts upward and unemployment moves back toward natural
The economy stays on the original SRPC at permanently lower unemployment
The LRPC shifts left because nominal wages increased
The SRPC shifts downward as expected inflation rises
PM2A-SRPC-LB-013.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
PM2A-SRPC-LB-013.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

PM2A-SRPC-LB-014.q: One episode has rising inflation with falling unemployment; another has rising inflation with rising unemployment. What distinguishes them?
options: Both are identical movements along one unchanged SRPC despite their opposite unemployment changes in the two episodes
The first shifts LRPC left while the second shifts aggregate demand right
Both establish a permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff without expectations adjustment
The first can be demand movement along SRPC; the second can be an adverse supply shift
PM2A-SRPC-LB-014.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
PM2A-SRPC-LB-014.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

PM2A-SRPC-LB-015.q: A government maintains a fixed unemployment gap below the natural rate through successive demand expansions. Expectations adapt to observed inflation, the Phillips slope is unchanged, and no supply or structural shock occurs. Which distinction explains why a permanently higher but stable inflation rate is insufficient?
options: Maintaining the gap requires only a one-time increase in inflation; expectations adjustment then preserves the lower unemployment.
Maintaining the gap shifts LRPC left even though the prompt holds labor-market structure fixed.
Maintaining the gap requires continuing positive inflation surprises; once inflation stabilizes and expectations catch up, unemployment returns toward natural.
Maintaining the gap requires falling actual inflation while expected inflation rises.
PM2A-SRPC-LB-015.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
PM2A-SRPC-LB-015.feedback: A fixed below-natural unemployment gap requires a positive actual-minus-expected inflation gap. Adaptive expectations catch up to a stable inflation rate, eliminating that gap. Continued surprises and a return to natural are alternative policy paths, not simultaneous endpoints.

ECON-SP-DEFINE-PHILLIPS-CURVE-5048.q: A demand increase raises inflation and lowers unemployment while expectations are unchanged. Is this a movement or a shift?
options: A movement along the current SRPC
An upward shift of the entire SRPC
A leftward shift of the LRPC
A downward shift of the entire SRPC
ECON-SP-DEFINE-PHILLIPS-CURVE-5048.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.
ECON-SP-DEFINE-PHILLIPS-CURVE-5048.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.

ECON-SP-MOVE-ALONG-SRPC-5050.q: Expected inflation rises while unemployment is held fixed. What happens to the SRPC?
options: The economy moves up the same SRPC
It shifts downward
The LRPC becomes horizontal
It shifts upward
ECON-SP-MOVE-ALONG-SRPC-5050.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.
ECON-SP-MOVE-ALONG-SRPC-5050.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.

ECON-SP-NATURAL-RATE-HYPOTHESIS-5052.q: On a Phillips graph, moving upward and left along one SRPC means what?
options: Inflation falls while unemployment rises
Inflation and unemployment both fall
Inflation rises while unemployment falls
Inflation and unemployment both rise
ECON-SP-NATURAL-RATE-HYPOTHESIS-5052.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.
ECON-SP-NATURAL-RATE-HYPOTHESIS-5052.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.

ECON-SP-READ-PC-AXES-5049.q: Can a downward-sloping SRPC guarantee permanently lower unemployment from higher inflation?
options: No, because demand never affects unemployment
No, because expected inflation adjusts
Yes, because the same SRPC is permanent
Yes, because natural unemployment becomes zero
ECON-SP-READ-PC-AXES-5049.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.
ECON-SP-READ-PC-AXES-5049.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.

ECON-SP-READ-PC-POINTS-5091.q: An adverse supply shock raises inflation and unemployment together. What curve change is indicated?
options: An upward shift of the SRPC
Movement up-left along the same SRPC
A downward shift of the SRPC
A vertical movement along the LRPC
ECON-SP-READ-PC-POINTS-5091.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.
ECON-SP-READ-PC-POINTS-5091.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.

ECON-SP-DEFINE-PHILLIPS-CURVE-6039.q: Aggregate demand expands unexpectedly, raising output and the price level. What linked Phillips result follows first?
options: Lower unemployment and higher inflation along the current SRPC
Higher unemployment and higher inflation from an SRPC shift
Lower unemployment and lower inflation from an LRPC shift
Unchanged unemployment with a downward SRPC shift
ECON-SP-DEFINE-PHILLIPS-CURVE-6039.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.
ECON-SP-DEFINE-PHILLIPS-CURVE-6039.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.

ECON-SP-MOVE-ALONG-SRPC-6041.q: After a move to lower unemployment and higher inflation, wage setters revise inflation forecasts upward. What happens to the short-run Phillips curve?
options: Aggregate demand shifts the LRPC left
Productivity makes the SRPC vertical
Money demand shifts the SRPC downward
Expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward
ECON-SP-MOVE-ALONG-SRPC-6041.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.
ECON-SP-MOVE-ALONG-SRPC-6041.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.

ECON-SP-NATURAL-RATE-HYPOTHESIS-6043.q: A short-run unemployment gain disappears as expectations adjust. Which family destination explains the long-run endpoint?
options: A horizontal LRPC at zero inflation
A sacrifice ratio equal to unemployment
The vertical LRPC at the natural rate
A permanently flatter SRPC
ECON-SP-NATURAL-RATE-HYPOTHESIS-6043.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
ECON-SP-NATURAL-RATE-HYPOTHESIS-6043.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.

ECON-SP-READ-PC-AXES-6040.q: A contraction moves the economy down the SRPC toward lower inflation and higher unemployment. Which applied destination studies that policy path?
options: Bank reserve creation through repeated lending and redepositing
Disinflation and its short-run costs
GDP accounting identities for measuring current national output
Comparative advantage from differences in opportunity cost
ECON-SP-READ-PC-AXES-6040.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.
ECON-SP-READ-PC-AXES-6040.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.

ECON-SP-EASY-64.q: The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at:
options: The natural rate of unemployment
Zero inflation
The money supply
The highest price level
ECON-SP-EASY-64.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

ECON-SP-EASY-65.q: Refer to the graph. Which unemployment rate is the natural rate?
options: U1
U2
U3
I1
ECON-SP-EASY-65.feedback: The LRPC is drawn at U2, so U2 is the natural rate of unemployment.

options: I1
I2
I3
I4

ECON-SP-EASY-72.feedback: The lower point at U4 on SRPC1 is at I1.

PM2A-LRPC-E-001.q: Where is the long-run Phillips curve drawn?
options: Vertically at the natural rate of unemployment
Horizontally at the current inflation rate
Downward sloping through every short-run point
Vertically at zero unemployment
PM2A-LRPC-E-001.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
PM2A-LRPC-E-001.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

PM2A-LRPC-E-002.q: What does a vertical LRPC imply?
options: Higher inflation permanently lowers unemployment
Inflation is fixed in the long run
The natural rate always equals zero
There is no permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff
PM2A-LRPC-E-002.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
PM2A-LRPC-E-002.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-159.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which pair of points are long-run equilibria?
options: a and d
b and c
a and b
c and d
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-159.commonError: Treating all SRPC points as long-run equilibria.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-159.feedback: Points b and c lie on the vertical LRPC at U2.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-159.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.

Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

P52B-S1-LRPC-M-001.q: Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 5 percent while unemployment remains at its natural rate. Which long-run outcome fits the vertical Phillips curve?
options: Inflation is higher, but unemployment is unchanged at the natural rate.
Inflation is higher and unemployment is permanently lower.
Inflation is unchanged and unemployment falls to zero.
Both inflation and unemployment are permanently higher.
P52B-S1-LRPC-M-001.commonError: Treating a higher expected inflation rate as a permanent way to lower unemployment.
P52B-S1-LRPC-M-001.feedback: Along the long-run Phillips curve, different inflation rates can coexist with the same natural rate of unemployment.

PG5-PC-M-003.q: What natural rate of unemployment is shown by the LRPC?
options: 3 percent
6 percent
5 percent
10 percent
PG5-PC-M-003.feedback: The vertical LRPC is drawn at 5 percent unemployment, so that is the natural rate.

PG5-PC-M-009.q: If inflation rises while the economy remains on the LRPC, what happens to unemployment in this graph?
options: It remains at 5 percent
It falls below 5 percent

It becomes equal to the inflation rate
PG5-PC-M-009.feedback: A vertical long-run Phillips curve means the long-run unemployment rate is pinned at the natural rate.

PM2A-LRPC-M-003.q: Demand expansion temporarily pushes unemployment below natural. After expected inflation adjusts, where does unemployment tend to go?
options: To zero regardless of labor institutions
Above natural forever with no inflation change
Back toward the natural rate
Permanently farther below the natural rate
PM2A-LRPC-M-003.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
PM2A-LRPC-M-003.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

PM2A-LRPC-M-004.q: Job-matching technology improves and lowers structural unemployment. What Phillips-curve change can follow?
options: The LRPC becomes downward sloping
The LRPC shifts left to a lower natural rate
The economy moves left along the same LRPC
The SRPC must shift upward at every point
PM2A-LRPC-M-004.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
PM2A-LRPC-M-004.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

PM2A-LRPC-M-005.q: A rise in long-term mismatch raises the natural rate. What happens to the LRPC?
options: It shifts right
It shifts left
It rotates to horizontal
It stays fixed at the old natural rate
PM2A-LRPC-M-005.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
PM2A-LRPC-M-005.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

PM2A-LRPC-M-006.q: Why can many inflation rates appear on the same vertical LRPC?
options: Inflation is unable to change nominal wages
Every point has zero expected inflation
Aggregate demand fixes the natural rate
Long-run unemployment equals natural after expectations adjust
PM2A-LRPC-M-006.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
PM2A-LRPC-M-006.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

ECON-SP-HARD-239.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which point reflects high inflation with unemployment at the natural rate?
options: a
b
c
d
ECON-SP-HARD-239.feedback: Point b lies on the LRPC at U2 and inflation I2.

ECON-SP-HARD-246.q: In the standard expectations-augmented Phillips model with no supply-shock offset, actual inflation equals expected inflation. What does the equation imply about unemployment?
options: At the natural rate
Below the natural rate
Above the natural rate
Equal to zero
ECON-SP-HARD-246.commonError: Missing the role of inflation surprises.
ECON-SP-HARD-246.feedback: With no inflation surprise, unemployment equals the natural rate. The no-offset assumption matters: an independent supply shock can also affect the relationship.

ECON-SP-HARD-259.q: Which event is most likely to shift the LRPC right?
options: Higher natural unemployment
Lower actual inflation
Temporary AD expansion
Unexpected money growth
ECON-SP-HARD-259.commonError: Confusing inflation changes with natural-rate changes.
ECON-SP-HARD-259.feedback: The LRPC shifts when the natural rate of unemployment changes.

ECON-SP-HARD-260.q: Which event is most likely to shift the LRPC left?
options: Better labor-market matching
Higher expected inflation
Unexpected AD expansion
Higher oil prices only
ECON-SP-HARD-260.commonError: Treating expected inflation as a natural-rate change.
ECON-SP-HARD-260.feedback: Better labor-market matching can lower the natural rate and shift the LRPC left.

PM2A-LRPC-H-007.q: Inflation rises permanently after repeated demand expansion, but labor-market structure is unchanged. Which long-run statement is strongest?
options: Unemployment remains permanently below natural after expectations fully adjust
The LRPC shifts right because the price level rose over time
Unemployment returns toward the same natural rate on an unchanged LRPC
The LRPC shifts left because higher inflation permanently improves job matching
PM2A-LRPC-H-007.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
PM2A-LRPC-H-007.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

PM2A-LRPC-H-008.q: The natural rate falls because job search becomes faster. How should SRPC and LRPC reasoning be separated?
options: LRPC stays fixed while unemployment permanently departs from its vertical location
LRPC shifts left; short-run curves may also reposition around the new natural rate
The economy merely moves upward along the old LRPC as inflation changes
Only inflation expectations can shift LRPC in the long-run model
PM2A-LRPC-H-008.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.

P52B-S1-LRPC-EL-001.q: Assume a fixed natural rate, no supply shocks, and an unchanged Phillips slope. Each year expected inflation equals the previous year’s actual inflation. Policy keeps unemployment the same fixed distance below natural. What must happen to actual inflation and the inflation surprise?
options: Both actual inflation and the size of the positive surprise must rise each year.
Actual inflation rises each year, but the required positive surprise can remain constant.
Actual inflation stays fixed while expected inflation falls each year.
Actual and expected inflation can remain equal while unemployment stays below natural.
P52B-S1-LRPC-EL-001.commonError: Assuming one expansion can hold unemployment below the natural rate forever.
P52B-S1-LRPC-EL-001.feedback: With an unchanged slope and unemployment gap, the required actual-minus-expected inflation gap is constant. Because expectations catch up to the previous actual rate, actual inflation must rise again by that same amount. Ever-higher inflation does not require ever-larger forecast errors.

P52B-S1-LRPC-L-001.q: Two economies have the same natural unemployment rate but very different average inflation rates over many years. Which observation is most consistent with a vertical long-run Phillips curve?
options: The higher-inflation economy must have permanently lower unemployment because inflation buys a lasting tradeoff.
The lower-inflation economy must have permanently higher unemployment because prices grow more slowly.
Both can remain at the same long-run unemployment rate despite different inflation rates.
Different inflation rates require different natural unemployment rates even when labor markets are otherwise alike.
P52B-S1-LRPC-L-001.commonError: Inferring a permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff from cross-country inflation differences.
P52B-S1-LRPC-L-001.feedback: The vertical LRPC allows different steady inflation rates at the same natural unemployment rate.

P52B-S1-LRPC-L-002.q: A matching reform lowers the natural unemployment rate from 6.4 percent to 5.6 percent. At the same time, an unexpected demand expansion lowers actual unemployment to 4.9 percent. Later inflation expectations fully adjust while the reform remains in place and no new surprises occur. Which decomposition separates the durable change from the initial cyclical change?
options: LRPC shifts left by 1.5 percentage points; actual unemployment at 4.9 percent is the new permanent natural rate.
LRPC stays at 6.4 percent; both the reform and demand expansion are temporary movements along SRPC.
LRPC shifts to 5.6 percent, but expectations adjustment permanently fixes unemployment at 4.9 percent.
LRPC shifts left by 0.8 percentage point; the initial gap is 0.7 point below the new natural rate, and long-run unemployment returns to 5.6 percent.
P52B-S1-LRPC-L-002.commonError: Confusing a change in the natural rate with a movement caused by inflation.
P52B-S1-LRPC-L-002.feedback: The structural shift is 6.4 − 5.6 = 0.8 percentage point. Actual unemployment is temporarily 5.6 − 4.9 = 0.7 point below the new natural rate. Once the demand surprise disappears, the long-run anchor is 5.6, not the old 6.4 or temporary 4.9.

P52B-S1-LRPC-L-003.q: An unexpected monetary expansion temporarily lowers unemployment. Inflation expectations then fully adjust while the higher inflation rate persists. What is the long-run result?

Unemployment remains permanently below the natural rate.
Unemployment rises permanently above the natural rate.
Inflation returns automatically to its original rate while unemployment stays low.
P52B-S1-LRPC-L-003.commonError: Stopping the analysis before expectations adjust.
P52B-S1-LRPC-L-003.feedback: The short-run unemployment effect disappears when expectations adjust, leaving higher inflation and natural-rate unemployment.

PM2A-LRPC-L-009.q: Policy holds unemployment below natural with successive demand expansions. Expected inflation rises each round. The repeated expansions then stop and actual inflation stabilizes at its higher rate. Which subsequent path is consistent with the natural-rate model?

One unchanged SRPC delivering permanently lower unemployment after every contract renewal
A leftward LRPC shift caused solely by faster inflation with unchanged labor structure
A downward SRPC shift ending in deflation and a lower natural unemployment rate
PM2A-LRPC-L-009.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
PM2A-LRPC-L-009.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate. Return to natural is conditional on ending the repeated effort to maintain a surprise.

PM2A-LRPC-L-010.q: Economy A lowers its natural rate through better job matching; Economy B only creates an unexpected demand boom. Which comparison is correct?

Only Economy B changes long-run unemployment by raising aggregate demand
Neither economy can affect unemployment at either a short or long horizon
A can shift LRPC left; B can only move unemployment below natural temporarily
PM2A-LRPC-L-010.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
PM2A-LRPC-L-010.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

PM2A-LRPC-L-011.q: Inflation expectations instantly match a fully anticipated monetary expansion in the model. What Phillips prediction is most consistent?

A guaranteed fall in both inflation and unemployment after expectations adjust
Little or no temporary unemployment movement away from the natural rate
A permanent unemployment decline along the SRPC once nominal spending increases
PM2A-LRPC-L-011.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
PM2A-LRPC-L-011.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-163.q: An adverse supply shock affects the Phillips curve by:
options: Shifting SRPC up and right
Moving down along the same SRPC
Shifting LRPC to zero unemployment
Eliminating expected inflation
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-163.commonError: Treating supply shocks as normal AD movements.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-163.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-164.q: If policymakers expand AD to reduce unemployment below the natural rate, what happens after expectations adjust?
options: Unemployment returns to natural and inflation stays higher
Unemployment stays permanently lower
Inflation falls below expected inflation
LRPC becomes downward sloping
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-164.commonError: Believing in a permanent policy tradeoff.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-164.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC up, returning unemployment to natural at higher inflation.

PG5-PC-M-002.q: Suppose expected inflation rises while the natural rate is unchanged. Which curve change shown is consistent with that assumption?
options: SRPC0 shifts downward away from SRPC1
SRPC0 shifts upward to SRPC1
LRPC shifts left to a lower natural rate
The economy only moves along unchanged SRPC0
PG5-PC-M-002.feedback: An upward shift of the short-run Phillips curve is the standard way to show higher expected inflation or an adverse supply shock with the natural rate unchanged.
PG5-PC-M-002.imageAlt: Phillips graph with two downward-sloping SRPCs, vertical LRPC, and points A and B.

Solid blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6), A at (5,3), and (10,0). Dashed purple SRPC1 is parallel above it, running through (0,9.6), B at (6,6), and (10,3.6). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and intersects SRPC0 at A and SRPC1 at inflation 6.6. Dashed guides mark A at (5,3) and B at (6,6).

ECON-SP-HARD-236.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at c, which sequence matches expansionary policy and expectations adjustment?
options: c to a to b
c to b to a
c to d to b
c to a to d
ECON-SP-HARD-236.commonError: Skipping the short-run movement along SRPC.
ECON-SP-HARD-236.feedback: Expansion moves from c to a in the short run; expected inflation rises and moves the economy to b.
ECON-SP-HARD-236.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.

Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

ECON-SP-HARD-240.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which movement shows expectations falling after contractionary policy?
options: d to c
c to a
a to b
b to a
ECON-SP-HARD-240.feedback: Moving from d to c reflects lower expected inflation and return to the natural unemployment rate.
ECON-SP-HARD-240.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
ECON-SP-HARD-240.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

ECON-SP-HARD-242.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. At U3, moving from SRPC1 to SRPC2 changes inflation from:
options: I2 to I4
I4 to I2
I1 to I3
I3 to I1
ECON-SP-HARD-242.commonError: Reading the wrong inflation level at U3.
ECON-SP-HARD-242.feedback: At U3, the lower curve is at I2 and the upper curve is at I4.
ECON-SP-HARD-242.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.

On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

ECON-SP-HARD-243.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. At inflation I3, the move from SRPC1 to SRPC2 implies unemployment is:
options: Higher on SRPC2
Lower on SRPC2
The same on both curves
Zero on both curves
ECON-SP-HARD-243.commonError: Missing worse tradeoff at the same inflation rate.
ECON-SP-HARD-243.feedback: At a given inflation rate, the higher SRPC implies a higher unemployment rate.
ECON-SP-HARD-243.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.

On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

ECON-SP-HARD-244.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A shift from SRPC1 to SRPC2 is most consistent with:
options: Higher expected inflation or adverse supply shock
Lower expected inflation or favorable supply shock
Higher money supply with expectations fixed
Lower unemployment at every inflation rate
ECON-SP-HARD-244.commonError: Treating SRPC shifts as ordinary movement along a curve.
ECON-SP-HARD-244.feedback: The upward SRPC shift reflects higher expected inflation or a worsened supply-side tradeoff.
ECON-SP-HARD-244.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.

SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

ECON-SP-HARD-245.q: If the Fed unexpectedly increases inflation while expected inflation is fixed, unemployment moves:
options: Below the natural rate temporarily
Above the natural rate permanently
To zero permanently
Unchanged in every period
ECON-SP-HARD-245.commonError: Ignoring the gap between actual and expected inflation.
ECON-SP-HARD-245.feedback: When actual inflation exceeds expected inflation, unemployment can temporarily fall below the natural rate.

ECON-SP-HARD-257.q: Which event shifts both SRAS left and SRPC up-right?
options: Oil price surge
Tax cut
Open-market purchase
Consumer confidence boom
ECON-SP-HARD-257.commonError: Confusing supply shocks with AD shocks.
ECON-SP-HARD-257.feedback: An oil price surge raises production costs and worsens the inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

ECON-SP-HARD-263.q: Initially actual inflation equals expected inflation and unemployment is at its natural rate. Supply conditions and the natural rate stay unchanged. If expected inflation rises while actual inflation is held at its original rate, what happens to unemployment?
options: Rise above natural
Fall below natural
Stay zero
Become inflation
ECON-SP-HARD-263.commonError: Ignoring expected inflation in the Phillips curve equation.
ECON-SP-HARD-263.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts SRPC up, so unchanged actual inflation corresponds to higher unemployment. The stated initial equality makes the new inflation surprise negative.

ECON-SP-HARD-264.q: Initially actual inflation equals expected inflation and unemployment is at its natural rate. Supply conditions and the natural rate stay unchanged. If expected inflation falls while actual inflation is held at its original rate, what happens to unemployment?
options: Fall below natural
Rise above natural
Stay at zero
Equal the price level
ECON-SP-HARD-264.commonError: Reversing the effect of lower expected inflation.
ECON-SP-HARD-264.feedback: Lower expected inflation shifts SRPC down, so the same actual inflation can mean lower unemployment. The stated initial equality makes the new inflation surprise positive.

ECON-SP-HARD-265.q: A student says an oil shock causes only movement along the SRPC. What is the correction?
options: It shifts SRPC because costs and prices change directly
It shifts only AD because spending changes directly
It shifts only LRPC because inflation changes
It moves only along LRAS because output changes
ECON-SP-HARD-265.commonError: Treating supply shocks as AD movements.
ECON-SP-HARD-265.feedback: A supply shock shifts the SRPC because it directly changes firms' costs and inflation pressure.

ECON-SP-HARD-267.q: A student says higher expected inflation lowers unemployment permanently. What is the correction?
options: It shifts SRPC upward and worsens the short-run tradeoff
It shifts LRPC left and improves the long-run tradeoff
It shifts AD right and lowers prices
It raises money demand and lowers rates
ECON-SP-HARD-267.commonError: Treating expected inflation as beneficial stimulus.
ECON-SP-HARD-267.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward, giving higher inflation at each unemployment rate.

PG5-PC-H-004.q: At a given unemployment rate, how does SRPC1 compare with SRPC0?
options: SRPC1 shows a lower inflation rate
SRPC1 shows the same inflation rate
SRPC1 shows a lower natural rate
SRPC1 shows a higher inflation rate
PG5-PC-H-004.feedback: Point B lies on a different short-run Phillips curve, SRPC1, so the graph is showing a curve shift rather than a movement along SRPC0.
PG5-PC-H-004.imageAlt: Phillips graph with two downward-sloping SRPCs, vertical LRPC, and points A and B.
PG5-PC-H-004.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from 0 to 10. Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and intersects SRPC0 at A and SRPC1 at inflation 6.6. Dashed guides mark A at (5,3) and B at (6,6).

ECON-SP-ELITE-326.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A move from c on SRPC1 to the upper point at U3 on SRPC2 means:
options: Same unemployment with higher inflation
Same inflation with lower unemployment
Lower inflation with same unemployment
Higher unemployment with same inflation
ECON-SP-ELITE-326.commonError: Reading the curve shift as movement along SRPC1.
ECON-SP-ELITE-326.feedback: At U3, SRPC2 shows a higher inflation rate than SRPC1.
ECON-SP-ELITE-326.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
ECON-SP-ELITE-326.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

ECON-SP-ELITE-327.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. At inflation I3, comparing SRPC1 and SRPC2 shows:
options: SRPC2 has higher unemployment
SRPC2 has lower unemployment
Both curves have U3
Both curves have U1
ECON-SP-ELITE-327.commonError: Missing the worse tradeoff after SRPC shifts upward.
ECON-SP-ELITE-327.feedback: At the same inflation rate, the higher SRPC shows higher unemployment.
ECON-SP-ELITE-327.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
ECON-SP-ELITE-327.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

ECON-SP-ELITE-328.q: A central bank unexpectedly expands AD. Later, workers build the higher inflation into wage demands. Which sequence is most accurate?
options: Move along SRPC, then SRPC shifts up
SRPC shifts down, then move along LRPC
LRPC shifts left, then AD falls
Move along LRAS, then M1 falls
ECON-SP-ELITE-328.commonError: Confusing immediate inflation surprise with later expectation adjustment.
ECON-SP-ELITE-328.feedback: Unexpected AD expansion first moves along the SRPC; later expected inflation rises and shifts SRPC upward.

ECON-SP-ELITE-350.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Which labeled move isolates an upward SRPC shift at unemployment U3?
options: The move from point c to point f
The move from point a to point f
The move from point b to point e
The move from point c to point a
ECON-SP-ELITE-350.commonError: Compares points with different unemployment rates, so movement and shift effects are mixed.
ECON-SP-ELITE-350.feedback: Points c and f share unemployment U3; moving from c on SRPC1 to f on SRPC2 isolates higher inflation at the same unemployment rate.
ECON-SP-ELITE-350.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
ECON-SP-ELITE-350.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9009.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. The economy moves from SRPC1 to SRPC2. Which statement should be rejected?
options: The tradeoff improved because higher inflation now buys lower unemployment at every point.
The tradeoff worsened because inflation is higher at a given unemployment rate.
Expected inflation may have increased and shifted the curve upward.
An adverse supply shock may have raised both inflation pressure and unemployment risk.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9009.commonError: Calling an upward SRPC shift an improvement.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9009.feedback: An upward SRPC shift worsens the tradeoff because inflation is higher at the same unemployment rate.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9009.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9009.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9018.q: A policymaker says, 'Inflation is high, so unemployment must be low.' What is the best correction?
options: That only fits demand pressure; supply shocks can raise inflation and unemployment together.
That is always true because the Phillips curve never shifts.
That is false only when M1 is larger than M2.
That is true in the long run because LRPC slopes downward.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9018.commonError: Treating the Phillips curve as fixed under every shock.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9018.feedback: The short-run tradeoff can worsen when SRPC shifts up, so inflation and unemployment can rise together.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9048.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. The economy is on SRPC2 rather than SRPC1. Which conclusion is most careful?
options: The tradeoff worsened, but the cause could be expected inflation or a supply shock.
The tradeoff improved, and policymakers can now lower unemployment without cost.
The LRPC shifted left, so natural unemployment must have fallen.
AD must have shifted right, so SRPC cannot have moved.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9048.commonError: Assuming every SRPC shift has only one cause.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9048.feedback: An upward SRPC shift can come from higher expected inflation or an adverse supply shock, and both worsen the tradeoff.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9048.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9048.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

PG5-PC-L-006.q: Refer to the graph with SRPC0, SRPC1, A and B. Use the model inflation = expected inflation − 0.6 × (unemployment − 5) + supply offset, with all rates in percent and differences in percentage points. At B the separately measured supply offset is +1.1 points. What expected inflation is consistent with B, and could the graph alone identify that expectation if the supply offset were unknown?
options: Expected inflation is 6 percent; actual inflation equals expectations at every point on an SRPC.
Expected inflation is 5.5 percent; without the supply-offset measurement, only expected inflation plus the offset is identified.
Expected inflation is 6.6 percent; the supply offset can be ignored even though it is positive.
Expected inflation is 4.3 percent; both the unemployment gap and the supply offset must be subtracted from actual inflation.
PG5-PC-L-006.feedback: B has unemployment 6 and actual inflation 6. Thus 6 = expected inflation − 0.6 + 1.1, implying expected inflation 5.5. Without the offset measurement the graph identifies only expected inflation + offset = 6.6. The higher curve does not by itself isolate an expectations change.
PG5-PC-L-006.imageAlt: Phillips graph with two downward-sloping SRPCs, vertical LRPC, and points A and B.
PG5-PC-L-006.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from 0 to 10. Solid blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6), A at (5,3), and (10,0). Dashed purple SRPC1 is parallel above it, running through (0,9.6), B at (6,6), and (10,3.6). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and intersects SRPC0 at A and SRPC1 at inflation 6.6. Dashed guides mark A at (5,3) and B at (6,6).

PG5-PC-L-018.q: Refer to the graph with A and B on SRPC0. Initially expected inflation is the inflation rate at A, and the economy is at B. Next period expected inflation equals this period’s actual inflation. Hold the natural rate and supply conditions fixed; each one-point expectations change shifts the SRPC vertically by one point with slope unchanged. Compare keeping unemployment at B’s rate with instead keeping actual inflation at B’s current rate. Which next-period outcome follows?
options: Keeping unemployment at 3 percent requires unchanged 3.5 percent inflation; holding inflation fixed shifts LRPC to 3 percent.
Keeping unemployment at 3 percent requires 4.5 percent inflation; holding inflation at 3.5 percent instead returns unemployment to 5 percent.
Keeping unemployment at 3 percent requires 2.5 percent inflation; holding inflation at 3.5 percent raises unemployment to 7 percent.
Both targets give the same unchanged point B because adaptive expectations cannot shift an SRPC.
PG5-PC-L-018.feedback: Expectations rise from 2.5 to 3.5, shifting the curve up one point. At unemployment 3, inflation therefore rises from 3.5 to 4.5. Alternatively, actual inflation equal to the new expectation gives natural unemployment at 5. A fixed unemployment target and a fixed inflation target are different continuations.
PG5-PC-L-018.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
PG5-PC-L-018.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through B at (3,3.5) and A at (5,2.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies above and left of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

PG5-PC-L-024.q: Refer to the graph with B to the right of A on SRPC0. Initially actual inflation is B’s rate and expected inflation is A’s rate. Each period expectations equal the previous period’s actual inflation; each one-point expectations change shifts SRPC vertically by one point with slope unchanged. Natural unemployment and supply conditions stay fixed. Policy holds unemployment at B’s rate for one additional period, then requires inflation to be nonnegative in the following period. What inflation occurs in the additional period, and what is the highest unemployment rate compatible with that later inflation constraint?
options: Inflation stays 1.5 percent, then unemployment can remain at 7 percent.
Inflation is 0.5 percent, then unemployment can remain at 7 percent without deflation.
Inflation is 2.5 percent, then unemployment can be at most 5 percent.
Inflation is 0.5 percent, then unemployment can be at most 6 percent.
PG5-PC-L-024.feedback: The plotted slope is (1.5 − 2.5)/(7 − 5) = −0.5. Expectations first fall from 2.5 to 1.5, so holding unemployment at 7 gives inflation 0.5. Next expectations are 0.5; nonnegative inflation requires 0.5 − 0.5 × (unemployment − 5) ≥ 0, or unemployment no greater than 6. Maintaining 7 would instead produce −0.5 percent inflation.
PG5-PC-L-024.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
PG5-PC-L-024.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through A at (5,2.5) and B at (7,1.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies below and right of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

PM2A-EXP-L-002.q: A temporary supply disruption raises inflation while existing contracts still reflect the original expected inflation. Wage setters update forecasts using the observed inflation, but the disruption ends before the new contracts take effect. Expected inflation nevertheless remains above its original level. With natural unemployment unchanged, what can be concluded about the final SRPC relative to its original position and its position during the disruption?
options: It must return exactly to its original position because the physical disruption ended.
It must lie above the disruption-period curve because any expectations rise exceeds any removed supply offset.
It must lie below the original curve because the original supply shock was temporary.
It remains above its original position, but its position relative to the disruption-period curve depends on the expectations rise versus the removed supply offset.
PM2A-EXP-L-002.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
PM2A-EXP-L-002.feedback: The original curve has neither the supply offset nor the higher expectation. The final curve retains only the expectation increase, so it is above the original. Comparing it with the disruption-period curve requires the two offset magnitudes. Observed inflation alone does not identify their relative sizes.

PM2A-EXP-L-003.q: Two central banks announce the same lower inflation target. One has a stronger record of meeting targets. Under otherwise similar conditions, what can differ?
options: Actual inflation must reach zero with no output cost
The less credible bank must cause immediate deflation
Expected inflation may fall faster where the announcement is more credible
The natural rate must immediately fall only in the credible economy
PM2A-EXP-L-003.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
PM2A-EXP-L-003.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

PM2A-EXP-L-004.q: Actual inflation is 5% while wage setters expected 3%, temporarily pushing unemployment below natural. What erodes that effect?
options: The price level returns to its initial value automatically
Forecasts adjust upward, shifting the SRPC until unemployment returns toward natural
The LRPC shifts left because actual inflation is above expected
Forecasts adjust downward, moving unemployment farther below natural
PM2A-EXP-L-004.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
PM2A-EXP-L-004.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.commonError: Treating expected inflation as movement along the same SRPC.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.q: What happens to the short-run Phillips curve when expected inflation rises?
options: It shifts downward
It shifts upward
It becomes horizontal
It becomes the money demand curve
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the short-run Phillips curve upward.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.commonError: Keeping unemployment below natural forever after an inflation surprise.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at c, expansionary policy moves the economy to a. After expected inflation rises, where does the economy move?
options: b
c
d
U1
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.feedback: After expected inflation rises, the SRPC shifts up and the economy moves to b at the natural rate of unemployment.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

P52B-S2-PCEXP-B2-001.q: A sharp oil-price increase raises firms’ costs. What happens to the short-run Phillips curve, other things equal?
options: It shifts down and to the left.
The economy only moves along an unchanged curve.
It shifts up and to the right.
It becomes vertical at zero unemployment.
P52B-S2-PCEXP-B2-001.commonError: Treating an adverse supply shock as a movement along a fixed SRPC.
P52B-S2-PCEXP-B2-001.feedback: An adverse supply shock can raise both inflation and unemployment, shifting the SRPC up-right.

PM2A-EXP-EB-005.q: If expected inflation increases, which SRPC change follows?
options: An upward shift
A downward shift
Only movement down the same curve
A horizontal LRPC shift
PM2A-EXP-EB-005.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
PM2A-EXP-EB-005.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

PM2A-EXP-EB-006.q: If expected inflation decreases, which SRPC change follows?
options: An upward shift
Only movement up the same curve
A vertical AD shift
A downward shift
PM2A-EXP-EB-006.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
PM2A-EXP-EB-006.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

PM2A-EXP-EB-007.q: Why can actual inflation above expected inflation temporarily reduce unemployment?
options: Higher inflation permanently raises labor productivity
The LRPC becomes downward sloping
Some wages and prices were set using the lower forecast
The natural rate immediately becomes lower
PM2A-EXP-EB-007.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
PM2A-EXP-EB-007.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

PM2A-EXP-FB-008.q: Under rational expectations, wage setters use available information, including credible policy announcements; forecasts can still be wrong when new information arrives. A credible lower-inflation target changes their forecasts before much demand contraction occurs, but some contracts remain fixed. Which assessment follows?
options: Rational expectations guarantee exact forecasts and eliminate every unemployment cost even with fixed contracts.
The SRPC can shift downward sooner, reducing the transition cost, while fixed contracts can leave some temporary unemployment increase.
Expected inflation must wait for past inflation to decline because announcements cannot enter a forecast.
A credible nominal target permanently shifts LRPC left even when labor-market structure is unchanged.
PM2A-EXP-FB-008.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
PM2A-EXP-FB-008.feedback: Available-information forecasting can incorporate credible policy news before actual inflation falls. It does not imply perfect foresight or instantly flexible contracts. Earlier expectations adjustment can reduce disinflation costs without guaranteeing zero costs.

PM2A-EXP-FB-009.q: Actual inflation remains above expected inflation for several contract cycles. Which sequence best fits adaptive expectations?
options: Expected inflation rises, shifting SRPC upward and undoing the temporary unemployment gain
Expected inflation falls, shifting SRPC downward and preserving the unemployment gain indefinitely
LRPC shifts left, locking in unemployment below natural after contracts renew
SRPC stays fixed because only actual inflation matters for wage setting
PM2A-EXP-FB-009.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
PM2A-EXP-FB-009.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

PM2A-EXP-FB-010.q: A supply shock raises inflation without a demand boom. Why might a simple expectations-only diagnosis be incomplete?
options: Expected inflation is the only possible SRPC shifter in the introductory model
Every inflation increase is movement along a fixed SRPC regardless of its cause
Supply shocks shift only the vertical LRPC while leaving SRPC unchanged
The shock can shift the SRPC even before expectations adapt
PM2A-EXP-FB-010.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
PM2A-EXP-FB-010.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

PM2A-EXP-LB-011.q: A surprise expansion lifts inflation from 2% to 5% while expected inflation remains 2%. What makes the unemployment effect temporary?
options: Expected inflation falls below 2% and shifts SRPC downward after workers observe prices
The LRPC becomes flatter as actual inflation rises above expected inflation
Expected inflation eventually rises toward actual inflation and shifts the SRPC upward
The natural rate permanently falls three points once actual inflation exceeds its forecast
PM2A-EXP-LB-011.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
PM2A-EXP-LB-011.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

PM2A-EXP-LB-012.q: A disinflation announcement is only partly credible and wage contracts reset slowly. Which conclusion is appropriately bounded?
options: The announcement necessarily causes the price level to fall for several years
Expectations may fall gradually, so some short-run output cost can remain
Partial credibility must eliminate every unemployment cost as soon as policy is announced
Expected inflation cannot change until actual inflation reaches the announced target
PM2A-EXP-LB-012.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
PM2A-EXP-LB-012.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

PM2A-EXP-LB-013.q: An adverse supply shock raises actual inflation, then wage setters incorporate it into next year’s contracts. What are the two stages?
options: An initial SRPC shift followed by reinforcement through higher expected inflation
Two movements along one fixed SRPC with no change in the inflation-unemployment relation
An LRPC shift followed by lower expected inflation when contracts renew
A demand contraction followed by an SRPC shift downward at each unemployment rate
PM2A-EXP-LB-013.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
PM2A-EXP-LB-013.feedback: The supply shock first shifts SRPC upward even with expectations unchanged. Incorporating the higher observed inflation into contracts adds an expectations-driven upward shift. This reinforces inflation pressure rather than describing the disappearance of a demand-created unemployment gain.

ECON-SP-EXPECTED-INFLATION-SHIFT-5053.q: Expected inflation rises from 2% to 4%. At a given unemployment rate, how does the SRPC move?
options: It shifts upward
It shifts downward
The economy moves down the same SRPC
The LRPC shifts right
ECON-SP-EXPECTED-INFLATION-SHIFT-5053.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.
ECON-SP-EXPECTED-INFLATION-SHIFT-5053.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.

ECON-SP-SUPPLY-SHOCK-PC-SHIFT-5055.q: Actual inflation repeatedly exceeds the rate workers expected. Which forecast adjustment is likely?
options: Expected inflation falls
Expected inflation becomes permanently zero
Expected inflation cannot respond
Expected inflation rises
ECON-SP-SUPPLY-SHOCK-PC-SHIFT-5055.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.
ECON-SP-SUPPLY-SHOCK-PC-SHIFT-5055.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.

ECON-SP-TRACE-EXPECTATIONS-ADJUSTMENT-50.q: Does a credible announcement guarantee costless disinflation?
options: Yes; unemployment must immediately fall
No; credibility can never affect expectations
No; it can reduce costs without always eliminating them
Yes; credibility removes all nominal rigidities
ECON-SP-TRACE-EXPECTATIONS-ADJUSTMENT-50.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
ECON-SP-TRACE-EXPECTATIONS-ADJUSTMENT-50.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

ECON-SP-EXPECTED-INFLATION-SHIFT-6044.q: The economy moves up-left along SRPC after a demand surprise. Wage setters then revise forecasts upward. What connection is required?
options: A movement along SRPC becomes an upward shift as expectations adjust
The LRPC shifts left as aggregate demand rises and nominal wages renew
The same fixed SRPC supports permanently lower unemployment after forecasts update
A downward expectations shift reinforces the initial unemployment gain
ECON-SP-EXPECTED-INFLATION-SHIFT-6044.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.
ECON-SP-EXPECTED-INFLATION-SHIFT-6044.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.

ECON-SP-SUPPLY-SHOCK-PC-SHIFT-6046.q: Expected inflation falls during a credible disinflation. Which applied family slice uses that change to assess policy costs?
options: GDP components
Money creation
Economic growth policy
Disinflation and policy
ECON-SP-SUPPLY-SHOCK-PC-SHIFT-6046.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
ECON-SP-SUPPLY-SHOCK-PC-SHIFT-6046.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

ECON-SP-TRACE-EXPECTATIONS-ADJUSTMENT-60.q: Expectations fully catch up after repeated inflation surprises. Which curve summarizes the long-run unemployment result?
options: The money-demand curve
The production possibilities frontier
The LRPC at the natural rate
The SRPC as a permanent menu
ECON-SP-TRACE-EXPECTATIONS-ADJUSTMENT-60.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
ECON-SP-TRACE-EXPECTATIONS-ADJUSTMENT-60.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.

ECON-SP-EASY-75.q: If the Fed reduces money growth to fight inflation, unemployment usually:
options: Falls immediately
Rises temporarily
Stays permanently at zero
Becomes the price level
ECON-SP-EASY-75.commonError: Ignoring the short-run cost of disinflation.
ECON-SP-EASY-75.feedback: Disinflation usually raises unemployment temporarily as the economy moves along the SRPC.

options: The overall price level is falling because average prices are declining.
Unemployment is falling even though output remains below potential.
Inflation is slowing, although the price level may still be rising.
Nominal wages are fixed while real wages rise automatically.
P52B-S1-DIS-E-001.feedback: Disinflation is slower price growth; deflation is a falling price level.

P52B-S1-DIS-E-002.q: Why can a credible anti-inflation announcement reduce the short-run cost of disinflation?
options: It permanently eliminates the natural rate of unemployment.
It guarantees that the price level falls immediately.
It makes aggregate demand irrelevant.
Expected inflation may adjust downward more quickly.
P52B-S1-DIS-E-002.commonError: Ignoring the role of expected inflation in the transition.
P52B-S1-DIS-E-002.feedback: When expectations fall sooner, wage and price setting can adjust with less output and unemployment loss.

options: Cumulative output lost per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
The permanent unemployment rate created by a recession.
The price-level increase caused by one point of money growth.
The share of public spending financed by current taxes.
P52B-S1-DIS-E-003.commonError: Treating the sacrifice ratio as a permanent unemployment rate.
P52B-S1-DIS-E-003.feedback: The sacrifice ratio summarizes the output cost of lowering inflation.

PM2A-DIS-E-001.q: Inflation slows from 6% to 3%, so the price level still rises more slowly. What is this?
options: Disinflation
Deflation
Hyperinflation
A falling real interest rate by definition
PM2A-DIS-E-001.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
PM2A-DIS-E-001.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

PM2A-DIS-E-002.q: Which short-run effect commonly accompanies contractionary disinflation policy?
options: Higher output and lower unemployment
A permanently lower natural unemployment rate
An immediate rise in aggregate demand
Lower output and higher unemployment
PM2A-DIS-E-002.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
PM2A-DIS-E-002.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-157.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point b, contractionary policy that lowers inflation below expectations moves the economy in the short run to:
options: a
c
d
U1
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-157.commonError: Moving directly to lower expected inflation.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-157.feedback: Contractionary policy moves along SRPC2 from b to d: lower inflation and higher unemployment.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-165.q: If the Fed reduces money growth to lower inflation, the short-run Phillips curve predicts:
options: Lower inflation and temporarily higher unemployment
Higher inflation and lower unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment immediately
No short-run cost at all
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-165.feedback: Disinflation usually moves the economy toward lower inflation and higher unemployment in the short run.

PM2A-DIS-M-003.q: A central bank reduces aggregate demand to lower inflation. What Phillips movement is expected before expectations adjust?
options: An immediate leftward LRPC shift
An upward SRPC shift from lower expected inflation
Down and right along the current SRPC
Up and left along the current SRPC
PM2A-DIS-M-003.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
PM2A-DIS-M-003.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

PM2A-DIS-M-004.q: Why can a credible lower-inflation target reduce the short-run cost of disinflation?
options: It causes aggregate demand to expand during contraction
It may lower expected inflation and shift the SRPC downward sooner
It permanently lowers the natural rate by announcement
It guarantees wages and prices adjust instantly
PM2A-DIS-M-004.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
PM2A-DIS-M-004.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

PM2A-DIS-M-005.q: Inflation falls from 4% to 1%, but prices continue rising. Which statement is correct?
options: The economy has disinflation, not deflation
The economy has deflation because inflation fell
The price level must be below its initial level
The natural rate must have declined
PM2A-DIS-M-005.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
PM2A-DIS-M-005.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

PM2A-DIS-M-006.q: Why might gradual disinflation be chosen instead of a rapid contraction?
options: It always produces zero cumulative output loss
It guarantees expected inflation never changes
It permanently shifts LRPC left
It can spread adjustment and reduce a severe short-run output gap
PM2A-DIS-M-006.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.
PM2A-DIS-M-006.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.

ECON-SP-HARD-237.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, which sequence matches disinflation and expectations adjustment?
options: b to d to c
b to c to d
b to a to c
b to d to a
ECON-SP-HARD-237.feedback: Disinflation moves from b to d in the short run; expected inflation falls and the economy moves to c.
