Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

ECON-SP-HARD-247.q: If actual inflation is less than expected inflation, unemployment is likely:
options: Above the natural rate
Below the natural rate
Equal to zero
Equal to inflation
ECON-SP-HARD-247.commonError: Reversing the effect of unexpectedly low inflation.
ECON-SP-HARD-247.feedback: When actual inflation is below expected inflation, unemployment tends to rise above the natural rate.

ECON-SP-HARD-256.q: A policymaker wants lower inflation but ignores unemployment during transition. What model warns about this cost?
options: Short-run Phillips curve
Money multiplier only
M1 definition only
Classical dichotomy only
ECON-SP-HARD-256.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows that reducing inflation can temporarily raise unemployment.

P52B-S1-DIS-H-001.q: A central bank announces a gradual disinflation, but households and firms doubt that the plan will continue. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The natural unemployment rate immediately falls to zero.
High expected inflation can prolong the output and job losses.
The price level must begin falling throughout the adjustment.
Unemployment cannot rise because the disinflation is gradual.
P52B-S1-DIS-H-001.commonError: Assuming gradualism automatically produces low transition costs.
P52B-S1-DIS-H-001.feedback: If the plan lacks credibility, expected inflation can adjust slowly and make the disinflation more costly.

PM2A-DIS-H-007.q: A disinflation announcement is not credible, and wage contracts embed 6% inflation. What makes immediate costless adjustment unlikely?
options: Aggregate demand cannot affect inflation
Deflation is required before unemployment changes
Expected inflation and nominal contracts may adjust slowly
The LRPC must shift left before policy begins
PM2A-DIS-H-007.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
PM2A-DIS-H-007.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

PM2A-DIS-H-008.q: Two paths reach 2% inflation. The rapid path has a deep one-year recession; the gradual path has smaller gaps for several years. What must be compared?
options: The price levels at the start, without output data
Their cumulative output losses and inflation reductions
Only the largest annual unemployment rate
Only the final year’s output level
PM2A-DIS-H-008.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.
PM2A-DIS-H-008.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.

ECON-SP-ELITE-324.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, which sequence best shows disinflation with temporary unemployment costs?
options: b to d to c
b to a to c
b to c to d
b to d to b
ECON-SP-ELITE-324.commonError: Skipping the temporary move above natural unemployment.
ECON-SP-ELITE-324.feedback: Disinflation lowers actual inflation first, moving to d, then expectations fall and the economy returns to c.

ECON-SP-ELITE-349.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which policy lesson fits the move from b to d to c?
options: Disinflation has temporary unemployment costs
Inflation permanently lowers unemployment
Expected inflation must rise after contraction
Supply shocks lower unemployment immediately
ECON-SP-ELITE-349.commonError: Missing the temporary cost of disinflation.
ECON-SP-ELITE-349.feedback: The move from b to d shows higher unemployment during disinflation; d to c shows expectations adjusting downward.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9008.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Compare two disinflations from b to the lower sustained inflation rate I1 with supply conditions and natural unemployment unchanged. In one, existing contracts keep expected inflation at I2 initially. In the other, a credible announcement and immediate contract adjustment lower expected inflation to I1 before spending adjusts. Which pair of paths is consistent with these assumptions?
options: The first can pass through d before c; the second can reach c without the same initial unemployment excursion.
Both must pass through d because credibility cannot change expected inflation before actual inflation falls.
The first reaches c immediately; the second must shift LRPC right before inflation can fall.
Both finish at a because lower inflation permanently lowers natural unemployment.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9008.commonError: Skipping the short-run unemployment cost of disinflation.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9008.feedback: With old expectations, lower actual inflation moves b to d along SRPC2 before expectations shift the curve down toward c. If expectations and contracts already incorporate I1, the lower SRPC can support c without that initial gap. Credibility alone would not guarantee this outcome without the stated contract adjustment.

Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9047.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. The economy has moved b to d during disinflation. Inflation is then held at I1, the natural rate stays U2, and the adverse-supply offset is unchanged. A forecast shows unemployment returning to U2. Which evidence is necessary to reconcile this forecast with the diagram?
options: Expected inflation must fall enough to place an SRPC through c; contraction along unchanged SRPC2 would leave unemployment at d.
Expected inflation must rise enough to place an SRPC above SRPC2 while actual inflation remains I1.
The return requires moving from d to b along unchanged SRPC2 while inflation remains I1.
The return requires LRPC to shift right to U3 even though the natural rate stays U2.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9047.commonError: Missing the expectation adjustment needed after disinflation.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9047.feedback: At I1 the original SRPC2 locates d, not c. With natural unemployment and the supply offset fixed, a lower expected-inflation schedule is needed to reach c at U2. A forecast of unemployment recovery is therefore conditional on the expected-inflation adjustment, not just continued contraction.

P52B-S1-DIS-L-001.q: Country A has a sacrifice ratio of 2, while Country B has a sacrifice ratio of 5. If both reduce inflation by 3 percentage points, which comparison is correct?
options: A loses about 15% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 6%.
Both lose about 3% of annual GDP because the inflation reduction is equal.
A loses about 6% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 15%.
A has no output loss because its sacrifice ratio is below the inflation reduction.
P52B-S1-DIS-L-001.commonError: Reversing the sacrifice ratios or treating equal inflation reductions as equal output costs.
P52B-S1-DIS-L-001.feedback: Cumulative output loss equals the sacrifice ratio times the inflation reduction: 2 × 3 = 6 for A and 5 × 3 = 15 for B.

PM2A-DIS-L-009.q: A credible central bank announces a lower inflation target, expected inflation falls partly, and policy still contracts demand. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: The downward SRPC shift may reduce but need not eliminate the short-run output cost
Credibility guarantees unemployment never rises during the contractionary adjustment
The LRPC shifts left because the announced target permanently lowers natural unemployment
Disinflation necessarily becomes deflation before expected inflation can decline
PM2A-DIS-L-009.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
PM2A-DIS-L-009.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

PM2A-DIS-L-010.q: Inflation falls 3 points while cumulative output loss equals 6% of annual GDP. Unemployment later returns to natural. Which synthesis is correct?
options: The sacrifice ratio is 0.5, and unemployment stays permanently high
The ratio is 3, and LRPC shifts right permanently
The ratio is 6, and the price level must have fallen
The sacrifice ratio is 2, and the unemployment cost was temporary in the model
PM2A-DIS-L-010.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-DIS-L-010.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-DIS-L-011.q: An adverse supply shock has raised inflation and unemployment. Why can disinflation policy face a harder near-term tradeoff than after a demand boom?
options: The LRPC becomes downward sloping during supply shocks
Contraction shifts the SRPC downward with no demand effect
Contraction can lower inflation pressure while worsening an already weak output position
Supply shocks automatically lower the sacrifice ratio to zero
PM2A-DIS-L-011.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
PM2A-DIS-L-011.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3009.commonError: Ignoring the short-run unemployment cost of reducing inflation.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3009.q: What does contractionary monetary policy do on the short-run Phillips curve?
options: It lowers inflation but raises unemployment in the short run
It raises inflation and lowers unemployment in the short run
It lowers both inflation and unemployment immediately
It raises both inflation and unemployment immediately
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3009.feedback: Contractionary monetary policy can reduce inflation, but it usually raises unemployment temporarily.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3010.commonError: Skipping the short-run move before expectations adjust.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3010.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at b, the Fed reduces inflation below expectations. Where does the economy move in the short run?
options: a
c
d
U2
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3010.feedback: Starting at b, lower actual inflation moves the economy to d: lower inflation and higher unemployment.

Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

P52B-S1-DIS-B3-001.q: Two central banks pursue the same reduction in inflation. One has strong credibility and expected inflation falls quickly. Compared with the less credible bank, what is the likely transition?
options: A permanently lower natural rate of unemployment.
A larger price-level increase caused by credibility.
No change in expected inflation.
A smaller temporary output and unemployment cost.
P52B-S1-DIS-B3-001.commonError: Assuming credibility changes the long-run natural rate rather than the transition cost.
P52B-S1-DIS-B3-001.feedback: Faster adjustment of expected inflation can reduce the sacrifice required to lower actual inflation.

PM2A-DIS-EB-012.q: Inflation drops from 5% to 2% while prices still rise. What is occurring?
options: A permanent output boom
Disinflation
Deflation
A price-level collapse
PM2A-DIS-EB-012.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
PM2A-DIS-EB-012.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

PM2A-DIS-EB-013.q: Which policy direction normally lowers aggregate demand to pursue disinflation?
options: Contractionary policy
Expansionary policy
A permanent supply restriction
A higher inflation target
PM2A-DIS-EB-013.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
PM2A-DIS-EB-013.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

PM2A-DIS-EB-014.q: What is the usual short-run Phillips cost of disinflation?
options: Lower unemployment while inflation falls
Permanently higher natural unemployment
Higher inflation with higher output
Higher unemployment while inflation falls
PM2A-DIS-EB-014.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
PM2A-DIS-EB-014.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

PM2A-DIS-FB-016.q: A rapid plan loses 5% of annual GDP to cut inflation 2 points; a gradual plan loses 6% to cut it 3 points. Which has the lower sacrifice ratio?
options: The gradual plan has ratio 3 versus the rapid plan’s 2
The gradual plan has ratio 2 versus the rapid plan’s 2.5
The rapid plan has ratio 2 versus the gradual plan’s 3
Both plans have a sacrifice ratio of 2.5
PM2A-DIS-FB-016.commonError: Compares total output losses without scaling each by its own inflation reduction.
PM2A-DIS-FB-016.feedback: The rapid path ratio is 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5; the gradual path ratio is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

PM2A-DIS-FB-017.q: After contraction raises unemployment above natural, expected inflation falls. What long-run adjustment is expected?
options: SRPC shifts downward and unemployment returns toward natural
LRPC shifts right and locks in higher unemployment
SRPC shifts upward and inflation rises
Unemployment remains above natural permanently
PM2A-DIS-FB-017.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
PM2A-DIS-FB-017.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

PM2A-DIS-MB-015.q: A trusted announcement lowers expected inflation. What is the relevant Phillips mechanism?
options: SRPC shifts upward because credibility raises the announced inflation target
Aggregate demand expands automatically without any change in policy instruments
SRPC can shift downward before all actual inflation adjustment occurs
LRPC shifts left and eliminates the natural rate before contracts reset
PM2A-DIS-MB-015.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
PM2A-DIS-MB-015.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

PM2A-DIS-LB-018.q: A central bank with mixed credibility begins rapid disinflation. Which full chain is most model-consistent?
options: Demand expands, unemployment falls, and inflation drops immediately without any wage, price, or expectations adjustment
LRPC shifts right permanently because lower inflation raises the natural unemployment rate
Expected inflation rises first and shifts SRPC upward before the contraction begins
Demand contracts, unemployment rises temporarily, expectations fall gradually, and output returns toward potential
PM2A-DIS-LB-018.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
PM2A-DIS-LB-018.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

PM2A-DIS-LB-019.q: Policy A cuts inflation 4 points with 8% cumulative output loss. Policy B cuts 2.5 points with 4% loss. Which cost comparison is correct?
options: A has ratio 4; B has ratio 2.5, using final inflation as denominator
Both have ratio 2 because each lowers inflation from a positive starting rate
A has ratio 2; B has ratio 1.6, so B loses less output per point
A has ratio 0.5; B has ratio 0.625, so A has the lower cost
PM2A-DIS-LB-019.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-DIS-LB-019.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-DIS-LB-020.q: Inflation is down to 1% after disinflation, unemployment is back at natural, and the price level is higher than before. Which diagnosis is complete?
options: The price level should have returned to its starting value once unemployment normalized
Disinflation succeeded without requiring deflation; the short-run labor cost has unwound
Deflation occurred because the inflation rate fell even though prices remained higher
The natural rate must now be permanently lower because unemployment first increased
PM2A-DIS-LB-020.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
PM2A-DIS-LB-020.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

ECON-SP-DISINFLATION-UNEMPLOYMENT-COST-5.q: Inflation falls from 5% to 2% but remains positive. Did the price level fall?
options: No; it rose more slowly
Yes; any inflation decline lowers prices
Yes; disinflation and deflation are identical
No; the price level stayed exactly fixed
ECON-SP-DISINFLATION-UNEMPLOYMENT-COST-5.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.
ECON-SP-DISINFLATION-UNEMPLOYMENT-COST-5.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.

ECON-SP-MONETARY-POLICY-PC-TRANSITION-50.q: Contractionary disinflation raises unemployment in the short run. Is that necessarily permanent?
options: Yes; every contraction shifts LRPC right
Yes; the SRPC never shifts after policy
No; unemployment must fall below natural immediately
No; unemployment can return toward natural as expectations adjust
ECON-SP-MONETARY-POLICY-PC-TRANSITION-50.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.
ECON-SP-MONETARY-POLICY-PC-TRANSITION-50.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.

ECON-SP-DISINFLATION-UNEMPLOYMENT-COST-6.q: Contractionary monetary policy reduces spending and inflation pressure. Which Phillips connection follows initially?
options: Movement toward higher unemployment and lower inflation along SRPC
A permanent LRPC shift to higher unemployment after expected inflation adjusts
Movement toward lower unemployment and lower inflation along the same curve
An upward SRPC shift caused by lower expected inflation during contraction
ECON-SP-DISINFLATION-UNEMPLOYMENT-COST-6.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.
ECON-SP-DISINFLATION-UNEMPLOYMENT-COST-6.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.

ECON-SP-MONETARY-POLICY-PC-TRANSITION-60.q: Expected inflation falls and the economy later returns to natural unemployment. Which family links explain the transition?
options: A permanent move along one SRPC only
An LRPC shift caused by the price level
A sacrifice-ratio shift of aggregate demand
A downward SRPC shift followed by long-run return to LRPC
ECON-SP-MONETARY-POLICY-PC-TRANSITION-60.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.
ECON-SP-MONETARY-POLICY-PC-TRANSITION-60.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.

PM2A-DIS-BR-021.q: A policy team has computed cumulative output loss per inflation point. What applied question should that sacrifice ratio now inform?
options: How alternative disinflation paths trade speed against short-run cost
How to classify liquid assets between M1 and broader monetary aggregates
How to calculate nominal GDP from current prices and quantities
How to shift the production frontier through resource accumulation
PM2A-DIS-BR-021.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.
PM2A-DIS-BR-021.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.

ECON-SP-EASY-77.q: The sacrifice ratio measures the output cost of reducing:
options: Inflation
Unemployment
Money demand
Imports
ECON-SP-EASY-77.commonError: Confusing sacrifice ratio with unemployment rate.
ECON-SP-EASY-77.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures how much output is lost when inflation is reduced.

ECON-SP-EASY-79.q: Credible anti-inflation policy can reduce the sacrifice ratio by causing expected inflation to:
options: Rise faster
Fall faster
Stay above actual inflation forever
Turn into unemployment
ECON-SP-EASY-79.feedback: If expected inflation falls faster, the short-run cost of disinflation can be smaller.

PM2A-SAC-E-001.q: What does a sacrifice ratio of 3 mean?
options: About 3% of one year’s output is lost per 1-percentage-point inflation reduction
Inflation falls 3% whenever output falls 1%
Unemployment rises 3 percentage points permanently
The price level falls 3% during every disinflation
PM2A-SAC-E-001.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
PM2A-SAC-E-001.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

PM2A-SAC-E-002.q: An analyst divides output loss by the final 4% inflation rate after inflation began at 7%. What denominator should replace 4%?
options: The initial 7% inflation rate before policy
The 11% sum of the two inflation rates
The final 4% inflation rate already used
The 3-percentage-point reduction in inflation
PM2A-SAC-E-002.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
PM2A-SAC-E-002.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

PM2A-SAC-E-003.q: Which loss belongs in the usual sacrifice-ratio numerator?
options: The total fall in the price level
The final year’s inflation rate
Cumulative output lost relative to potential during disinflation
The permanent increase in the unemployment rate
PM2A-SAC-E-003.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
PM2A-SAC-E-003.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

PM2A-SAC-E-004.q: A disinflation has a lower sacrifice ratio than another. Under comparable measurement, what does that indicate?
options: A higher inflation target after policy ends
Less cumulative output loss per inflation point reduced
A larger fall in the price level
A permanently higher natural unemployment rate
PM2A-SAC-E-004.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
PM2A-SAC-E-004.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-166.q: If expected inflation falls quickly after a credible policy announcement, the sacrifice ratio is likely to be:
options: Lower
Higher
Unchanged by expectations
Equal to M1
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-166.feedback: Faster adjustment of expected inflation reduces the output cost of disinflation.

PM2A-SAC-M-005.q: Cumulative output loss is 12% of one year’s GDP while inflation falls 3 percentage points. What is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 4% of one year’s output per inflation point
3% of output per inflation point
9% of output per inflation point
36% of output per inflation point
PM2A-SAC-M-005.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-M-005.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-M-006.q: A planned inflation reduction is 2.5 percentage points and the estimated sacrifice ratio is 3. What cumulative output loss is implied?
options: 1.2% of one year’s output
5.5% of one year’s output
8.3% of one year’s output
7.5% of one year’s output
PM2A-SAC-M-006.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-M-006.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-M-007.q: The output gap is −1.5% in year one and −2.5% in year two while inflation falls 2 percentage points. Using the sum of annual gaps, what is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 4% of output per inflation point
8% of output per inflation point
2% of one year’s output per inflation point
1% of output per inflation point
PM2A-SAC-M-007.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-M-007.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-M-008.q: Inflation declines from 8% to 5%. Which calculation uses the correct denominator?
options: Final output divided by 13 percentage points
Cumulative output loss divided by 3 percentage points
Cumulative output loss divided by the final 5%
Cumulative output loss divided by the initial 8%
PM2A-SAC-M-008.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
PM2A-SAC-M-008.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

PM2A-SAC-M-009.q: Path A loses 6% of one year’s output to cut inflation 3 points. Path B loses 5% to cut inflation 2 points. Which has the lower sacrifice ratio?
options: Path A has a ratio of 2; Path B has a ratio of 2.5
Path B has a ratio of 2; Path A has a ratio of 2.5
Both paths have a sacrifice ratio of 2
Path A has a ratio of 3; Path B has a ratio of 2
PM2A-SAC-M-009.commonError: Compares total losses without dividing each by its own inflation-point reduction.
PM2A-SAC-M-009.feedback: Path A: 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Path B: 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5, so Path A has the lower sacrifice ratio.

ECON-SP-HARD-248.q: A credible disinflation lowers expected inflation before unemployment rises much. What happens to the sacrifice ratio?
options: It falls
It rises
It becomes infinite
It equals MPC
ECON-SP-HARD-248.feedback: Credibility lowers expected inflation faster and can reduce the output cost of disinflation.

ECON-SP-HARD-266.q: A student says disinflation has no cost if the Fed announces it. What is the correction?
options: Credibility can lower the cost, not guarantee zero cost
Announcements always raise inflation first
The sacrifice ratio ignores expectations
Unemployment must fall during disinflation
ECON-SP-HARD-266.feedback: Credibility can reduce the sacrifice ratio, but it does not automatically make disinflation costless.

PM2A-SAC-H-010.q: Potential GDP remains $500 billion in each of the three years. Output is 2% below potential for one year and 1% below for two more years while inflation falls 4 points. What is the loss per inflation point?
options: $2.5 billion per inflation point
$10 billion per inflation point
$20 billion per inflation point
$5 billion per inflation point
PM2A-SAC-H-010.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-H-010.feedback: The cumulative loss is $10 billion + $5 billion + $5 billion = $20 billion; $20 billion ÷ 4 = $5 billion per inflation point.

PM2A-SAC-H-011.q: A disinflation creates cumulative output loss equal to 9% of annual GDP. If the sacrifice ratio is 3, how far did inflation fall?
options: 6 percentage points
27 percentage points
3 percentage points
2 percentage points
PM2A-SAC-H-011.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-H-011.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-H-012.q: Real GDP growth slows from 4% to 1%, but output remains above potential. Why can the 3-point growth slowdown not automatically be the sacrifice-ratio numerator?
options: Only the final inflation rate belongs in the numerator of this measure
The numerator measures an output-level loss relative to a benchmark, not merely slower growth
Any growth slowdown is exactly the cumulative output gap relative to potential
The numerator must be a permanent unemployment-rate change rather than output
PM2A-SAC-H-012.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
PM2A-SAC-H-012.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

PM2A-SAC-H-013.q: Cumulative output loss is 6.5% of one year’s GDP and inflation falls 3 percentage points. Round the sacrifice ratio to two decimals.
options: 2.17% of one year’s output per inflation point
2.16% of output per inflation point
2.20% of output per inflation point
3.50% of output per inflation point
PM2A-SAC-H-013.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-H-013.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

ECON-SP-ELITE-329.q: The Fed announces disinflation, but workers doubt it and expected inflation stays high. What happens to the sacrifice ratio?
options: It is likely higher
It is automatically zero
It becomes the MPC
It shifts LRAS right
ECON-SP-ELITE-329.commonError: Assuming announcements alone make policy credible.
ECON-SP-ELITE-329.feedback: If expected inflation does not fall quickly, reducing actual inflation tends to require more output loss.

ECON-SP-ELITE-330.q: If inflation falls from 12 percent to 7 percent and the sacrifice ratio is 3.5, output loss equals:
options: 17.5 percent of one year's output
15.5 percent of one year's output
8.5 percent of one year's output
5 percent of one year's output
ECON-SP-ELITE-330.commonError: Adding the sacrifice ratio to the inflation reduction.
ECON-SP-ELITE-330.feedback: Inflation falls by 5 points, so output loss is 3.5 x 5 = 17.5 percent of one year's output.

ECON-SP-ELITE-331.q: If cumulative output loss is 14 percent of one year’s potential GDP and inflation falls by 4 percentage points, the sacrifice ratio is:
options: 3.5% of one year’s output per inflation point
4% of one year’s output per inflation point
10% of one year’s output per inflation point
18% of one year’s output per inflation point
ECON-SP-ELITE-331.commonError: Uses the inflation change or output loss alone rather than dividing cumulative loss by the percentage-point reduction.
ECON-SP-ELITE-331.feedback: Divide the 14% cumulative output loss by the 4-percentage-point inflation reduction: 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5% of one year’s output per point.

ECON-SP-ELITE-354.q: A disinflation plan is credible, wage contracts adjust quickly, and expected inflation falls fast. Which path is most likely?
options: Smaller unemployment increase for the same inflation reduction
Larger unemployment increase for the same inflation reduction
No change in expected inflation despite credibility
Permanent unemployment below natural
ECON-SP-ELITE-354.feedback: Credibility and fast expectation adjustment reduce the output and unemployment cost of lowering inflation.

ECON-SP-ELITE-355.q: A disinflation plan lacks credibility, wage contracts are slow, and expected inflation remains high. Which path is most likely?
options: Larger output loss for the same inflation reduction
Smaller output loss for the same inflation reduction
Immediate movement to lower unemployment
LRPC becomes downward sloping
ECON-SP-ELITE-355.commonError: Assuming disinflation costs vanish without credibility.
ECON-SP-ELITE-355.feedback: If expected inflation stays high, lowering actual inflation usually requires a larger output loss.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9020.q: A disinflation lowers inflation from 10 percent to 6 percent. Cumulative output loss is 18 percent of one year’s potential GDP, of which 11 percent occurred before the final year. An analyst reports a sacrifice ratio using only the final-year loss. Which audit correction is needed?
options: Use all 18 percent: the ratio is 4.5; using only the final year would understate it as 1.75.
Use only 7 percent: the ratio is 1.75 because earlier output losses are already over.
Use the final inflation rate: the ratio is 3 because the target is 6 percent.
Add initial and final inflation: the ratio is 1.125 because the full window contains both rates.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9020.commonError: Dividing by the wrong inflation change.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9020.feedback: The inflation reduction is 4 percentage points. Cumulative loss gives 18/4 = 4.5. Final-year loss is 18 − 11 = 7, giving 7/4 = 1.75 if earlier losses are wrongly omitted. Returning toward potential does not erase earlier lost production.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9021.q: A plan must reduce inflation by 5 percentage points with cumulative output loss no greater than 14 percent of one year’s potential GDP. Its first stage has already reduced inflation by 2 percentage points at a cumulative loss of 7 percent. What maximum sacrifice ratio can the remaining stage have if the full plan is to meet both targets?
options: About 2.33 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
2.8 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
3.5 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
7 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9021.feedback: There are 3 inflation points and 7 percent of output-loss allowance remaining. The remaining-stage ceiling is 7/3 = 2.333..., about 2.33. Applying the overall allowance ratio 14/5 = 2.8 to the remaining stage would exceed the total loss limit because the first stage used more loss per point.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9049.q: A disinflation lowers inflation from 9 percent to 5 percent with cumulative output loss of 10 percent of one year’s potential GDP. A second plan is projected to lower inflation by only 2.5 percentage points with loss of 7 percent on the same output benchmark. Which comparison avoids confusing a smaller total loss with a lower loss per inflation point?
options: The completed plan has ratio 2.5 versus 2.8 for the second; the second has less total loss but a higher loss per point.
The second plan has the lower ratio because 7 is less than 10, regardless of the inflation reductions.
Both have ratio 2.5 because the second plan’s inflation reduction is its denominator and also its ratio.
The completed plan has ratio 0.4 and therefore no output cost; the second has ratio 2.8.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9049.commonError: Using the ending inflation rate instead of the inflation reduction.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9049.feedback: The completed reduction is 9 − 5 = 4 points, so 10/4 = 2.5. The second ratio is 7/2.5 = 2.8. A lower cumulative cost can accompany a higher per-point cost when the inflation reductions differ; neither statistic alone proves a universally better policy.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9050.q: Two stages jointly reduce inflation by 6 percentage points with a combined sacrifice ratio of 1.75. The first stage loses 3 percent of one year’s potential GDP while reducing inflation by 2 percentage points. Use the same output benchmark for both stages. What is the second-stage ratio, and how does it compare with the first?
options: 1.875 for the second versus 1.5 for the first; the second has the higher loss per point.
1.75 for both stages, because a combined ratio must equal each stage’s ratio.
3.75 for the second versus 1.5 for the first, using only 2 remaining inflation points.
0.533 for the second versus 0.667 for the first, using inflation reduction divided by loss.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9050.commonError: Adding the inflation reduction and sacrifice ratio.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9050.feedback: Total loss is 6 × 1.75 = 10.5 percent. The second stage accounts for 10.5 − 3 = 7.5 percent loss and 6 − 2 = 4 inflation points, giving 1.875. The first-stage ratio is 3/2 = 1.5. The combined ratio is weighted by the reductions, not a mandate for equal stage ratios.

PM2A-SAC-L-014.q: A three-year disinflation produces annual output gaps of −2%, −1%, and 0%, cutting inflation from 6.5% to 4.5%. A faster path produces one year at −4% and cuts inflation the same amount. Which comparison is correct?
options: The gradual path ratio is 3; the fast path ratio is 4
Both paths have a ratio of 2
The gradual path ratio is 2; the fast path ratio is 1.5
The gradual path ratio is 1.5; the fast path ratio is 2
PM2A-SAC-L-014.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-L-014.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-L-015.q: Economy A loses 8% of one year’s GDP while inflation falls from 9% to 5%. Economy B loses 6% while inflation falls from 5% to 2%. What can be concluded?
options: A has a ratio of 0.5 and B has a ratio of 0.67
A has a lower ratio because its inflation drop is larger
A has a ratio of 2 and B also has a ratio of 2
A has a ratio of 4 and B has a ratio of 3
PM2A-SAC-L-015.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-L-015.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

ECON-SP-EASY-78.q: If the sacrifice ratio is 4 and inflation falls by 2 percentage points, the output cost is:
options: 2 percent of one year's output
4 percent of one year's output
8 percent of one year's output
16 percent of one year's output
ECON-SP-EASY-78.feedback: The output cost is 4 x 2 = 8 percent of one year's output.

ECON-SP-HARD-249.q: Potential GDP is $400 billion. Cumulative output loss is $24 billion while inflation falls from 8% to 5%. What is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 3% of output per inflation point
6% of output per inflation point
8% of output per inflation point
2% of one year’s output per inflation point
ECON-SP-HARD-249.commonError: Divides the dollar loss directly by the inflation change without converting loss to a share of potential output.
ECON-SP-HARD-249.feedback: The $24 billion loss is 6% of $400 billion. Inflation falls 3 percentage points, so the ratio is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

ECON-SP-HARD-250.q: If inflation falls by 3 points and the output loss is 12 percent of one year’s GDP, the sacrifice ratio is:
options: 12% of one year’s output per inflation point
4% of one year’s output per inflation point
3% of one year’s output per inflation point
9% of one year’s output per inflation point
ECON-SP-HARD-250.commonError: Uses the inflation reduction or cumulative output loss alone rather than dividing loss by points reduced.
ECON-SP-HARD-250.feedback: Divide cumulative output loss by the inflation reduction: 12 ÷ 3 = 4% of one year’s output per inflation point.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-167.q: If the sacrifice ratio is 3 and inflation falls from 8 percent to 5 percent, the output cost is:
options: 3 percent of one year's output
6 percent of one year's output
9 percent of one year's output
15 percent of one year's output
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-167.feedback: Inflation falls by 3 percentage points, so output loss is 3 x 3 = 9 percent of one year's output.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3012.commonError: Confusing the sacrifice ratio with the inflation rate itself.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3012.q: What does the sacrifice ratio measure?
options: The output cost of reducing inflation
The unemployment rate at zero inflation
The money multiplier after disinflation
The tax increase needed to raise AD
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3012.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures the output cost of reducing inflation.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3013.q: Inflation falls by 3 percentage points. If the sacrifice ratio is 4, what output loss should be expected?
options: 7 percent of one year's output
12 percent of one year's output
3 percent of one year's output
4 percent of one year's output
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3013.feedback: Output loss equals sacrifice ratio times inflation reduction, so 4 x 3 = 12 percent of one year's output.

PM2A-SAC-EB-016.q: Which formula states the sacrifice ratio?
options: Price-level decline over the episode ÷ nominal GDP growth
Cumulative output loss ÷ inflation reduction in percentage points
Inflation reduction in points ÷ cumulative output loss relative to potential
Permanent unemployment increase ÷ the final positive inflation rate
PM2A-SAC-EB-016.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
PM2A-SAC-EB-016.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

PM2A-SAC-EB-017.q: Inflation falls from 6% to 4%. What is the denominator?
options: 2 percentage points
4 percent
6 percent
10 percentage points
PM2A-SAC-EB-017.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
PM2A-SAC-EB-017.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

PM2A-SAC-EB-018.q: A ratio of 2 is best read as what?
options: Inflation falls two percent for every percentage point of unemployment added
Unemployment stays two points above natural after expectations completely adjust
The price level declines two percent in each year of disinflation
Two percent of one year’s output lost per inflation point reduced
PM2A-SAC-EB-018.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
PM2A-SAC-EB-018.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

PM2A-SAC-FB-020.q: Use the sum of annual percentage output shortfalls as the cumulative-loss convention. Annual output gaps are −1%, −2%, and −1%; inflation falls from 7% to 5%. What is the ratio?
options: 6% of output per inflation point
2% of one year’s output per inflation point
0.5% of output per inflation point
3% of output per inflation point
PM2A-SAC-FB-020.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-FB-020.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-FB-021.q: A report divides cumulative output loss by the final inflation rate. What correction is required?
options: Divide by the percentage-point reduction in inflation
Divide by the initial inflation rate before the policy began
Multiply by the final inflation rate
Use the permanent unemployment rate
PM2A-SAC-FB-021.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
PM2A-SAC-FB-021.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

PM2A-SAC-FB-022.q: Path X loses 7.2% of annual GDP to reduce inflation 3 points. Path Y loses 5% to reduce inflation 2 points. Which is more output-efficient?
options: Path Y, with a ratio of 2 versus 2.4
Path X, with a ratio of 3 versus 2
They are equal because both lower inflation
Path X, with a ratio of 2.4 versus 2.5
PM2A-SAC-FB-022.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-FB-022.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-MB-019.q: Loss is 10% of annual GDP and inflation falls 4 points. What is the ratio?
options: 4% of output per inflation point
14% of output per inflation point
2.5% of one year’s output per inflation point
1.5% of output per inflation point
PM2A-SAC-MB-019.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-MB-019.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-LB-023.q: A two-year policy creates output gaps of −2.4% and −1.8%, lowering inflation from 7.0% to 5.2%. Round the sacrifice ratio to two decimals.
options: 2.34% of output per inflation point
4.20% of output per inflation point
2.33% of one year’s output per inflation point
1.80% of output per inflation point
PM2A-SAC-LB-023.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-LB-023.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-LB-024.q: A credible plan lowers expected inflation and produces a 3% cumulative output loss for a 2-point inflation reduction. A less credible plan loses 7.5% for a 3-point reduction. Which comparison is correct?
options: The plans are equal because both reduce inflation
The credible plan ratio is 1.5; the other is 2.5
The credible plan ratio is 2; the other is 2.5
The credible plan ratio is 0.67; the other is 0.4
PM2A-SAC-LB-024.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-LB-024.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-LB-025.q: Potential output remains $800 billion each year. Actual output is below potential by 1.5% for two years and 0.5% for one year while inflation falls 2.8 points. What is cumulative loss per inflation point?
options: $10 billion per inflation point
$4 billion per inflation point
$14 billion per inflation point
$28 billion per inflation point
PM2A-SAC-LB-025.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-LB-025.feedback: The cumulative loss is 3.5% of $800 billion = $28 billion. Dividing by 2.8 inflation points gives $10 billion per point.
PM2A-SAC-LB-025.roundingRule: Report the exact dollar amount per inflation point.

ECON-SP-CALCULATE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5059.q: Inflation falls from 8% to 5%. What number belongs in the sacrifice-ratio denominator?
options: 3 percentage points
5 percent
8 percent
13 percentage points
ECON-SP-CALCULATE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5059.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.
ECON-SP-CALCULATE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5059.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.

ECON-SP-DEFINE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5058.q: Should annual output gaps be added before calculating a multi-year sacrifice ratio?
options: No, only the worst year counts
No, only the final year counts
Yes, but add inflation rates too
Yes, to obtain cumulative output loss
ECON-SP-DEFINE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5058.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.
ECON-SP-DEFINE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5058.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.

ECON-SP-INTERPRET-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5060.q: Does the sacrifice ratio normally measure an unemployment increase per inflation point?
options: Yes, but only when inflation stays positive
No, it measures the fall in the price level
No, it measures cumulative output loss per inflation point
Yes, unemployment is always the numerator
ECON-SP-INTERPRET-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5060.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
ECON-SP-INTERPRET-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5060.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.

ECON-SP-CALCULATE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6050.q: The economy temporarily moves above natural unemployment during disinflation. How is this cost measured?
options: Sum the output losses and divide by the inflation-point reduction
Divide the unemployment increase by the final positive inflation rate
Treat the change in the price level as the cumulative output numerator
Shift LRPC right by the cumulative inflation reduction during policy
ECON-SP-CALCULATE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6050.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.
ECON-SP-CALCULATE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6050.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.

ECON-SP-DEFINE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6049.q: Expected inflation falls faster after a credible announcement. How can that connect to the sacrifice ratio?
options: A lower final inflation rate automatically raises the ratio even with unchanged loss
Credibility changes the denominator from inflation reduction to unemployment
The ratio must become zero in every credible disinflation plan
A smaller cumulative output loss can lower the measured ratio
ECON-SP-DEFINE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6049.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
ECON-SP-DEFINE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6049.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

ECON-SP-INTERPRET-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6051.q: Two disinflation paths reach the same inflation target. Which family destination uses their sacrifice ratios to compare costs?
options: GDP component classification
Bank reserve accounting
Disinflation and policy
Short-run curve axis reading
ECON-SP-INTERPRET-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6051.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.
ECON-SP-INTERPRET-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6051.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.

short-run-phillips-curve.title: Short-Run Phillips Curve
short-run-phillips-curve.description: Interpret movements along the short-run inflation–unemployment tradeoff.

easy.q: The Phillips curve shows a short-run trade-off between:
options: Inflation and unemployment
Taxes and spending
Money supply and money demand
Imports and exports
easy.commonError: Confusing the Phillips curve with the money market.
easy.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows a trade-off between inflation and unemployment.

easy.q: In the standard Phillips-curve convention, the vertical axis measures:
options: Unemployment rate
Inflation rate
Real GDP
Money supply
easy.commonError: Reversing the Phillips curve axes.
easy.feedback: The vertical axis measures the inflation rate.

easy.q: In the standard Phillips-curve convention, the horizontal axis measures:
options: Inflation rate
Price level
Unemployment rate
Money demand
easy.commonError: Reversing the Phillips curve axes.
easy.feedback: The horizontal axis measures the unemployment rate.

easy.q: In the short run, expansionary policy usually moves the economy toward:
options: Higher inflation and lower unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment
Higher unemployment and lower inflation
No change in either variable
easy.commonError: Missing the short-run tradeoff.
easy.feedback: Expansionary policy raises inflation pressure and lowers unemployment in the short run.

easy.q: In the short run, contractionary policy usually moves the economy toward:
options: Higher inflation and lower unemployment
Lower inflation and higher unemployment
Higher inflation and higher unemployment
Lower unemployment and higher output
easy.commonError: Reversing contractionary policy effects.
easy.feedback: Contractionary policy lowers inflation but raises unemployment in the short run.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Point a has:
options: Lower unemployment and higher inflation than point c
Higher unemployment and lower inflation than point c
The same unemployment and lower inflation than point c
No inflation
easy.commonError: Reading the Phillips curve axes backward.
easy.feedback: Point a is at U1 and I2, while point c is at U2 and I1.
easy.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from point c to point a shows:
options: Lower inflation and higher unemployment
Higher inflation and lower unemployment
Higher inflation and higher unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment
easy.commonError: Reversing movement along SRPC.
easy.feedback: Moving from c to a raises inflation and lowers unemployment in the short run.
easy.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

easy.q: In the long run, unemployment returns to:
options: The natural rate
Zero
The inflation rate
The money multiplier
easy.commonError: Thinking policymakers can permanently hold unemployment below natural.
easy.feedback: The natural-rate hypothesis says unemployment returns to its natural rate in the long run.

easy.q: At point A, what is the unemployment rate?
options: 2.5 percent
8 percent
5 percent
10 percent
easy.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
easy.feedback: Point A lies directly above 5 on the unemployment axis.
easy.imageAlt: Phillips graph with downward SRPC0, vertical LRPC, and their intersection A.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from −2.5 to 10. Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6.5), A at (5,2.5), and (10,−1.5). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5. Dashed guides from A mark 5 on the horizontal axis and 2.5 on the vertical axis.

easy.q: Relative to point A, what does point B show on SRPC0?
options: Lower unemployment and higher inflation
Higher unemployment and lower inflation
Lower unemployment and lower inflation
Higher unemployment and higher inflation
easy.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
easy.feedback: Point B is left of A on the unemployment axis and above A on the inflation axis.
easy.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through B at (3,3.5) and A at (5,2.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies above and left of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

easy.q: How does point B compare with the natural-rate point A in the displayed Phillips-curve graph?
options: Lower unemployment and higher inflation
Higher unemployment and higher inflation
Higher unemployment and lower inflation
Lower unemployment and lower inflation
easy.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
easy.feedback: Point B is to the right of A on the unemployment axis and below A on the inflation axis.
easy.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through A at (5,2.5) and B at (7,1.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies below and right of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

medium.q: The short-run Phillips curve slopes downward because higher AD tends to:
options: Raise output, lower unemployment, and raise inflation
Lower output, lower unemployment, and lower inflation
Raise unemployment while lowering inflation forever
Shift LRPC left immediately
medium.commonError: Missing the AD-to-unemployment channel.
medium.feedback: Higher AD raises output and prices, which maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation.

medium.q: Why is there no permanent Phillips-curve tradeoff?
options: Expectations adjust; unemployment returns to normal
Money demand becomes zero
AD stops affecting the short run
Inflation cannot change wages
medium.commonError: Treating the short-run tradeoff as permanent.
medium.feedback: Once expectations adjust, unemployment returns to the natural rate.

medium.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point c, expansionary policy that raises inflation above expectations moves the economy to:
options: a
b
c
d
medium.commonError: Moving to the long-run point immediately.
medium.feedback: Expansionary policy moves the economy along SRPC1 from c to a: higher inflation and lower unemployment.
medium.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

medium.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A move along SRPC1 from c toward b means:
options: Inflation rises and unemployment falls
Inflation falls and unemployment rises
Both inflation and unemployment rise
Both inflation and unemployment fall
medium.commonError: Reading movement along the curve backward.
medium.feedback: Moving up-left along SRPC1 raises inflation and lowers unemployment.
medium.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

medium.q: At point A, what is the inflation rate?
options: 5 percent
0 percent
6.5 percent
2.5 percent
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: The horizontal guide through point A hits the inflation axis at 2.5 percent.
medium.imageAlt: Phillips graph with downward SRPC0, vertical LRPC, and their intersection A.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from −2.5 to 10. Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6.5), A at (5,2.5), and (10,−1.5). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5. Dashed guides from A mark 5 on the horizontal axis and 2.5 on the vertical axis.

medium.q: How far below the natural rate is unemployment at point B?
options: 0.5 percentage point
2 percentage points
1 percentage point
3.5 percentage points
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: The natural rate is 5 percent at point A on the LRPC, while point B has 3 percent unemployment.
medium.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through B at (3,3.5) and A at (5,2.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies above and left of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

medium.q: What type of change is the move from A to B?
options: An upward shift from SRPC0 to another SRPC
A leftward shift of the LRPC
A movement along the same SRPC0
A movement along the vertical LRPC
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: Both A and B lie on the same SRPC0, so the graph shows a movement along the curve, not a curve shift.
medium.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through B at (3,3.5) and A at (5,2.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies above and left of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

medium.q: Point B is to the right of the LRPC. By how many percentage points does its unemployment rate exceed the natural rate?
options: 0.5 percentage point
1 percentage point
4.5 percentage points
2 percentage points
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: The natural rate is 5 percent at A, and point B is at 7 percent unemployment.
medium.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through A at (5,2.5) and B at (7,1.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies below and right of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

medium.q: Points A and B lie on the same short-run Phillips curve. How should the change from A to B be classified?
options: A movement along the same SRPC0
A downward shift from SRPC0 to another SRPC
A rightward shift of the LRPC
A movement along the vertical LRPC
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: A and B lie on the same SRPC0, so the graph shows a movement along the short-run curve.
medium.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through A at (5,2.5) and B at (7,1.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies below and right of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

medium.q: Aggregate demand rises unexpectedly while expected inflation is fixed. Which Phillips-curve change best represents the immediate effect?
options: A move up and left along the current SRPC
An upward shift of the SRPC at every unemployment rate
A rightward shift of the vertical LRPC
A move down and right along the current SRPC
medium.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.
medium.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.

medium.q: Inflation and unemployment both rise after a sharp increase in energy costs. What is the best diagnosis?
options: Aggregate demand causes movement up one unchanged SRPC
Lower expected inflation shifts the SRPC downward
The natural rate necessarily falls and shifts LRPC left
The adverse supply shock shifts the SRPC upward
medium.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
medium.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

hard.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which point reflects unemployment below the natural rate with inflation above I1?
options: a
b
c
d
hard.commonError: Ignoring the LRPC natural rate.
hard.feedback: Point a is at U1 and I2, so unemployment is below the natural rate U2 and inflation is above I1.
hard.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
hard.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

hard.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Moving from b to c along SRPC1 means:
options: Inflation falls and unemployment rises
Inflation rises and unemployment falls
Both inflation and unemployment rise
Both inflation and unemployment fall
hard.commonError: Reading movement along SRPC backward.
hard.feedback: Moving down-right along SRPC1 lowers inflation and raises unemployment.
hard.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
hard.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

hard.q: A policymaker claims higher inflation can permanently hold unemployment below natural. What is the flaw?
options: Expected inflation adjusts over time
Money demand is always zero
LRAS shifts right automatically
M1 excludes currency
hard.commonError: Believing in a permanent Phillips curve menu.
hard.feedback: Once expected inflation adjusts, unemployment returns to the natural rate.

hard.q: Which event moves along SRPC rather than shifting SRPC?
options: Unexpected AD expansion
Higher expected inflation
Adverse oil shock
Rising natural unemployment
hard.commonError: Confusing movement along SRPC with shifts of SRPC.
hard.feedback: Unexpected AD expansion moves the economy along the existing SRPC in the short run.

hard.q: Which answer best separates short-run and long-run Phillips curve logic?
options: Policy can move unemployment temporarily, but expectations restore the natural rate
Policy cannot affect unemployment even briefly, because money is neutral in every period
Policy permanently lowers unemployment whenever inflation rises above zero
Policy shifts LRPC whenever actual inflation changes
hard.commonError: Confusing short-run effects with long-run neutrality.
hard.feedback: Demand policy can move unemployment in the short run, but expectations adjust and unemployment returns to natural.

hard.q: Moving leftward along SRPC0 from point A implies which short-run relationship?
options: Lower unemployment with lower inflation
Lower unemployment with higher inflation
Higher unemployment with higher inflation
No change in unemployment as inflation changes
hard.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
hard.feedback: A downward-sloping SRPC shows an inverse short-run relationship: less unemployment comes with more inflation.
hard.imageAlt: Phillips graph with downward SRPC0, vertical LRPC, and their intersection A.
hard.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from −2.5 to 10. Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6.5), A at (5,2.5), and (10,−1.5). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5. Dashed guides from A mark 5 on the horizontal axis and 2.5 on the vertical axis.

hard.q: Refer to the graph with points A and B on SRPC0. The natural rate and supply conditions are unchanged, and inflation expectations have not yet adjusted. Consumer spending unexpectedly strengthens. Which interpretation links the demand event to the graph and distinguishes current unemployment from its natural rate?
options: The economy shifts to a different SRPC because any change in actual inflation changes expectations immediately.
LRPC shifts left to 3 percent unemployment because stronger demand permanently improves matching.
The economy moves B to A because stronger demand reduces inflation and raises unemployment.
The economy moves A to B along SRPC0; unemployment is 2 percentage points below natural while inflation is 1 percentage point higher.
hard.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
hard.feedback: A is (5,2.5) and B is (3,3.5). A demand change with expectations and supply fixed moves along SRPC0. Compare the unemployment coordinate with LRPC at 5, and compare inflation with A; the cyclical gap does not move natural unemployment.
hard.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
hard.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through B at (3,3.5) and A at (5,2.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies above and left of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

hard.q: Refer to the graph with points A and B on SRPC0. The natural rate and supply conditions are unchanged, and inflation expectations have not yet adjusted. Planned investment unexpectedly contracts. Which interpretation links the demand event to the graph and distinguishes current unemployment from its natural rate?
options: The economy shifts to a different SRPC because any change in actual inflation changes expectations immediately.
The economy moves A to B along SRPC0; unemployment is 2 percentage points above natural while inflation is 1 percentage point lower.
LRPC shifts right to 7 percent unemployment because weaker demand permanently worsens matching.
The economy moves B to A because weaker demand raises inflation and reduces unemployment.
hard.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
hard.feedback: A is (5,2.5) and B is (7,1.5). A demand change with expectations and supply fixed moves along SRPC0. Compare the unemployment coordinate with LRPC at 5, and compare inflation with A; the cyclical gap does not move natural unemployment.
hard.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
hard.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through A at (5,2.5) and B at (7,1.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies below and right of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

hard.q: Two years have the same unemployment rate, but inflation is higher in the second after wage setters revise expected inflation upward. What changed?
options: The LRPC became downward sloping
Aggregate demand alone fixed both outcomes
The economy is on a higher SRPC
The economy moved up one unchanged SRPC
hard.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
hard.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at c, which sequence best shows an attempted permanent unemployment reduction through expansionary policy?
options: c to a to b
c to b to d
c to d to c
c to a to c
elite.commonError: Thinking point a can be held permanently.
elite.feedback: Expansion lowers unemployment at a temporarily, but expectations adjust and unemployment returns to natural at b.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which policy mistake is shown by treating point a as permanent?
options: Ignoring expected inflation adjustment
Ignoring the money multiplier
Ignoring M2 near monies
Ignoring nominal GDP accounting
elite.commonError: Believing unemployment can stay below natural without expectations changing.
elite.feedback: Point a is temporary because expected inflation eventually rises and moves the economy toward point b.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.

SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

elite.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. If policy moves the economy from c to b on SRPC1, what must be true?
options: Actual inflation rises while unemployment falls
Expected inflation rises while unemployment stays fixed
Natural unemployment rises while inflation falls
Output falls while inflation rises
elite.commonError: Confusing movement along SRPC with a shift of SRPC.
elite.feedback: Movement up-left along the same SRPC means higher inflation and lower unemployment.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
