Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

medium.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Moving from d to c most likely reflects:
options: Expected inflation falling
Expected inflation rising
Natural unemployment rising
AD shifting right
medium.commonError: Missing downward expectations adjustment.
medium.feedback: As expected inflation falls, the SRPC shifts downward and unemployment returns to U2 at point c.
medium.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

medium.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Moving from SRPC1 to SRPC2 at the same unemployment rate means:
options: Inflation is higher at the same unemployment rate
Inflation is lower at the same unemployment rate
Unemployment disappears
LRPC shifts right
medium.commonError: Missing the upward SRPC shift.
medium.feedback: SRPC2 is above SRPC1, so inflation is higher for a given unemployment rate.
medium.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

medium.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Assume supply conditions and the natural rate are unchanged; only expected inflation can shift the curve. If the economy moves from c on SRPC1 to the upper point at the same unemployment rate, the likely cause is:
options: Higher expected inflation
Lower expected inflation
A fall in actual inflation only
A lower natural rate
medium.commonError: Confusing a curve shift with movement along one curve.
medium.feedback: At the same unemployment rate, a higher SRPC reflects higher expected inflation or a worse tradeoff. With other shifters explicitly excluded, the upward shift identifies higher expected inflation.
medium.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

medium.q: An adverse supply shock affects the Phillips curve by:
options: Shifting SRPC up and right
Moving down along the same SRPC
Shifting LRPC to zero unemployment
Eliminating expected inflation
medium.commonError: Treating supply shocks as normal AD movements.
medium.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

medium.q: If policymakers expand AD to reduce unemployment below the natural rate, what happens after expectations adjust?
options: Unemployment returns to natural and inflation stays higher
Unemployment stays permanently lower
Inflation falls below expected inflation
LRPC becomes downward sloping
medium.commonError: Believing in a permanent policy tradeoff.
medium.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC up, returning unemployment to natural at higher inflation.

medium.q: Suppose expected inflation rises while the natural rate is unchanged. Which curve change shown is consistent with that assumption?
options: SRPC0 shifts downward away from SRPC1
SRPC0 shifts upward to SRPC1
LRPC shifts left to a lower natural rate
The economy only moves along unchanged SRPC0
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: An upward shift of the short-run Phillips curve is the standard way to show higher expected inflation or an adverse supply shock with the natural rate unchanged.
medium.imageAlt: Phillips graph with two downward-sloping SRPCs, vertical LRPC, and points A and B.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from 0 to 10. Solid blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6), A at (5,3), and (10,0). Dashed purple SRPC1 is parallel above it, running through (0,9.6), B at (6,6), and (10,3.6). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and intersects SRPC0 at A and SRPC1 at inflation 6.6. Dashed guides mark A at (5,3) and B at (6,6).

hard.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at c, which sequence matches expansionary policy and expectations adjustment?
options: c to a to b
c to b to a
c to d to b
c to a to d
hard.commonError: Skipping the short-run movement along SRPC.
hard.feedback: Expansion moves from c to a in the short run; expected inflation rises and moves the economy to b.
hard.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
hard.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

hard.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which movement shows expectations falling after contractionary policy?
options: d to c
c to a
a to b
b to a
hard.commonError: Reversing expectation shifts.
hard.feedback: Moving from d to c reflects lower expected inflation and return to the natural unemployment rate.
hard.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
hard.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

hard.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. At U3, moving from SRPC1 to SRPC2 changes inflation from:
options: I2 to I4
I4 to I2
I1 to I3
I3 to I1
hard.commonError: Reading the wrong inflation level at U3.
hard.feedback: At U3, the lower curve is at I2 and the upper curve is at I4.
hard.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
hard.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

hard.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. At inflation I3, the move from SRPC1 to SRPC2 implies unemployment is:
options: Higher on SRPC2
Lower on SRPC2
The same on both curves
Zero on both curves
hard.commonError: Missing worse tradeoff at the same inflation rate.
hard.feedback: At a given inflation rate, the higher SRPC implies a higher unemployment rate.
hard.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
hard.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

hard.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A shift from SRPC1 to SRPC2 is most consistent with:
options: Higher expected inflation or adverse supply shock
Lower expected inflation or favorable supply shock
Higher money supply with expectations fixed
Lower unemployment at every inflation rate
hard.commonError: Treating SRPC shifts as ordinary movement along a curve.
hard.feedback: The upward SRPC shift reflects higher expected inflation or a worsened supply-side tradeoff.
hard.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
hard.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

hard.q: If the Fed unexpectedly increases inflation while expected inflation is fixed, unemployment moves:
options: Below the natural rate temporarily
Above the natural rate permanently
To zero permanently
Unchanged in every period
hard.commonError: Ignoring the gap between actual and expected inflation.
hard.feedback: When actual inflation exceeds expected inflation, unemployment can temporarily fall below the natural rate.

hard.q: Which event shifts both SRAS left and SRPC up-right?
options: Oil price surge
Tax cut
Open-market purchase
Consumer confidence boom
hard.commonError: Confusing supply shocks with AD shocks.
hard.feedback: An oil price surge raises production costs and worsens the inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

hard.q: Initially actual inflation equals expected inflation and unemployment is at its natural rate. Supply conditions and the natural rate stay unchanged. If expected inflation rises while actual inflation is held at its original rate, what happens to unemployment?
options: Rise above natural
Fall below natural
Stay zero
Become inflation
hard.commonError: Ignoring expected inflation in the Phillips curve equation.
hard.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts SRPC up, so unchanged actual inflation corresponds to higher unemployment. The stated initial equality makes the new inflation surprise negative.

hard.q: Initially actual inflation equals expected inflation and unemployment is at its natural rate. Supply conditions and the natural rate stay unchanged. If expected inflation falls while actual inflation is held at its original rate, what happens to unemployment?
options: Fall below natural
Rise above natural
Stay at zero
Equal the price level
hard.commonError: Reversing the effect of lower expected inflation.
hard.feedback: Lower expected inflation shifts SRPC down, so the same actual inflation can mean lower unemployment. The stated initial equality makes the new inflation surprise positive.

hard.q: A student says an oil shock causes only movement along the SRPC. What is the correction?
options: It shifts SRPC because costs and prices change directly
It shifts only AD because spending changes directly
It shifts only LRPC because inflation changes
It moves only along LRAS because output changes
hard.commonError: Treating supply shocks as AD movements.
hard.feedback: A supply shock shifts the SRPC because it directly changes firms' costs and inflation pressure.

hard.q: A student says higher expected inflation lowers unemployment permanently. What is the correction?
options: It shifts SRPC upward and worsens the short-run tradeoff
It shifts LRPC left and improves the long-run tradeoff
It shifts AD right and lowers prices
It raises money demand and lowers rates
hard.commonError: Treating expected inflation as beneficial stimulus.
hard.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward, giving higher inflation at each unemployment rate.

hard.q: At a given unemployment rate, how does SRPC1 compare with SRPC0?
options: SRPC1 shows a lower inflation rate
SRPC1 shows the same inflation rate
SRPC1 shows a lower natural rate
SRPC1 shows a higher inflation rate
hard.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
hard.feedback: Point B lies on a different short-run Phillips curve, SRPC1, so the graph is showing a curve shift rather than a movement along SRPC0.
hard.imageAlt: Phillips graph with two downward-sloping SRPCs, vertical LRPC, and points A and B.
hard.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from 0 to 10. Solid blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6), A at (5,3), and (10,0). Dashed purple SRPC1 is parallel above it, running through (0,9.6), B at (6,6), and (10,3.6). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and intersects SRPC0 at A and SRPC1 at inflation 6.6. Dashed guides mark A at (5,3) and B at (6,6).

elite.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A move from c on SRPC1 to the upper point at U3 on SRPC2 means:
options: Same unemployment with higher inflation
Same inflation with lower unemployment
Lower inflation with same unemployment
Higher unemployment with same inflation
elite.commonError: Reading the curve shift as movement along SRPC1.
elite.feedback: At U3, SRPC2 shows a higher inflation rate than SRPC1.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

elite.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. At inflation I3, comparing SRPC1 and SRPC2 shows:
options: SRPC2 has higher unemployment
SRPC2 has lower unemployment
Both curves have U3
Both curves have U1
elite.commonError: Missing the worse tradeoff after SRPC shifts upward.
elite.feedback: At the same inflation rate, the higher SRPC shows higher unemployment.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

elite.q: A central bank unexpectedly expands AD. Later, workers build the higher inflation into wage demands. Which sequence is most accurate?
options: Move along SRPC, then SRPC shifts up
SRPC shifts down, then move along LRPC
LRPC shifts left, then AD falls
Move along LRAS, then M1 falls
elite.commonError: Confusing immediate inflation surprise with later expectation adjustment.
elite.feedback: Unexpected AD expansion first moves along the SRPC; later expected inflation rises and shifts SRPC upward.

elite.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Which labeled move isolates an upward SRPC shift at unemployment U3?
options: The move from point c to point f
The move from point a to point f
The move from point b to point e
The move from point c to point a
elite.commonError: Compares points with different unemployment rates, so movement and shift effects are mixed.
elite.feedback: Points c and f share unemployment U3; moving from c on SRPC1 to f on SRPC2 isolates higher inflation at the same unemployment rate.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

legendary.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. The economy moves from SRPC1 to SRPC2. Which statement should be rejected?
options: The tradeoff improved because higher inflation now buys lower unemployment at every point.
The tradeoff worsened because inflation is higher at a given unemployment rate.
Expected inflation may have increased and shifted the curve upward.
An adverse supply shock may have raised both inflation pressure and unemployment risk.
legendary.commonError: Calling an upward SRPC shift an improvement.
legendary.feedback: An upward SRPC shift worsens the tradeoff because inflation is higher at the same unemployment rate.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

legendary.q: A policymaker says, 'Inflation is high, so unemployment must be low.' What is the best correction?
options: That only fits demand pressure; supply shocks can raise inflation and unemployment together.
That is always true because the Phillips curve never shifts.
That is false only when M1 is larger than M2.
That is true in the long run because LRPC slopes downward.
legendary.commonError: Treating the Phillips curve as fixed under every shock.
legendary.feedback: The short-run tradeoff can worsen when SRPC shifts up, so inflation and unemployment can rise together.

legendary.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. The economy is on SRPC2 rather than SRPC1. Which conclusion is most careful?
options: The tradeoff worsened, but the cause could be expected inflation or a supply shock.
The tradeoff improved, and policymakers can now lower unemployment without cost.
The LRPC shifted left, so natural unemployment must have fallen.
AD must have shifted right, so SRPC cannot have moved.
legendary.commonError: Assuming every SRPC shift has only one cause.
legendary.feedback: An upward SRPC shift can come from higher expected inflation or an adverse supply shock, and both worsen the tradeoff.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph with SRPC0, SRPC1, A and B. Use the model inflation = expected inflation − 0.6 × (unemployment − 5) + supply offset, with all rates in percent and differences in percentage points. At B the separately measured supply offset is +1.1 points. What expected inflation is consistent with B, and could the graph alone identify that expectation if the supply offset were unknown?
options: Expected inflation is 6 percent; actual inflation equals expectations at every point on an SRPC.
Expected inflation is 5.5 percent; without the supply-offset measurement, only expected inflation plus the offset is identified.
Expected inflation is 6.6 percent; the supply offset can be ignored even though it is positive.
Expected inflation is 4.3 percent; both the unemployment gap and the supply offset must be subtracted from actual inflation.
legendary.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
legendary.feedback: B has unemployment 6 and actual inflation 6. Thus 6 = expected inflation − 0.6 + 1.1, implying expected inflation 5.5. Without the offset measurement the graph identifies only expected inflation + offset = 6.6. The higher curve does not by itself isolate an expectations change.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips graph with two downward-sloping SRPCs, vertical LRPC, and points A and B.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from 0 to 10. Solid blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6), A at (5,3), and (10,0). Dashed purple SRPC1 is parallel above it, running through (0,9.6), B at (6,6), and (10,3.6). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and intersects SRPC0 at A and SRPC1 at inflation 6.6. Dashed guides mark A at (5,3) and B at (6,6).

legendary.q: Refer to the graph with A and B on SRPC0. Initially expected inflation is the inflation rate at A, and the economy is at B. Next period expected inflation equals this period’s actual inflation. Hold the natural rate and supply conditions fixed; each one-point expectations change shifts the SRPC vertically by one point with slope unchanged. Compare keeping unemployment at B’s rate with instead keeping actual inflation at B’s current rate. Which next-period outcome follows?
options: Keeping unemployment at 3 percent requires unchanged 3.5 percent inflation; holding inflation fixed shifts LRPC to 3 percent.
Keeping unemployment at 3 percent requires 4.5 percent inflation; holding inflation at 3.5 percent instead returns unemployment to 5 percent.
Keeping unemployment at 3 percent requires 2.5 percent inflation; holding inflation at 3.5 percent raises unemployment to 7 percent.
Both targets give the same unchanged point B because adaptive expectations cannot shift an SRPC.
legendary.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
legendary.feedback: Expectations rise from 2.5 to 3.5, shifting the curve up one point. At unemployment 3, inflation therefore rises from 3.5 to 4.5. Alternatively, actual inflation equal to the new expectation gives natural unemployment at 5. A fixed unemployment target and a fixed inflation target are different continuations.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through B at (3,3.5) and A at (5,2.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies above and left of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph with B to the right of A on SRPC0. Initially actual inflation is B’s rate and expected inflation is A’s rate. Each period expectations equal the previous period’s actual inflation; each one-point expectations change shifts SRPC vertically by one point with slope unchanged. Natural unemployment and supply conditions stay fixed. Policy holds unemployment at B’s rate for one additional period, then requires inflation to be nonnegative in the following period. What inflation occurs in the additional period, and what is the highest unemployment rate compatible with that later inflation constraint?
options: Inflation stays 1.5 percent, then unemployment can remain at 7 percent.
Inflation is 0.5 percent, then unemployment can remain at 7 percent without deflation.
Inflation is 2.5 percent, then unemployment can be at most 5 percent.
Inflation is 0.5 percent, then unemployment can be at most 6 percent.
legendary.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
legendary.feedback: The plotted slope is (1.5 − 2.5)/(7 − 5) = −0.5. Expectations first fall from 2.5 to 1.5, so holding unemployment at 7 gives inflation 0.5. Next expectations are 0.5; nonnegative inflation requires 0.5 − 0.5 × (unemployment − 5) ≥ 0, or unemployment no greater than 6. Maintaining 7 would instead produce −0.5 percent inflation.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through A at (5,2.5) and B at (7,1.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies below and right of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

legendary.q: A temporary supply disruption raises inflation while existing contracts still reflect the original expected inflation. Wage setters update forecasts using the observed inflation, but the disruption ends before the new contracts take effect. Expected inflation nevertheless remains above its original level. With natural unemployment unchanged, what can be concluded about the final SRPC relative to its original position and its position during the disruption?
options: It must return exactly to its original position because the physical disruption ended.
It must lie above the disruption-period curve because any expectations rise exceeds any removed supply offset.
It must lie below the original curve because the original supply shock was temporary.
It remains above its original position, but its position relative to the disruption-period curve depends on the expectations rise versus the removed supply offset.
legendary.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
legendary.feedback: The original curve has neither the supply offset nor the higher expectation. The final curve retains only the expectation increase, so it is above the original. Comparing it with the disruption-period curve requires the two offset magnitudes. Observed inflation alone does not identify their relative sizes.

legendary.q: Two central banks announce the same lower inflation target. One has a stronger record of meeting targets. Under otherwise similar conditions, what can differ?
options: Actual inflation must reach zero with no output cost
The less credible bank must cause immediate deflation
Expected inflation may fall faster where the announcement is more credible
The natural rate must immediately fall only in the credible economy
legendary.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
legendary.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

legendary.q: Actual inflation is 5% while wage setters expected 3%, temporarily pushing unemployment below natural. What erodes that effect?
options: The price level returns to its initial value automatically
Forecasts adjust upward, shifting the SRPC until unemployment returns toward natural
The LRPC shifts left because actual inflation is above expected
Forecasts adjust downward, moving unemployment farther below natural
legendary.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
legendary.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

boss.commonError: Treating expected inflation as movement along the same SRPC.
boss.q: What happens to the short-run Phillips curve when expected inflation rises?
options: It shifts downward
It shifts upward
It becomes horizontal
It becomes the money demand curve
boss.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the short-run Phillips curve upward.

boss.commonError: Keeping unemployment below natural forever after an inflation surprise.
boss.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at c, expansionary policy moves the economy to a. After expected inflation rises, where does the economy move?
options: b
c
d
U1
boss.feedback: After expected inflation rises, the SRPC shifts up and the economy moves to b at the natural rate of unemployment.
boss.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
boss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

boss.q: A sharp oil-price increase raises firms’ costs. What happens to the short-run Phillips curve, other things equal?
options: It shifts down and to the left.
The economy only moves along an unchanged curve.
It shifts up and to the right.
It becomes vertical at zero unemployment.
boss.commonError: Treating an adverse supply shock as a movement along a fixed SRPC.
boss.feedback: An adverse supply shock can raise both inflation and unemployment, shifting the SRPC up-right.

boss.q: If expected inflation increases, which SRPC change follows?
options: An upward shift
A downward shift
Only movement down the same curve
A horizontal LRPC shift
boss.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
boss.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

boss.q: If expected inflation decreases, which SRPC change follows?
options: An upward shift
Only movement up the same curve
A vertical AD shift
A downward shift
boss.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
boss.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

boss.q: Why can actual inflation above expected inflation temporarily reduce unemployment?
options: Higher inflation permanently raises labor productivity
The LRPC becomes downward sloping
Some wages and prices were set using the lower forecast
The natural rate immediately becomes lower
boss.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
boss.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

boss.q: Under rational expectations, wage setters use available information, including credible policy announcements; forecasts can still be wrong when new information arrives. A credible lower-inflation target changes their forecasts before much demand contraction occurs, but some contracts remain fixed. Which assessment follows?
options: Rational expectations guarantee exact forecasts and eliminate every unemployment cost even with fixed contracts.
The SRPC can shift downward sooner, reducing the transition cost, while fixed contracts can leave some temporary unemployment increase.
Expected inflation must wait for past inflation to decline because announcements cannot enter a forecast.
A credible nominal target permanently shifts LRPC left even when labor-market structure is unchanged.
boss.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
boss.feedback: Available-information forecasting can incorporate credible policy news before actual inflation falls. It does not imply perfect foresight or instantly flexible contracts. Earlier expectations adjustment can reduce disinflation costs without guaranteeing zero costs.

boss.q: Actual inflation remains above expected inflation for several contract cycles. Which sequence best fits adaptive expectations?
options: Expected inflation rises, shifting SRPC upward and undoing the temporary unemployment gain
Expected inflation falls, shifting SRPC downward and preserving the unemployment gain indefinitely
LRPC shifts left, locking in unemployment below natural after contracts renew
SRPC stays fixed because only actual inflation matters for wage setting
boss.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
boss.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

boss.q: A supply shock raises inflation without a demand boom. Why might a simple expectations-only diagnosis be incomplete?
options: Expected inflation is the only possible SRPC shifter in the introductory model
Every inflation increase is movement along a fixed SRPC regardless of its cause
Supply shocks shift only the vertical LRPC while leaving SRPC unchanged
The shock can shift the SRPC even before expectations adapt
boss.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
boss.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

legendaryBoss.q: A surprise expansion lifts inflation from 2% to 5% while expected inflation remains 2%. What makes the unemployment effect temporary?
options: Expected inflation falls below 2% and shifts SRPC downward after workers observe prices
The LRPC becomes flatter as actual inflation rises above expected inflation
Expected inflation eventually rises toward actual inflation and shifts the SRPC upward
The natural rate permanently falls three points once actual inflation exceeds its forecast
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
legendaryBoss.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

legendaryBoss.q: A disinflation announcement is only partly credible and wage contracts reset slowly. Which conclusion is appropriately bounded?
options: The announcement necessarily causes the price level to fall for several years
Expectations may fall gradually, so some short-run output cost can remain
Partial credibility must eliminate every unemployment cost as soon as policy is announced
Expected inflation cannot change until actual inflation reaches the announced target
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

legendaryBoss.q: An adverse supply shock raises actual inflation, then wage setters incorporate it into next year’s contracts. What are the two stages?
options: An initial SRPC shift followed by reinforcement through higher expected inflation
Two movements along one fixed SRPC with no change in the inflation-unemployment relation
An LRPC shift followed by lower expected inflation when contracts renew
A demand contraction followed by an SRPC shift downward at each unemployment rate
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The supply shock first shifts SRPC upward even with expectations unchanged. Incorporating the higher observed inflation into contracts adds an expectations-driven upward shift. This reinforces inflation pressure rather than describing the disappearance of a demand-created unemployment gain.

repairQuestions.q: Expected inflation rises from 2% to 4%. At a given unemployment rate, how does the SRPC move?
options: It shifts upward
It shifts downward
The economy moves down the same SRPC
The LRPC shifts right
repairQuestions.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.
repairQuestions.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.

repairQuestions.q: Actual inflation repeatedly exceeds the rate workers expected. Which forecast adjustment is likely?
options: Expected inflation falls
Expected inflation becomes permanently zero
Expected inflation cannot respond
Expected inflation rises
repairQuestions.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.
repairQuestions.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.

repairQuestions.q: Does a credible announcement guarantee costless disinflation?
options: Yes; unemployment must immediately fall
No; credibility can never affect expectations
No; it can reduce costs without always eliminating them
Yes; credibility removes all nominal rigidities
repairQuestions.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
repairQuestions.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: The economy moves up-left along SRPC after a demand surprise. Wage setters then revise forecasts upward. What connection is required?
options: A movement along SRPC becomes an upward shift as expectations adjust
The LRPC shifts left as aggregate demand rises and nominal wages renew
The same fixed SRPC supports permanently lower unemployment after forecasts update
A downward expectations shift reinforces the initial unemployment gain
bridgeQuestions.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.

bridgeQuestions.q: Expected inflation falls during a credible disinflation. Which applied family slice uses that change to assess policy costs?
options: GDP components
Money creation
Economic growth policy
Disinflation and policy
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Expectations fully catch up after repeated inflation surprises. Which curve summarizes the long-run unemployment result?
options: The money-demand curve
The production possibilities frontier
The LRPC at the natural rate
The SRPC as a permanent menu
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.

disinflation-and-policy.title: Disinflation and Policy
disinflation-and-policy.description: Trace monetary disinflation, unemployment costs, and expectations adjustment.

easy.q: If the Fed reduces money growth to fight inflation, unemployment usually:
options: Falls immediately
Rises temporarily
Stays permanently at zero
Becomes the price level
easy.commonError: Ignoring the short-run cost of disinflation.
easy.feedback: Disinflation usually raises unemployment temporarily as the economy moves along the SRPC.

easy.q: Disinflation means that:
options: The overall price level is falling because average prices are declining.
Unemployment is falling even though output remains below potential.
Inflation is slowing, although the price level may still be rising.
Nominal wages are fixed while real wages rise automatically.
easy.commonError: Confusing disinflation with deflation.
easy.feedback: Disinflation is slower price growth; deflation is a falling price level.

easy.q: Why can a credible anti-inflation announcement reduce the short-run cost of disinflation?
options: It permanently eliminates the natural rate of unemployment.
It guarantees that the price level falls immediately.
It makes aggregate demand irrelevant.
Expected inflation may adjust downward more quickly.
easy.commonError: Ignoring the role of expected inflation in the transition.
easy.feedback: When expectations fall sooner, wage and price setting can adjust with less output and unemployment loss.

easy.q: The sacrifice ratio measures the:
options: Cumulative output lost per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
The permanent unemployment rate created by a recession.
The price-level increase caused by one point of money growth.
The share of public spending financed by current taxes.
easy.commonError: Treating the sacrifice ratio as a permanent unemployment rate.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio summarizes the output cost of lowering inflation.

easy.q: Inflation slows from 6% to 3%, so the price level still rises more slowly. What is this?
options: Disinflation
Deflation
Hyperinflation
A falling real interest rate by definition
easy.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
easy.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

easy.q: Which short-run effect commonly accompanies contractionary disinflation policy?
options: Higher output and lower unemployment
A permanently lower natural unemployment rate
An immediate rise in aggregate demand
Lower output and higher unemployment
easy.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
easy.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

medium.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point b, contractionary policy that lowers inflation below expectations moves the economy in the short run to:
options: a
c
d
U1
medium.commonError: Moving directly to lower expected inflation.
medium.feedback: Contractionary policy moves along SRPC2 from b to d: lower inflation and higher unemployment.
medium.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

medium.q: If the Fed reduces money growth to lower inflation, the short-run Phillips curve predicts:
options: Lower inflation and temporarily higher unemployment
Higher inflation and lower unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment immediately
No short-run cost at all
medium.commonError: Ignoring the short-run unemployment cost.
medium.feedback: Disinflation usually moves the economy toward lower inflation and higher unemployment in the short run.

medium.q: A central bank reduces aggregate demand to lower inflation. What Phillips movement is expected before expectations adjust?
options: An immediate leftward LRPC shift
An upward SRPC shift from lower expected inflation
Down and right along the current SRPC
Up and left along the current SRPC
medium.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
medium.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

medium.q: Why can a credible lower-inflation target reduce the short-run cost of disinflation?
options: It causes aggregate demand to expand during contraction
It may lower expected inflation and shift the SRPC downward sooner
It permanently lowers the natural rate by announcement
It guarantees wages and prices adjust instantly
medium.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
medium.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

medium.q: Inflation falls from 4% to 1%, but prices continue rising. Which statement is correct?
options: The economy has disinflation, not deflation
The economy has deflation because inflation fell
The price level must be below its initial level
The natural rate must have declined
medium.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
medium.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

medium.q: Why might gradual disinflation be chosen instead of a rapid contraction?
options: It always produces zero cumulative output loss
It guarantees expected inflation never changes
It permanently shifts LRPC left
It can spread adjustment and reduce a severe short-run output gap
medium.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.
medium.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.

hard.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, which sequence matches disinflation and expectations adjustment?
options: b to d to c
b to c to d
b to a to c
b to d to a
hard.commonError: Skipping the temporary unemployment cost.
hard.feedback: Disinflation moves from b to d in the short run; expected inflation falls and the economy moves to c.
hard.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
hard.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

hard.q: If actual inflation is less than expected inflation, unemployment is likely:
options: Above the natural rate
Below the natural rate
Equal to zero
Equal to inflation
hard.commonError: Reversing the effect of unexpectedly low inflation.
hard.feedback: When actual inflation is below expected inflation, unemployment tends to rise above the natural rate.

hard.q: A policymaker wants lower inflation but ignores unemployment during transition. What model warns about this cost?
options: Short-run Phillips curve
Money multiplier only
M1 definition only
Classical dichotomy only
hard.commonError: Ignoring short-run disinflation costs.
hard.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows that reducing inflation can temporarily raise unemployment.

hard.q: A central bank announces a gradual disinflation, but households and firms doubt that the plan will continue. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The natural unemployment rate immediately falls to zero.
High expected inflation can prolong the output and job losses.
The price level must begin falling throughout the adjustment.
Unemployment cannot rise because the disinflation is gradual.
hard.commonError: Assuming gradualism automatically produces low transition costs.
hard.feedback: If the plan lacks credibility, expected inflation can adjust slowly and make the disinflation more costly.

hard.q: A disinflation announcement is not credible, and wage contracts embed 6% inflation. What makes immediate costless adjustment unlikely?
options: Aggregate demand cannot affect inflation
Deflation is required before unemployment changes
Expected inflation and nominal contracts may adjust slowly
The LRPC must shift left before policy begins
hard.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
hard.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

hard.q: Two paths reach 2% inflation. The rapid path has a deep one-year recession; the gradual path has smaller gaps for several years. What must be compared?
options: The price levels at the start, without output data
Their cumulative output losses and inflation reductions
Only the largest annual unemployment rate
Only the final year’s output level
hard.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.
hard.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, which sequence best shows disinflation with temporary unemployment costs?
options: b to d to c
b to a to c
b to c to d
b to d to b
elite.commonError: Skipping the temporary move above natural unemployment.
elite.feedback: Disinflation lowers actual inflation first, moving to d, then expectations fall and the economy returns to c.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which policy lesson fits the move from b to d to c?
options: Disinflation has temporary unemployment costs
Inflation permanently lowers unemployment
Expected inflation must rise after contraction
Supply shocks lower unemployment immediately
elite.commonError: Missing the temporary cost of disinflation.
elite.feedback: The move from b to d shows higher unemployment during disinflation; d to c shows expectations adjusting downward.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

legendary.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Compare two disinflations from b to the lower sustained inflation rate I1 with supply conditions and natural unemployment unchanged. In one, existing contracts keep expected inflation at I2 initially. In the other, a credible announcement and immediate contract adjustment lower expected inflation to I1 before spending adjusts. Which pair of paths is consistent with these assumptions?
options: The first can pass through d before c; the second can reach c without the same initial unemployment excursion.
Both must pass through d because credibility cannot change expected inflation before actual inflation falls.
The first reaches c immediately; the second must shift LRPC right before inflation can fall.
Both finish at a because lower inflation permanently lowers natural unemployment.
legendary.commonError: Skipping the short-run unemployment cost of disinflation.
legendary.feedback: With old expectations, lower actual inflation moves b to d along SRPC2 before expectations shift the curve down toward c. If expectations and contracts already incorporate I1, the lower SRPC can support c without that initial gap. Credibility alone would not guarantee this outcome without the stated contract adjustment.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

legendary.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. The economy has moved b to d during disinflation. Inflation is then held at I1, the natural rate stays U2, and the adverse-supply offset is unchanged. A forecast shows unemployment returning to U2. Which evidence is necessary to reconcile this forecast with the diagram?
options: Expected inflation must fall enough to place an SRPC through c; contraction along unchanged SRPC2 would leave unemployment at d.
Expected inflation must rise enough to place an SRPC above SRPC2 while actual inflation remains I1.
The return requires moving from d to b along unchanged SRPC2 while inflation remains I1.
The return requires LRPC to shift right to U3 even though the natural rate stays U2.
legendary.commonError: Missing the expectation adjustment needed after disinflation.
legendary.feedback: At I1 the original SRPC2 locates d, not c. With natural unemployment and the supply offset fixed, a lower expected-inflation schedule is needed to reach c at U2. A forecast of unemployment recovery is therefore conditional on the expected-inflation adjustment, not just continued contraction.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

legendary.q: Country A has a sacrifice ratio of 2, while Country B has a sacrifice ratio of 5. If both reduce inflation by 3 percentage points, which comparison is correct?
options: A loses about 15% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 6%.
Both lose about 3% of annual GDP because the inflation reduction is equal.
A loses about 6% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 15%.
A has no output loss because its sacrifice ratio is below the inflation reduction.
legendary.commonError: Reversing the sacrifice ratios or treating equal inflation reductions as equal output costs.
legendary.feedback: Cumulative output loss equals the sacrifice ratio times the inflation reduction: 2 × 3 = 6 for A and 5 × 3 = 15 for B.

legendary.q: A credible central bank announces a lower inflation target, expected inflation falls partly, and policy still contracts demand. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: The downward SRPC shift may reduce but need not eliminate the short-run output cost
Credibility guarantees unemployment never rises during the contractionary adjustment
The LRPC shifts left because the announced target permanently lowers natural unemployment
Disinflation necessarily becomes deflation before expected inflation can decline
legendary.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
legendary.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

legendary.q: Inflation falls 3 points while cumulative output loss equals 6% of annual GDP. Unemployment later returns to natural. Which synthesis is correct?
options: The sacrifice ratio is 0.5, and unemployment stays permanently high
The ratio is 3, and LRPC shifts right permanently
The ratio is 6, and the price level must have fallen
The sacrifice ratio is 2, and the unemployment cost was temporary in the model
legendary.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendary.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendary.q: An adverse supply shock has raised inflation and unemployment. Why can disinflation policy face a harder near-term tradeoff than after a demand boom?
options: The LRPC becomes downward sloping during supply shocks
Contraction shifts the SRPC downward with no demand effect
Contraction can lower inflation pressure while worsening an already weak output position
Supply shocks automatically lower the sacrifice ratio to zero
legendary.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
legendary.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

boss.commonError: Ignoring the short-run unemployment cost of reducing inflation.
boss.q: What does contractionary monetary policy do on the short-run Phillips curve?
options: It lowers inflation but raises unemployment in the short run
It raises inflation and lowers unemployment in the short run
It lowers both inflation and unemployment immediately
It raises both inflation and unemployment immediately
boss.feedback: Contractionary monetary policy can reduce inflation, but it usually raises unemployment temporarily.

boss.commonError: Skipping the short-run move before expectations adjust.
boss.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at b, the Fed reduces inflation below expectations. Where does the economy move in the short run?
options: a
c
d
U2
boss.feedback: Starting at b, lower actual inflation moves the economy to d: lower inflation and higher unemployment.
boss.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
boss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

boss.q: Two central banks pursue the same reduction in inflation. One has strong credibility and expected inflation falls quickly. Compared with the less credible bank, what is the likely transition?
options: A permanently lower natural rate of unemployment.
A larger price-level increase caused by credibility.
No change in expected inflation.
A smaller temporary output and unemployment cost.
boss.commonError: Assuming credibility changes the long-run natural rate rather than the transition cost.
boss.feedback: Faster adjustment of expected inflation can reduce the sacrifice required to lower actual inflation.

boss.q: Inflation drops from 5% to 2% while prices still rise. What is occurring?
options: A permanent output boom
Disinflation
Deflation
A price-level collapse
boss.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
boss.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

boss.q: Which policy direction normally lowers aggregate demand to pursue disinflation?
options: Contractionary policy
Expansionary policy
A permanent supply restriction
A higher inflation target
boss.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
boss.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

boss.q: What is the usual short-run Phillips cost of disinflation?
options: Lower unemployment while inflation falls
Permanently higher natural unemployment
Higher inflation with higher output
Higher unemployment while inflation falls
boss.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
boss.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

boss.q: A rapid plan loses 5% of annual GDP to cut inflation 2 points; a gradual plan loses 6% to cut it 3 points. Which has the lower sacrifice ratio?
options: The gradual plan has ratio 3 versus the rapid plan’s 2
The gradual plan has ratio 2 versus the rapid plan’s 2.5
The rapid plan has ratio 2 versus the gradual plan’s 3
Both plans have a sacrifice ratio of 2.5
boss.commonError: Compares total output losses without scaling each by its own inflation reduction.
boss.feedback: The rapid path ratio is 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5; the gradual path ratio is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

boss.q: After contraction raises unemployment above natural, expected inflation falls. What long-run adjustment is expected?
options: SRPC shifts downward and unemployment returns toward natural
LRPC shifts right and locks in higher unemployment
SRPC shifts upward and inflation rises
Unemployment remains above natural permanently
boss.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
boss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

boss.q: A trusted announcement lowers expected inflation. What is the relevant Phillips mechanism?
options: SRPC shifts upward because credibility raises the announced inflation target
Aggregate demand expands automatically without any change in policy instruments
SRPC can shift downward before all actual inflation adjustment occurs
LRPC shifts left and eliminates the natural rate before contracts reset
boss.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
boss.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

legendaryBoss.q: A central bank with mixed credibility begins rapid disinflation. Which full chain is most model-consistent?
options: Demand expands, unemployment falls, and inflation drops immediately without any wage, price, or expectations adjustment
LRPC shifts right permanently because lower inflation raises the natural unemployment rate
Expected inflation rises first and shifts SRPC upward before the contraction begins
Demand contracts, unemployment rises temporarily, expectations fall gradually, and output returns toward potential
legendaryBoss.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

legendaryBoss.q: Policy A cuts inflation 4 points with 8% cumulative output loss. Policy B cuts 2.5 points with 4% loss. Which cost comparison is correct?
options: A has ratio 4; B has ratio 2.5, using final inflation as denominator
Both have ratio 2 because each lowers inflation from a positive starting rate
A has ratio 2; B has ratio 1.6, so B loses less output per point
A has ratio 0.5; B has ratio 0.625, so A has the lower cost
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendaryBoss.q: Inflation is down to 1% after disinflation, unemployment is back at natural, and the price level is higher than before. Which diagnosis is complete?
options: The price level should have returned to its starting value once unemployment normalized
Disinflation succeeded without requiring deflation; the short-run labor cost has unwound
Deflation occurred because the inflation rate fell even though prices remained higher
The natural rate must now be permanently lower because unemployment first increased
legendaryBoss.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

repairQuestions.q: Inflation falls from 5% to 2% but remains positive. Did the price level fall?
options: No; it rose more slowly
Yes; any inflation decline lowers prices
Yes; disinflation and deflation are identical
No; the price level stayed exactly fixed
repairQuestions.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.
repairQuestions.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.

repairQuestions.q: Contractionary disinflation raises unemployment in the short run. Is that necessarily permanent?
options: Yes; every contraction shifts LRPC right
Yes; the SRPC never shifts after policy
No; unemployment must fall below natural immediately
No; unemployment can return toward natural as expectations adjust
repairQuestions.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.
repairQuestions.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Contractionary monetary policy reduces spending and inflation pressure. Which Phillips connection follows initially?
options: Movement toward higher unemployment and lower inflation along SRPC
A permanent LRPC shift to higher unemployment after expected inflation adjusts
Movement toward lower unemployment and lower inflation along the same curve
An upward SRPC shift caused by lower expected inflation during contraction
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Expected inflation falls and the economy later returns to natural unemployment. Which family links explain the transition?
options: A permanent move along one SRPC only
An LRPC shift caused by the price level
A sacrifice-ratio shift of aggregate demand
A downward SRPC shift followed by long-run return to LRPC
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.

bridgeQuestions.q: A policy team has computed cumulative output loss per inflation point. What applied question should that sacrifice ratio now inform?
options: How alternative disinflation paths trade speed against short-run cost
How to classify liquid assets between M1 and broader monetary aggregates
How to calculate nominal GDP from current prices and quantities
How to shift the production frontier through resource accumulation
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.
