SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which policy mistake is shown by treating point a as permanent?
options: Ignoring expected inflation adjustment
Ignoring the money multiplier
Ignoring M2 near monies
Ignoring nominal GDP accounting
elite.commonError: Believing unemployment can stay below natural without expectations changing.
elite.feedback: Point a is temporary because expected inflation eventually rises and moves the economy toward point b.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

elite.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. If policy moves the economy from c to b on SRPC1, what must be true?
options: Actual inflation rises while unemployment falls
Expected inflation rises while unemployment stays fixed
Natural unemployment rises while inflation falls
Output falls while inflation rises
elite.commonError: Confusing movement along SRPC with a shift of SRPC.
elite.feedback: Movement up-left along the same SRPC means higher inflation and lower unemployment.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which comparison best captures the long-run result of higher expected inflation?
options: b and c have same unemployment but different inflation
a and b have same unemployment but different inflation
c and d have same inflation but different unemployment
a and d have same inflation but different unemployment
elite.commonError: Missing vertical long-run logic.
elite.feedback: Both b and c lie on the LRPC at U2, but b has higher inflation.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

elite.q: Assume a fixed natural rate, no supply shocks, and an unchanged Phillips slope. Each year expected inflation equals the previous year’s actual inflation. Policy keeps unemployment the same fixed distance below natural. What must happen to actual inflation and the inflation surprise?
options: Both actual inflation and the size of the positive surprise must rise each year.
Actual inflation rises each year, but the required positive surprise can remain constant.
Actual inflation stays fixed while expected inflation falls each year.
Actual and expected inflation can remain equal while unemployment stays below natural.
elite.commonError: Assuming one expansion can hold unemployment below the natural rate forever.
elite.feedback: With an unchanged slope and unemployment gap, the required actual-minus-expected inflation gap is constant. Because expectations catch up to the previous actual rate, actual inflation must rise again by that same amount. Ever-higher inflation does not require ever-larger forecast errors.

elite.q: Which feature of the graph shows that the natural rate is unchanged after the SRPC shift?
options: LRPC stays vertical at 5 percent unemployment
LRPC shifts left to 3 percent unemployment
SRPC1 becomes vertical at 6 percent unemployment
Point B moves to the right of point A
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: The LRPC staying fixed at 5 percent says the natural rate is unchanged, so inflation changes do not permanently buy lower unemployment.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips graph with two downward-sloping SRPCs, vertical LRPC, and points A and B.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from 0 to 10. Solid blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6), A at (5,3), and (10,0). Dashed purple SRPC1 is parallel above it, running through (0,9.6), B at (6,6), and (10,3.6). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and intersects SRPC0 at A and SRPC1 at inflation 6.6. Dashed guides mark A at (5,3) and B at (6,6).

elite.q: Which description of point A is correct?
options: A is only on SRPC0 and remains below the natural unemployment rate.
A is only on LRPC and remains above the natural unemployment rate.
A is on both SRPC0 and LRPC at the natural rate
A is the location where SRPC0 turns into a vertical Phillips curve.
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: Point A is where the short-run curve crosses the long-run curve, so unemployment equals the natural rate there.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips graph with downward SRPC0, vertical LRPC, and their intersection A.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from −2.5 to 10. Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6.5), A at (5,2.5), and (10,−1.5). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5. Dashed guides from A mark 5 on the horizontal axis and 2.5 on the vertical axis.

elite.q: If point B persists and expectations adjust, what long-run change is predicted?
options: SRPC shifts upward; unemployment returns to 5 percent
LRPC shifts left; unemployment stays at 3 percent
SRPC shifts downward; unemployment stays at 3 percent
LRPC shifts right; unemployment rises above 5 percent
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: With unemployment below the natural rate, expectations eventually adjust, shifting the SRPC and bringing unemployment back to the natural rate.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through B at (3,3.5) and A at (5,2.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies above and left of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

elite.q: With unemployment above the natural rate at B, what long-run Phillips-curve adjustment should follow?
options: LRPC shifts right; unemployment stays at 7 percent
SRPC shifts up; unemployment stays at 7 percent
SRPC shifts down; unemployment returns to 5 percent
LRPC shifts left; unemployment falls below 5 percent
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: With unemployment above the natural rate, inflation expectations tend to fall, shifting the SRPC downward and returning unemployment to the natural rate.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through A at (5,2.5) and B at (7,1.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies below and right of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

elite.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A move from c on SRPC1 to the upper point at U3 on SRPC2 means:
options: Same unemployment with higher inflation
Same inflation with lower unemployment
Lower inflation with same unemployment
Higher unemployment with same inflation
elite.commonError: Reading the curve shift as movement along SRPC1.
elite.feedback: At U3, SRPC2 shows a higher inflation rate than SRPC1.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

elite.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. At inflation I3, comparing SRPC1 and SRPC2 shows:
options: SRPC2 has higher unemployment
SRPC2 has lower unemployment
Both curves have U3
Both curves have U1
elite.commonError: Missing the worse tradeoff after SRPC shifts upward.
elite.feedback: At the same inflation rate, the higher SRPC shows higher unemployment.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

elite.q: A central bank unexpectedly expands AD. Later, workers build the higher inflation into wage demands. Which sequence is most accurate?
options: Move along SRPC, then SRPC shifts up
SRPC shifts down, then move along LRPC
LRPC shifts left, then AD falls
Move along LRAS, then M1 falls
elite.commonError: Confusing immediate inflation surprise with later expectation adjustment.
elite.feedback: Unexpected AD expansion first moves along the SRPC; later expected inflation rises and shifts SRPC upward.

elite.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Which labeled move isolates an upward SRPC shift at unemployment U3?
options: The move from point c to point f
The move from point a to point f
The move from point b to point e
The move from point c to point a
elite.commonError: Compares points with different unemployment rates, so movement and shift effects are mixed.
elite.feedback: Points c and f share unemployment U3; moving from c on SRPC1 to f on SRPC2 isolates higher inflation at the same unemployment rate.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, which sequence best shows disinflation with temporary unemployment costs?
options: b to d to c
b to a to c
b to c to d
b to d to b
elite.commonError: Skipping the temporary move above natural unemployment.
elite.feedback: Disinflation lowers actual inflation first, moving to d, then expectations fall and the economy returns to c.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which policy lesson fits the move from b to d to c?
options: Disinflation has temporary unemployment costs
Inflation permanently lowers unemployment
Expected inflation must rise after contraction
Supply shocks lower unemployment immediately
elite.commonError: Missing the temporary cost of disinflation.
elite.feedback: The move from b to d shows higher unemployment during disinflation; d to c shows expectations adjusting downward.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

elite.q: The Fed announces disinflation, but workers doubt it and expected inflation stays high. What happens to the sacrifice ratio?
options: It is likely higher
It is automatically zero
It becomes the MPC
It shifts LRAS right
elite.commonError: Assuming announcements alone make policy credible.
elite.feedback: If expected inflation does not fall quickly, reducing actual inflation tends to require more output loss.

elite.q: If inflation falls from 12 percent to 7 percent and the sacrifice ratio is 3.5, output loss equals:
options: 17.5 percent of one year's output
15.5 percent of one year's output
8.5 percent of one year's output
5 percent of one year's output
elite.commonError: Adding the sacrifice ratio to the inflation reduction.
elite.feedback: Inflation falls by 5 points, so output loss is 3.5 x 5 = 17.5 percent of one year's output.

elite.q: If cumulative output loss is 14 percent of one year’s potential GDP and inflation falls by 4 percentage points, the sacrifice ratio is:
options: 3.5% of one year’s output per inflation point
4% of one year’s output per inflation point
10% of one year’s output per inflation point
18% of one year’s output per inflation point
elite.commonError: Uses the inflation change or output loss alone rather than dividing cumulative loss by the percentage-point reduction.
elite.feedback: Divide the 14% cumulative output loss by the 4-percentage-point inflation reduction: 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5% of one year’s output per point.

elite.q: A disinflation plan is credible, wage contracts adjust quickly, and expected inflation falls fast. Which path is most likely?
options: Smaller unemployment increase for the same inflation reduction
Larger unemployment increase for the same inflation reduction
No change in expected inflation despite credibility
Permanent unemployment below natural
elite.commonError: Ignoring expectations in sacrifice-ratio logic.
elite.feedback: Credibility and fast expectation adjustment reduce the output and unemployment cost of lowering inflation.

elite.q: A disinflation plan lacks credibility, wage contracts are slow, and expected inflation remains high. Which path is most likely?
options: Larger output loss for the same inflation reduction
Smaller output loss for the same inflation reduction
Immediate movement to lower unemployment
LRPC becomes downward sloping
elite.commonError: Assuming disinflation costs vanish without credibility.
elite.feedback: If expected inflation stays high, lowering actual inflation usually requires a larger output loss.

legendary.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at c, policymakers try to keep unemployment at U1 through repeated demand expansion. What eventually breaks the plan?
options: Expected inflation rises and shifts the SRPC upward.
Actual inflation falls and shifts the SRPC downward.
The LRPC shifts left because inflation is higher.
The natural rate disappears because output rose once.
legendary.commonError: Believing policymakers can permanently buy lower unemployment with inflation.
legendary.feedback: Expansion can move unemployment below natural temporarily, but expected inflation adjusts and SRPC shifts upward.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

legendary.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. The economy moves from c to a, then policymakers mistake a as sustainable. What is the likely correction?
options: Expected inflation rises, SRPC shifts up, and the economy moves toward b.
Expected inflation falls, SRPC shifts down, and the economy moves toward d.
The natural rate falls, LRPC shifts left, and the economy stays at a.
The price level falls, AD shifts left, and unemployment stays at U1.
legendary.commonError: Treating a short-run Phillips curve point as permanent.
legendary.feedback: Point a is temporary. Expected inflation adjusts upward and the economy returns to the natural rate at higher inflation.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

legendary.q: Two episodes produce the same increase in inflation. In one, unemployment falls after aggregate demand expands; in the other, unemployment rises after an adverse supply shock. What explains the difference?
options: Both episodes are movements along one SRPC, but they begin from different unemployment rates.
Both episodes shift the LRPC because inflation changes the natural rate in opposite directions.
The supply shock lowers expected inflation and moves the economy down an unchanged SRPC.
The demand expansion moves along an SRPC, while the supply shock shifts the curve.
legendary.commonError: Assuming every inflation change is a movement along one fixed Phillips curve.
legendary.feedback: Demand changes can move the economy along a given SRPC; supply shocks alter the inflation-unemployment relationship and shift the SRPC.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph with A on SRPC0 and LRPC. Later observations show unemployment at A’s rate but persistently higher inflation. One analyst says the SRPC must have become vertical; another says the same vertical LRPC can coexist with a higher SRPC after contracts adjust. Which additional evidence would support the second interpretation?
options: Inflation rose once, which by itself proves that expectations already adjusted fully.
Current unemployment equals the natural rate, which requires every SRPC to be vertical.
The price level is higher, which proves that the natural unemployment rate permanently fell.
Wage-setting expectations have risen to match the sustained inflation while labor-market structure and supply conditions are unchanged.
legendary.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
legendary.feedback: An unchanged natural rate locates the same LRPC. Evidence that expected inflation caught up, with other shifters held fixed, supports a higher SRPC crossing it. Equal unemployment and a higher inflation observation alone do not establish the expectations mechanism.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips graph with downward SRPC0, vertical LRPC, and their intersection A.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from −2.5 to 10. Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6.5), A at (5,2.5), and (10,−1.5). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5. Dashed guides from A mark 5 on the horizontal axis and 2.5 on the vertical axis.

legendary.q: A demand expansion moves the economy to lower unemployment and higher inflation. A year later unemployment returns to its original rate while inflation remains higher. Which sequence fits?
options: A supply improvement followed by movement down the SRPC
Movement along an SRPC followed by an upward SRPC shift
Two movements along one permanently fixed SRPC
An LRPC shift left followed by falling expectations
legendary.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
legendary.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

legendary.q: An adverse supply shock raises inflation while output falls. How should the AD-AS result transfer to the Phillips model?
options: Higher inflation and unemployment indicate an upward SRPC shift
Higher inflation and lower unemployment indicate movement along SRPC
Lower inflation and unemployment indicate a downward SRPC shift
Unchanged inflation with lower unemployment indicates an LRPC shift
legendary.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
legendary.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

legendary.q: A policymaker cites the downward-sloping SRPC as proof that permanently higher inflation will secure permanently lower unemployment. What is the decisive flaw?
options: The SRPC actually slopes upward for every demand change
Inflation cannot respond to aggregate demand in the short run
The natural rate is always zero after an expansion
Expected inflation adjusts, so the short-run unemployment gain is not permanent
legendary.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
legendary.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

legendary.q: Two economies have the same natural unemployment rate but very different average inflation rates over many years. Which observation is most consistent with a vertical long-run Phillips curve?
options: The higher-inflation economy must have permanently lower unemployment because inflation buys a lasting tradeoff.
The lower-inflation economy must have permanently higher unemployment because prices grow more slowly.
Both can remain at the same long-run unemployment rate despite different inflation rates.
Different inflation rates require different natural unemployment rates even when labor markets are otherwise alike.
legendary.commonError: Inferring a permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff from cross-country inflation differences.
legendary.feedback: The vertical LRPC allows different steady inflation rates at the same natural unemployment rate.

legendary.q: A matching reform lowers the natural unemployment rate from 6.4 percent to 5.6 percent. At the same time, an unexpected demand expansion lowers actual unemployment to 4.9 percent. Later inflation expectations fully adjust while the reform remains in place and no new surprises occur. Which decomposition separates the durable change from the initial cyclical change?
options: LRPC shifts left by 1.5 percentage points; actual unemployment at 4.9 percent is the new permanent natural rate.
LRPC stays at 6.4 percent; both the reform and demand expansion are temporary movements along SRPC.
LRPC shifts to 5.6 percent, but expectations adjustment permanently fixes unemployment at 4.9 percent.
LRPC shifts left by 0.8 percentage point; the initial gap is 0.7 point below the new natural rate, and long-run unemployment returns to 5.6 percent.
legendary.commonError: Confusing a change in the natural rate with a movement caused by inflation.
legendary.feedback: The structural shift is 6.4 − 5.6 = 0.8 percentage point. Actual unemployment is temporarily 5.6 − 4.9 = 0.7 point below the new natural rate. Once the demand surprise disappears, the long-run anchor is 5.6, not the old 6.4 or temporary 4.9.

legendary.q: An unexpected monetary expansion temporarily lowers unemployment. Inflation expectations then fully adjust while the higher inflation rate persists. What is the long-run result?
options: Unemployment returns to the natural rate at a higher inflation rate.
Unemployment remains permanently below the natural rate.
Unemployment rises permanently above the natural rate.
Inflation returns automatically to its original rate while unemployment stays low.
legendary.commonError: Stopping the analysis before expectations adjust.
legendary.feedback: The short-run unemployment effect disappears when expectations adjust, leaving higher inflation and natural-rate unemployment.

legendary.q: Policy holds unemployment below natural with successive demand expansions. Expected inflation rises each round. The repeated expansions then stop and actual inflation stabilizes at its higher rate. Which subsequent path is consistent with the natural-rate model?
options: A sequence of upward-shifting SRPCs ending back at natural unemployment with higher inflation
One unchanged SRPC delivering permanently lower unemployment after every contract renewal
A leftward LRPC shift caused solely by faster inflation with unchanged labor structure
A downward SRPC shift ending in deflation and a lower natural unemployment rate
legendary.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
legendary.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate. Return to natural is conditional on ending the repeated effort to maintain a surprise.

legendary.q: Economy A lowers its natural rate through better job matching; Economy B only creates an unexpected demand boom. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both economies permanently shift LRPC left because unemployment initially declines
Only Economy B changes long-run unemployment by raising aggregate demand
Neither economy can affect unemployment at either a short or long horizon
A can shift LRPC left; B can only move unemployment below natural temporarily
legendary.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
legendary.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

legendary.q: Inflation expectations instantly match a fully anticipated monetary expansion in the model. What Phillips prediction is most consistent?
options: A rightward LRPC shift from higher money growth and unchanged labor institutions
A guaranteed fall in both inflation and unemployment after expectations adjust
Little or no temporary unemployment movement away from the natural rate
A permanent unemployment decline along the SRPC once nominal spending increases
legendary.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
legendary.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

legendary.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. The economy moves from SRPC1 to SRPC2. Which statement should be rejected?
options: The tradeoff improved because higher inflation now buys lower unemployment at every point.
The tradeoff worsened because inflation is higher at a given unemployment rate.
Expected inflation may have increased and shifted the curve upward.
An adverse supply shock may have raised both inflation pressure and unemployment risk.
legendary.commonError: Calling an upward SRPC shift an improvement.
legendary.feedback: An upward SRPC shift worsens the tradeoff because inflation is higher at the same unemployment rate.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

legendary.q: A policymaker says, 'Inflation is high, so unemployment must be low.' What is the best correction?
options: That only fits demand pressure; supply shocks can raise inflation and unemployment together.
That is always true because the Phillips curve never shifts.
That is false only when M1 is larger than M2.
That is true in the long run because LRPC slopes downward.
legendary.commonError: Treating the Phillips curve as fixed under every shock.
legendary.feedback: The short-run tradeoff can worsen when SRPC shifts up, so inflation and unemployment can rise together.

legendary.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. The economy is on SRPC2 rather than SRPC1. Which conclusion is most careful?
options: The tradeoff worsened, but the cause could be expected inflation or a supply shock.
The tradeoff improved, and policymakers can now lower unemployment without cost.
The LRPC shifted left, so natural unemployment must have fallen.
AD must have shifted right, so SRPC cannot have moved.
legendary.commonError: Assuming every SRPC shift has only one cause.
legendary.feedback: An upward SRPC shift can come from higher expected inflation or an adverse supply shock, and both worsen the tradeoff.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph with SRPC0, SRPC1, A and B. Use the model inflation = expected inflation − 0.6 × (unemployment − 5) + supply offset, with all rates in percent and differences in percentage points. At B the separately measured supply offset is +1.1 points. What expected inflation is consistent with B, and could the graph alone identify that expectation if the supply offset were unknown?
options: Expected inflation is 6 percent; actual inflation equals expectations at every point on an SRPC.
Expected inflation is 5.5 percent; without the supply-offset measurement, only expected inflation plus the offset is identified.
Expected inflation is 6.6 percent; the supply offset can be ignored even though it is positive.
Expected inflation is 4.3 percent; both the unemployment gap and the supply offset must be subtracted from actual inflation.
legendary.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
legendary.feedback: B has unemployment 6 and actual inflation 6. Thus 6 = expected inflation − 0.6 + 1.1, implying expected inflation 5.5. Without the offset measurement the graph identifies only expected inflation + offset = 6.6. The higher curve does not by itself isolate an expectations change.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips graph with two downward-sloping SRPCs, vertical LRPC, and points A and B.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from 0 to 10. Solid blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6), A at (5,3), and (10,0). Dashed purple SRPC1 is parallel above it, running through (0,9.6), B at (6,6), and (10,3.6). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and intersects SRPC0 at A and SRPC1 at inflation 6.6. Dashed guides mark A at (5,3) and B at (6,6).

legendary.q: Refer to the graph with A and B on SRPC0. Initially expected inflation is the inflation rate at A, and the economy is at B. Next period expected inflation equals this period’s actual inflation. Hold the natural rate and supply conditions fixed; each one-point expectations change shifts the SRPC vertically by one point with slope unchanged. Compare keeping unemployment at B’s rate with instead keeping actual inflation at B’s current rate. Which next-period outcome follows?
options: Keeping unemployment at 3 percent requires unchanged 3.5 percent inflation; holding inflation fixed shifts LRPC to 3 percent.
Keeping unemployment at 3 percent requires 4.5 percent inflation; holding inflation at 3.5 percent instead returns unemployment to 5 percent.
Keeping unemployment at 3 percent requires 2.5 percent inflation; holding inflation at 3.5 percent raises unemployment to 7 percent.
Both targets give the same unchanged point B because adaptive expectations cannot shift an SRPC.
legendary.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
legendary.feedback: Expectations rise from 2.5 to 3.5, shifting the curve up one point. At unemployment 3, inflation therefore rises from 3.5 to 4.5. Alternatively, actual inflation equal to the new expectation gives natural unemployment at 5. A fixed unemployment target and a fixed inflation target are different continuations.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through B at (3,3.5) and A at (5,2.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies above and left of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph with B to the right of A on SRPC0. Initially actual inflation is B’s rate and expected inflation is A’s rate. Each period expectations equal the previous period’s actual inflation; each one-point expectations change shifts SRPC vertically by one point with slope unchanged. Natural unemployment and supply conditions stay fixed. Policy holds unemployment at B’s rate for one additional period, then requires inflation to be nonnegative in the following period. What inflation occurs in the additional period, and what is the highest unemployment rate compatible with that later inflation constraint?
options: Inflation stays 1.5 percent, then unemployment can remain at 7 percent.
Inflation is 0.5 percent, then unemployment can remain at 7 percent without deflation.
Inflation is 2.5 percent, then unemployment can be at most 5 percent.
Inflation is 0.5 percent, then unemployment can be at most 6 percent.
legendary.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
legendary.feedback: The plotted slope is (1.5 − 2.5)/(7 − 5) = −0.5. Expectations first fall from 2.5 to 1.5, so holding unemployment at 7 gives inflation 0.5. Next expectations are 0.5; nonnegative inflation requires 0.5 − 0.5 × (unemployment − 5) ≥ 0, or unemployment no greater than 6. Maintaining 7 would instead produce −0.5 percent inflation.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through A at (5,2.5) and B at (7,1.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies below and right of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

legendary.q: A temporary supply disruption raises inflation while existing contracts still reflect the original expected inflation. Wage setters update forecasts using the observed inflation, but the disruption ends before the new contracts take effect. Expected inflation nevertheless remains above its original level. With natural unemployment unchanged, what can be concluded about the final SRPC relative to its original position and its position during the disruption?
options: It must return exactly to its original position because the physical disruption ended.
It must lie above the disruption-period curve because any expectations rise exceeds any removed supply offset.
It must lie below the original curve because the original supply shock was temporary.
It remains above its original position, but its position relative to the disruption-period curve depends on the expectations rise versus the removed supply offset.
legendary.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
legendary.feedback: The original curve has neither the supply offset nor the higher expectation. The final curve retains only the expectation increase, so it is above the original. Comparing it with the disruption-period curve requires the two offset magnitudes. Observed inflation alone does not identify their relative sizes.

legendary.q: Two central banks announce the same lower inflation target. One has a stronger record of meeting targets. Under otherwise similar conditions, what can differ?
options: Actual inflation must reach zero with no output cost
The less credible bank must cause immediate deflation
Expected inflation may fall faster where the announcement is more credible
The natural rate must immediately fall only in the credible economy
legendary.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
legendary.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

legendary.q: Actual inflation is 5% while wage setters expected 3%, temporarily pushing unemployment below natural. What erodes that effect?
options: The price level returns to its initial value automatically
Forecasts adjust upward, shifting the SRPC until unemployment returns toward natural
The LRPC shifts left because actual inflation is above expected
Forecasts adjust downward, moving unemployment farther below natural
legendary.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
legendary.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

legendary.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Compare two disinflations from b to the lower sustained inflation rate I1 with supply conditions and natural unemployment unchanged. In one, existing contracts keep expected inflation at I2 initially. In the other, a credible announcement and immediate contract adjustment lower expected inflation to I1 before spending adjusts. Which pair of paths is consistent with these assumptions?
options: The first can pass through d before c; the second can reach c without the same initial unemployment excursion.
Both must pass through d because credibility cannot change expected inflation before actual inflation falls.
The first reaches c immediately; the second must shift LRPC right before inflation can fall.
Both finish at a because lower inflation permanently lowers natural unemployment.
legendary.commonError: Skipping the short-run unemployment cost of disinflation.
legendary.feedback: With old expectations, lower actual inflation moves b to d along SRPC2 before expectations shift the curve down toward c. If expectations and contracts already incorporate I1, the lower SRPC can support c without that initial gap. Credibility alone would not guarantee this outcome without the stated contract adjustment.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

legendary.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. The economy has moved b to d during disinflation. Inflation is then held at I1, the natural rate stays U2, and the adverse-supply offset is unchanged. A forecast shows unemployment returning to U2. Which evidence is necessary to reconcile this forecast with the diagram?
options: Expected inflation must fall enough to place an SRPC through c; contraction along unchanged SRPC2 would leave unemployment at d.
Expected inflation must rise enough to place an SRPC above SRPC2 while actual inflation remains I1.
The return requires moving from d to b along unchanged SRPC2 while inflation remains I1.
The return requires LRPC to shift right to U3 even though the natural rate stays U2.
legendary.commonError: Missing the expectation adjustment needed after disinflation.
legendary.feedback: At I1 the original SRPC2 locates d, not c. With natural unemployment and the supply offset fixed, a lower expected-inflation schedule is needed to reach c at U2. A forecast of unemployment recovery is therefore conditional on the expected-inflation adjustment, not just continued contraction.
legendary.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

legendary.q: Country A has a sacrifice ratio of 2, while Country B has a sacrifice ratio of 5. If both reduce inflation by 3 percentage points, which comparison is correct?
options: A loses about 15% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 6%.
Both lose about 3% of annual GDP because the inflation reduction is equal.
A loses about 6% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 15%.
A has no output loss because its sacrifice ratio is below the inflation reduction.
legendary.commonError: Reversing the sacrifice ratios or treating equal inflation reductions as equal output costs.
legendary.feedback: Cumulative output loss equals the sacrifice ratio times the inflation reduction: 2 × 3 = 6 for A and 5 × 3 = 15 for B.

legendary.q: A credible central bank announces a lower inflation target, expected inflation falls partly, and policy still contracts demand. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: The downward SRPC shift may reduce but need not eliminate the short-run output cost
Credibility guarantees unemployment never rises during the contractionary adjustment
The LRPC shifts left because the announced target permanently lowers natural unemployment
Disinflation necessarily becomes deflation before expected inflation can decline
legendary.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
legendary.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

legendary.q: Inflation falls 3 points while cumulative output loss equals 6% of annual GDP. Unemployment later returns to natural. Which synthesis is correct?
options: The sacrifice ratio is 0.5, and unemployment stays permanently high
The ratio is 3, and LRPC shifts right permanently
The ratio is 6, and the price level must have fallen
The sacrifice ratio is 2, and the unemployment cost was temporary in the model
legendary.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendary.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendary.q: An adverse supply shock has raised inflation and unemployment. Why can disinflation policy face a harder near-term tradeoff than after a demand boom?
options: The LRPC becomes downward sloping during supply shocks
Contraction shifts the SRPC downward with no demand effect
Contraction can lower inflation pressure while worsening an already weak output position
Supply shocks automatically lower the sacrifice ratio to zero
legendary.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
legendary.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

legendary.q: A disinflation lowers inflation from 10 percent to 6 percent. Cumulative output loss is 18 percent of one year’s potential GDP, of which 11 percent occurred before the final year. An analyst reports a sacrifice ratio using only the final-year loss. Which audit correction is needed?
options: Use all 18 percent: the ratio is 4.5; using only the final year would understate it as 1.75.
Use only 7 percent: the ratio is 1.75 because earlier output losses are already over.
Use the final inflation rate: the ratio is 3 because the target is 6 percent.
Add initial and final inflation: the ratio is 1.125 because the full window contains both rates.
legendary.commonError: Dividing by the wrong inflation change.
legendary.feedback: The inflation reduction is 4 percentage points. Cumulative loss gives 18/4 = 4.5. Final-year loss is 18 − 11 = 7, giving 7/4 = 1.75 if earlier losses are wrongly omitted. Returning toward potential does not erase earlier lost production.

legendary.q: A plan must reduce inflation by 5 percentage points with cumulative output loss no greater than 14 percent of one year’s potential GDP. Its first stage has already reduced inflation by 2 percentage points at a cumulative loss of 7 percent. What maximum sacrifice ratio can the remaining stage have if the full plan is to meet both targets?
options: About 2.33 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
2.8 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
3.5 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
7 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
legendary.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
legendary.feedback: There are 3 inflation points and 7 percent of output-loss allowance remaining. The remaining-stage ceiling is 7/3 = 2.333..., about 2.33. Applying the overall allowance ratio 14/5 = 2.8 to the remaining stage would exceed the total loss limit because the first stage used more loss per point.

legendary.q: A disinflation lowers inflation from 9 percent to 5 percent with cumulative output loss of 10 percent of one year’s potential GDP. A second plan is projected to lower inflation by only 2.5 percentage points with loss of 7 percent on the same output benchmark. Which comparison avoids confusing a smaller total loss with a lower loss per inflation point?
options: The completed plan has ratio 2.5 versus 2.8 for the second; the second has less total loss but a higher loss per point.
The second plan has the lower ratio because 7 is less than 10, regardless of the inflation reductions.
Both have ratio 2.5 because the second plan’s inflation reduction is its denominator and also its ratio.
The completed plan has ratio 0.4 and therefore no output cost; the second has ratio 2.8.
legendary.commonError: Using the ending inflation rate instead of the inflation reduction.
legendary.feedback: The completed reduction is 9 − 5 = 4 points, so 10/4 = 2.5. The second ratio is 7/2.5 = 2.8. A lower cumulative cost can accompany a higher per-point cost when the inflation reductions differ; neither statistic alone proves a universally better policy.

legendary.q: Two stages jointly reduce inflation by 6 percentage points with a combined sacrifice ratio of 1.75. The first stage loses 3 percent of one year’s potential GDP while reducing inflation by 2 percentage points. Use the same output benchmark for both stages. What is the second-stage ratio, and how does it compare with the first?
options: 1.875 for the second versus 1.5 for the first; the second has the higher loss per point.
1.75 for both stages, because a combined ratio must equal each stage’s ratio.
3.75 for the second versus 1.5 for the first, using only 2 remaining inflation points.
0.533 for the second versus 0.667 for the first, using inflation reduction divided by loss.
legendary.commonError: Adding the inflation reduction and sacrifice ratio.
legendary.feedback: Total loss is 6 × 1.75 = 10.5 percent. The second stage accounts for 10.5 − 3 = 7.5 percent loss and 6 − 2 = 4 inflation points, giving 1.875. The first-stage ratio is 3/2 = 1.5. The combined ratio is weighted by the reductions, not a mandate for equal stage ratios.

legendary.q: A three-year disinflation produces annual output gaps of −2%, −1%, and 0%, cutting inflation from 6.5% to 4.5%. A faster path produces one year at −4% and cuts inflation the same amount. Which comparison is correct?
options: The gradual path ratio is 3; the fast path ratio is 4
Both paths have a ratio of 2
The gradual path ratio is 2; the fast path ratio is 1.5
The gradual path ratio is 1.5; the fast path ratio is 2
legendary.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendary.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendary.q: Economy A loses 8% of one year’s GDP while inflation falls from 9% to 5%. Economy B loses 6% while inflation falls from 5% to 2%. What can be concluded?
options: A has a ratio of 0.5 and B has a ratio of 0.67
A has a lower ratio because its inflation drop is larger
A has a ratio of 2 and B also has a ratio of 2
A has a ratio of 4 and B has a ratio of 3
legendary.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendary.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

easyBoss.q: On a given SRPC, which combination lies farther up and left?
options: Higher inflation and higher unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment
Higher inflation and lower unemployment
Lower inflation and higher unemployment
easyBoss.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
easyBoss.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

easyBoss.q: Expected inflation is unchanged and aggregate demand falls. What happens first?
options: The economy moves up and left along its SRPC
The economy moves down and right along its SRPC
The SRPC shifts upward at every unemployment rate
The LRPC shifts left of the natural rate
easyBoss.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.
easyBoss.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.

easyBoss.q: Which event most directly shifts rather than moves along the SRPC?
options: A change in expected inflation
An unexpected change in aggregate demand
A temporary change in real spending
A movement between two points on one curve
easyBoss.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
easyBoss.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

easyBoss.q: At what unemployment rate is the LRPC located?
options: The cyclical unemployment rate alone
The natural rate
Zero unemployment
The current inflation rate
easyBoss.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
easyBoss.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

options: Expected inflation adjusts in the long run
Aggregate demand never changes output even temporarily
Inflation must remain constant at every natural-rate point
Unemployment cannot change during a short-run demand surprise
easyBoss.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
easyBoss.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

easyBoss.q: Which event can shift the LRPC?
options: A one-time surprise demand expansion with fixed expectations
A movement along the current SRPC after demand changes
A temporary inflation forecast error in wage contracts
A structural change in the natural rate
easyBoss.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
easyBoss.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

easyBoss.q: If expected inflation increases, which SRPC change follows?
options: An upward shift
A downward shift
Only movement down the same curve
A horizontal LRPC shift
easyBoss.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
easyBoss.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

easyBoss.q: If expected inflation decreases, which SRPC change follows?
options: An upward shift
Only movement up the same curve
A vertical AD shift
A downward shift
easyBoss.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
easyBoss.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

easyBoss.q: Why can actual inflation above expected inflation temporarily reduce unemployment?
options: Higher inflation permanently raises labor productivity
The LRPC becomes downward sloping
Some wages and prices were set using the lower forecast
The natural rate immediately becomes lower
easyBoss.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
easyBoss.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

easyBoss.q: Inflation drops from 5% to 2% while prices still rise. What is occurring?
options: A permanent output boom
Disinflation
Deflation
A price-level collapse
easyBoss.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
easyBoss.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

easyBoss.q: Which policy direction normally lowers aggregate demand to pursue disinflation?
options: Contractionary policy
Expansionary policy
A permanent supply restriction
A higher inflation target
easyBoss.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
easyBoss.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

easyBoss.q: What is the usual short-run Phillips cost of disinflation?
options: Lower unemployment while inflation falls
Permanently higher natural unemployment
Higher inflation with higher output
Higher unemployment while inflation falls
easyBoss.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
easyBoss.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

easyBoss.q: Which formula states the sacrifice ratio?
options: Price-level decline over the episode ÷ nominal GDP growth
Cumulative output loss ÷ inflation reduction in percentage points
Inflation reduction in points ÷ cumulative output loss relative to potential
Permanent unemployment increase ÷ the final positive inflation rate
easyBoss.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
easyBoss.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

easyBoss.q: Inflation falls from 6% to 4%. What is the denominator?
options: 2 percentage points
4 percent
6 percent
10 percentage points
easyBoss.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
easyBoss.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

easyBoss.q: A ratio of 2 is best read as what?
options: Inflation falls two percent for every percentage point of unemployment added
Unemployment stays two points above natural after expectations completely adjust
The price level declines two percent in each year of disinflation
Two percent of one year’s output lost per inflation point reduced
easyBoss.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
easyBoss.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing the Phillips curve with the AD-AS model.
mediumBoss.q: What does the short-run Phillips curve show?
options: A short-run tradeoff between inflation and unemployment
A long-run tradeoff between inflation and output
A fixed relationship between money supply and GDP
A direct measure of government spending
mediumBoss.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows that lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation, and higher unemployment is associated with lower inflation.

mediumBoss.q: Expansionary policy raises aggregate demand. In the short run, what Phillips curve movement should follow?
options: Lower inflation and higher unemployment
Higher inflation and lower unemployment
Higher inflation and higher unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment
mediumBoss.feedback: Expansionary policy raises AD, which can lower unemployment but raises inflation in the short run.

mediumBoss.q: Aggregate demand contracts unexpectedly while expected inflation is initially fixed. What short-run Phillips-curve movement is most likely?
options: Toward lower inflation and higher unemployment.
Toward higher inflation and lower unemployment.
The entire SRPC shifts up-right immediately.
Unemployment stays fixed at the natural rate in the short run.
mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing a demand-driven movement along the SRPC with a shift of the curve.
mediumBoss.feedback: An unexpected demand contraction moves the economy down and right along the current SRPC.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing the short-run and long-run Phillips curves.
mediumBoss.q: What does the vertical long-run Phillips curve represent?
options: The natural rate of unemployment
The current inflation rate
The money supply target
The sacrifice ratio
mediumBoss.feedback: The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

mediumBoss.commonError: Reading the natural rate from the wrong point.
mediumBoss.q: On the graph, where does the LRPC identify the natural rate of unemployment?
options: U1
U2
U3
I2
mediumBoss.feedback: The LRPC is drawn at U2, so U2 is the natural rate of unemployment.

mediumBoss.q: Unemployment is below natural and actual inflation exceeds expected inflation. What long-run adjustment follows?
options: Expected inflation falls and SRPC shifts downward
Natural unemployment disappears as inflation continues
Expected inflation rises and unemployment returns toward natural
LRPC shifts left and locks in the lower unemployment
mediumBoss.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
mediumBoss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

mediumBoss.commonError: Treating expected inflation as movement along the same SRPC.
mediumBoss.q: What happens to the short-run Phillips curve when expected inflation rises?
options: It shifts downward
It shifts upward
It becomes horizontal
It becomes the money demand curve
mediumBoss.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the short-run Phillips curve upward.

mediumBoss.commonError: Keeping unemployment below natural forever after an inflation surprise.
mediumBoss.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at c, expansionary policy moves the economy to a. After expected inflation rises, where does the economy move?
options: b
c
d
U1
mediumBoss.feedback: After expected inflation rises, the SRPC shifts up and the economy moves to b at the natural rate of unemployment.

Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

mediumBoss.q: A sharp oil-price increase raises firms’ costs. What happens to the short-run Phillips curve, other things equal?
options: It shifts down and to the left.
The economy only moves along an unchanged curve.
It shifts up and to the right.
It becomes vertical at zero unemployment.
mediumBoss.commonError: Treating an adverse supply shock as a movement along a fixed SRPC.
mediumBoss.feedback: An adverse supply shock can raise both inflation and unemployment, shifting the SRPC up-right.

mediumBoss.commonError: Ignoring the short-run unemployment cost of reducing inflation.
mediumBoss.q: What does contractionary monetary policy do on the short-run Phillips curve?
options: It lowers inflation but raises unemployment in the short run
It raises inflation and lowers unemployment in the short run
It lowers both inflation and unemployment immediately
It raises both inflation and unemployment immediately
mediumBoss.feedback: Contractionary monetary policy can reduce inflation, but it usually raises unemployment temporarily.

mediumBoss.commonError: Skipping the short-run move before expectations adjust.
mediumBoss.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at b, the Fed reduces inflation below expectations. Where does the economy move in the short run?
options: a
c
d
U2
mediumBoss.feedback: Starting at b, lower actual inflation moves the economy to d: lower inflation and higher unemployment.
