sacrifice-ratio.title: Sacrifice Ratio
sacrifice-ratio.description: Calculate and interpret output losses associated with disinflation.

easy.q: The sacrifice ratio measures the output cost of reducing:
options: Inflation
Unemployment
Money demand
Imports
easy.commonError: Confusing sacrifice ratio with unemployment rate.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures how much output is lost when inflation is reduced.

easy.q: Credible anti-inflation policy can reduce the sacrifice ratio by causing expected inflation to:
options: Rise faster
Fall faster
Stay above actual inflation forever
Turn into unemployment
easy.commonError: Ignoring expectations in disinflation.
easy.feedback: If expected inflation falls faster, the short-run cost of disinflation can be smaller.

easy.q: What does a sacrifice ratio of 3 mean?
options: About 3% of one year’s output is lost per 1-percentage-point inflation reduction
Inflation falls 3% whenever output falls 1%
Unemployment rises 3 percentage points permanently
The price level falls 3% during every disinflation
easy.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

easy.q: An analyst divides output loss by the final 4% inflation rate after inflation began at 7%. What denominator should replace 4%?
options: The initial 7% inflation rate before policy
The 11% sum of the two inflation rates
The final 4% inflation rate already used
The 3-percentage-point reduction in inflation
easy.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
easy.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

easy.q: Which loss belongs in the usual sacrifice-ratio numerator?
options: The total fall in the price level
The final year’s inflation rate
Cumulative output lost relative to potential during disinflation
The permanent increase in the unemployment rate
easy.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

easy.q: A disinflation has a lower sacrifice ratio than another. Under comparable measurement, what does that indicate?
options: A higher inflation target after policy ends
Less cumulative output loss per inflation point reduced
A larger fall in the price level
A permanently higher natural unemployment rate
easy.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

medium.q: If expected inflation falls quickly after a credible policy announcement, the sacrifice ratio is likely to be:
options: Lower
Higher
Unchanged by expectations
Equal to M1
medium.commonError: Ignoring credibility and expectations.
medium.feedback: Faster adjustment of expected inflation reduces the output cost of disinflation.

medium.q: Cumulative output loss is 12% of one year’s GDP while inflation falls 3 percentage points. What is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 4% of one year’s output per inflation point
3% of output per inflation point
9% of output per inflation point
36% of output per inflation point
medium.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
medium.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

medium.q: A planned inflation reduction is 2.5 percentage points and the estimated sacrifice ratio is 3. What cumulative output loss is implied?
options: 1.2% of one year’s output
5.5% of one year’s output
8.3% of one year’s output
7.5% of one year’s output
medium.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
medium.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

medium.q: The output gap is −1.5% in year one and −2.5% in year two while inflation falls 2 percentage points. Using the sum of annual gaps, what is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 4% of output per inflation point
8% of output per inflation point
2% of one year’s output per inflation point
1% of output per inflation point
medium.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
medium.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

medium.q: Inflation declines from 8% to 5%. Which calculation uses the correct denominator?
options: Final output divided by 13 percentage points
Cumulative output loss divided by 3 percentage points
Cumulative output loss divided by the final 5%
Cumulative output loss divided by the initial 8%
medium.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
medium.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

medium.q: Path A loses 6% of one year’s output to cut inflation 3 points. Path B loses 5% to cut inflation 2 points. Which has the lower sacrifice ratio?
options: Path A has a ratio of 2; Path B has a ratio of 2.5
Path B has a ratio of 2; Path A has a ratio of 2.5
Both paths have a sacrifice ratio of 2
Path A has a ratio of 3; Path B has a ratio of 2
medium.commonError: Compares total losses without dividing each by its own inflation-point reduction.
medium.feedback: Path A: 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Path B: 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5, so Path A has the lower sacrifice ratio.

hard.q: A credible disinflation lowers expected inflation before unemployment rises much. What happens to the sacrifice ratio?
options: It falls
It rises
It becomes infinite
It equals MPC
hard.commonError: Ignoring credibility in disinflation costs.
hard.feedback: Credibility lowers expected inflation faster and can reduce the output cost of disinflation.

hard.q: A student says disinflation has no cost if the Fed announces it. What is the correction?
options: Credibility can lower the cost, not guarantee zero cost
Announcements always raise inflation first
The sacrifice ratio ignores expectations
Unemployment must fall during disinflation
hard.commonError: Overstating credibility effects.
hard.feedback: Credibility can reduce the sacrifice ratio, but it does not automatically make disinflation costless.

hard.q: Potential GDP remains $500 billion in each of the three years. Output is 2% below potential for one year and 1% below for two more years while inflation falls 4 points. What is the loss per inflation point?
options: $2.5 billion per inflation point
$10 billion per inflation point
$20 billion per inflation point
$5 billion per inflation point
hard.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
hard.feedback: The cumulative loss is $10 billion + $5 billion + $5 billion = $20 billion; $20 billion ÷ 4 = $5 billion per inflation point.

hard.q: A disinflation creates cumulative output loss equal to 9% of annual GDP. If the sacrifice ratio is 3, how far did inflation fall?
options: 6 percentage points
27 percentage points
3 percentage points
2 percentage points
hard.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
hard.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

hard.q: Real GDP growth slows from 4% to 1%, but output remains above potential. Why can the 3-point growth slowdown not automatically be the sacrifice-ratio numerator?
options: Only the final inflation rate belongs in the numerator of this measure
The numerator measures an output-level loss relative to a benchmark, not merely slower growth
Any growth slowdown is exactly the cumulative output gap relative to potential
The numerator must be a permanent unemployment-rate change rather than output
hard.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
hard.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

hard.q: Cumulative output loss is 6.5% of one year’s GDP and inflation falls 3 percentage points. Round the sacrifice ratio to two decimals.
options: 2.17% of one year’s output per inflation point
2.16% of output per inflation point
2.20% of output per inflation point
3.50% of output per inflation point
hard.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
hard.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

elite.q: The Fed announces disinflation, but workers doubt it and expected inflation stays high. What happens to the sacrifice ratio?
options: It is likely higher
It is automatically zero
It becomes the MPC
It shifts LRAS right
elite.commonError: Assuming announcements alone make policy credible.
elite.feedback: If expected inflation does not fall quickly, reducing actual inflation tends to require more output loss.

elite.q: If inflation falls from 12 percent to 7 percent and the sacrifice ratio is 3.5, output loss equals:
options: 17.5 percent of one year's output
15.5 percent of one year's output
8.5 percent of one year's output
5 percent of one year's output
elite.commonError: Adding the sacrifice ratio to the inflation reduction.
elite.feedback: Inflation falls by 5 points, so output loss is 3.5 x 5 = 17.5 percent of one year's output.

elite.q: If cumulative output loss is 14 percent of one year’s potential GDP and inflation falls by 4 percentage points, the sacrifice ratio is:
options: 3.5% of one year’s output per inflation point
4% of one year’s output per inflation point
10% of one year’s output per inflation point
18% of one year’s output per inflation point
elite.commonError: Uses the inflation change or output loss alone rather than dividing cumulative loss by the percentage-point reduction.
elite.feedback: Divide the 14% cumulative output loss by the 4-percentage-point inflation reduction: 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5% of one year’s output per point.

elite.q: A disinflation plan is credible, wage contracts adjust quickly, and expected inflation falls fast. Which path is most likely?
options: Smaller unemployment increase for the same inflation reduction
Larger unemployment increase for the same inflation reduction
No change in expected inflation despite credibility
Permanent unemployment below natural
elite.commonError: Ignoring expectations in sacrifice-ratio logic.
elite.feedback: Credibility and fast expectation adjustment reduce the output and unemployment cost of lowering inflation.

elite.q: A disinflation plan lacks credibility, wage contracts are slow, and expected inflation remains high. Which path is most likely?
options: Larger output loss for the same inflation reduction
Smaller output loss for the same inflation reduction
Immediate movement to lower unemployment
LRPC becomes downward sloping
elite.commonError: Assuming disinflation costs vanish without credibility.
elite.feedback: If expected inflation stays high, lowering actual inflation usually requires a larger output loss.

legendary.q: A disinflation lowers inflation from 10 percent to 6 percent. Cumulative output loss is 18 percent of one year’s potential GDP, of which 11 percent occurred before the final year. An analyst reports a sacrifice ratio using only the final-year loss. Which audit correction is needed?
options: Use all 18 percent: the ratio is 4.5; using only the final year would understate it as 1.75.
Use only 7 percent: the ratio is 1.75 because earlier output losses are already over.
Use the final inflation rate: the ratio is 3 because the target is 6 percent.
Add initial and final inflation: the ratio is 1.125 because the full window contains both rates.
legendary.commonError: Dividing by the wrong inflation change.
legendary.feedback: The inflation reduction is 4 percentage points. Cumulative loss gives 18/4 = 4.5. Final-year loss is 18 − 11 = 7, giving 7/4 = 1.75 if earlier losses are wrongly omitted. Returning toward potential does not erase earlier lost production.

legendary.q: A plan must reduce inflation by 5 percentage points with cumulative output loss no greater than 14 percent of one year’s potential GDP. Its first stage has already reduced inflation by 2 percentage points at a cumulative loss of 7 percent. What maximum sacrifice ratio can the remaining stage have if the full plan is to meet both targets?
options: About 2.33 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
2.8 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
3.5 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
7 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
legendary.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
legendary.feedback: There are 3 inflation points and 7 percent of output-loss allowance remaining. The remaining-stage ceiling is 7/3 = 2.333..., about 2.33. Applying the overall allowance ratio 14/5 = 2.8 to the remaining stage would exceed the total loss limit because the first stage used more loss per point.

legendary.q: A disinflation lowers inflation from 9 percent to 5 percent with cumulative output loss of 10 percent of one year’s potential GDP. A second plan is projected to lower inflation by only 2.5 percentage points with loss of 7 percent on the same output benchmark. Which comparison avoids confusing a smaller total loss with a lower loss per inflation point?
options: The completed plan has ratio 2.5 versus 2.8 for the second; the second has less total loss but a higher loss per point.
The second plan has the lower ratio because 7 is less than 10, regardless of the inflation reductions.
Both have ratio 2.5 because the second plan’s inflation reduction is its denominator and also its ratio.
The completed plan has ratio 0.4 and therefore no output cost; the second has ratio 2.8.
legendary.commonError: Using the ending inflation rate instead of the inflation reduction.
legendary.feedback: The completed reduction is 9 − 5 = 4 points, so 10/4 = 2.5. The second ratio is 7/2.5 = 2.8. A lower cumulative cost can accompany a higher per-point cost when the inflation reductions differ; neither statistic alone proves a universally better policy.

legendary.q: Two stages jointly reduce inflation by 6 percentage points with a combined sacrifice ratio of 1.75. The first stage loses 3 percent of one year’s potential GDP while reducing inflation by 2 percentage points. Use the same output benchmark for both stages. What is the second-stage ratio, and how does it compare with the first?
options: 1.875 for the second versus 1.5 for the first; the second has the higher loss per point.
1.75 for both stages, because a combined ratio must equal each stage’s ratio.
3.75 for the second versus 1.5 for the first, using only 2 remaining inflation points.
0.533 for the second versus 0.667 for the first, using inflation reduction divided by loss.
legendary.commonError: Adding the inflation reduction and sacrifice ratio.
legendary.feedback: Total loss is 6 × 1.75 = 10.5 percent. The second stage accounts for 10.5 − 3 = 7.5 percent loss and 6 − 2 = 4 inflation points, giving 1.875. The first-stage ratio is 3/2 = 1.5. The combined ratio is weighted by the reductions, not a mandate for equal stage ratios.

legendary.q: A three-year disinflation produces annual output gaps of −2%, −1%, and 0%, cutting inflation from 6.5% to 4.5%. A faster path produces one year at −4% and cuts inflation the same amount. Which comparison is correct?
options: The gradual path ratio is 3; the fast path ratio is 4
Both paths have a ratio of 2
The gradual path ratio is 2; the fast path ratio is 1.5
The gradual path ratio is 1.5; the fast path ratio is 2
legendary.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendary.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendary.q: Economy A loses 8% of one year’s GDP while inflation falls from 9% to 5%. Economy B loses 6% while inflation falls from 5% to 2%. What can be concluded?
options: A has a ratio of 0.5 and B has a ratio of 0.67
A has a lower ratio because its inflation drop is larger
A has a ratio of 2 and B also has a ratio of 2
A has a ratio of 4 and B has a ratio of 3
legendary.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendary.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

calculation.q: If the sacrifice ratio is 4 and inflation falls by 2 percentage points, the output cost is:
options: 2 percent of one year's output
4 percent of one year's output
8 percent of one year's output
16 percent of one year's output
calculation.feedback: The output cost is 4 x 2 = 8 percent of one year's output.

calculation.q: Potential GDP is $400 billion. Cumulative output loss is $24 billion while inflation falls from 8% to 5%. What is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 3% of output per inflation point
6% of output per inflation point
8% of output per inflation point
2% of one year’s output per inflation point
calculation.commonError: Divides the dollar loss directly by the inflation change without converting loss to a share of potential output.
calculation.feedback: The $24 billion loss is 6% of $400 billion. Inflation falls 3 percentage points, so the ratio is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

calculation.q: If inflation falls by 3 points and the output loss is 12 percent of one year’s GDP, the sacrifice ratio is:
options: 12% of one year’s output per inflation point
4% of one year’s output per inflation point
3% of one year’s output per inflation point
9% of one year’s output per inflation point
calculation.commonError: Uses the inflation reduction or cumulative output loss alone rather than dividing loss by points reduced.
calculation.feedback: Divide cumulative output loss by the inflation reduction: 12 ÷ 3 = 4% of one year’s output per inflation point.

calculation.q: If the sacrifice ratio is 3 and inflation falls from 8 percent to 5 percent, the output cost is:
options: 3 percent of one year's output
6 percent of one year's output
9 percent of one year's output
15 percent of one year's output
calculation.feedback: Inflation falls by 3 percentage points, so output loss is 3 x 3 = 9 percent of one year's output.

boss.commonError: Confusing the sacrifice ratio with the inflation rate itself.
boss.q: What does the sacrifice ratio measure?
options: The output cost of reducing inflation
The unemployment rate at zero inflation
The money multiplier after disinflation
The tax increase needed to raise AD
boss.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures the output cost of reducing inflation.

boss.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
boss.q: Inflation falls by 3 percentage points. If the sacrifice ratio is 4, what output loss should be expected?
options: 7 percent of one year's output
12 percent of one year's output
3 percent of one year's output
4 percent of one year's output
boss.feedback: Output loss equals sacrifice ratio times inflation reduction, so 4 x 3 = 12 percent of one year's output.

boss.q: Which formula states the sacrifice ratio?
options: Price-level decline over the episode ÷ nominal GDP growth
Cumulative output loss ÷ inflation reduction in percentage points
Inflation reduction in points ÷ cumulative output loss relative to potential
Permanent unemployment increase ÷ the final positive inflation rate
boss.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
boss.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

boss.q: Inflation falls from 6% to 4%. What is the denominator?
options: 2 percentage points
4 percent
6 percent
10 percentage points
boss.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
boss.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

boss.q: A ratio of 2 is best read as what?
options: Inflation falls two percent for every percentage point of unemployment added
Unemployment stays two points above natural after expectations completely adjust
The price level declines two percent in each year of disinflation
Two percent of one year’s output lost per inflation point reduced
boss.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
boss.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

boss.q: Use the sum of annual percentage output shortfalls as the cumulative-loss convention. Annual output gaps are −1%, −2%, and −1%; inflation falls from 7% to 5%. What is the ratio?
options: 6% of output per inflation point
2% of one year’s output per inflation point
0.5% of output per inflation point
3% of output per inflation point
boss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
boss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

boss.q: A report divides cumulative output loss by the final inflation rate. What correction is required?
options: Divide by the percentage-point reduction in inflation
Divide by the initial inflation rate before the policy began
Multiply by the final inflation rate
Use the permanent unemployment rate
boss.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
boss.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

boss.q: Path X loses 7.2% of annual GDP to reduce inflation 3 points. Path Y loses 5% to reduce inflation 2 points. Which is more output-efficient?
options: Path Y, with a ratio of 2 versus 2.4
Path X, with a ratio of 3 versus 2
They are equal because both lower inflation
Path X, with a ratio of 2.4 versus 2.5
boss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
boss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

boss.q: Loss is 10% of annual GDP and inflation falls 4 points. What is the ratio?
options: 4% of output per inflation point
14% of output per inflation point
2.5% of one year’s output per inflation point
1.5% of output per inflation point
boss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
boss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendaryBoss.q: A two-year policy creates output gaps of −2.4% and −1.8%, lowering inflation from 7.0% to 5.2%. Round the sacrifice ratio to two decimals.
options: 2.34% of output per inflation point
4.20% of output per inflation point
2.33% of one year’s output per inflation point
1.80% of output per inflation point
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendaryBoss.q: A credible plan lowers expected inflation and produces a 3% cumulative output loss for a 2-point inflation reduction. A less credible plan loses 7.5% for a 3-point reduction. Which comparison is correct?
options: The plans are equal because both reduce inflation
The credible plan ratio is 1.5; the other is 2.5
The credible plan ratio is 2; the other is 2.5
The credible plan ratio is 0.67; the other is 0.4
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendaryBoss.q: Potential output remains $800 billion each year. Actual output is below potential by 1.5% for two years and 0.5% for one year while inflation falls 2.8 points. What is cumulative loss per inflation point?
options: $10 billion per inflation point
$4 billion per inflation point
$14 billion per inflation point
$28 billion per inflation point
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The cumulative loss is 3.5% of $800 billion = $28 billion. Dividing by 2.8 inflation points gives $10 billion per point.
legendaryBoss.roundingRule: Report the exact dollar amount per inflation point.

repairQuestions.q: Inflation falls from 8% to 5%. What number belongs in the sacrifice-ratio denominator?
options: 3 percentage points
5 percent
8 percent
13 percentage points
repairQuestions.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.

repairQuestions.q: Should annual output gaps be added before calculating a multi-year sacrifice ratio?
options: No, only the worst year counts
No, only the final year counts
Yes, but add inflation rates too
Yes, to obtain cumulative output loss
repairQuestions.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.
repairQuestions.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.

repairQuestions.q: Does the sacrifice ratio normally measure an unemployment increase per inflation point?
options: Yes, but only when inflation stays positive
No, it measures the fall in the price level
No, it measures cumulative output loss per inflation point
Yes, unemployment is always the numerator
repairQuestions.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.

bridgeQuestions.q: The economy temporarily moves above natural unemployment during disinflation. How is this cost measured?
options: Sum the output losses and divide by the inflation-point reduction
Divide the unemployment increase by the final positive inflation rate
Treat the change in the price level as the cumulative output numerator
Shift LRPC right by the cumulative inflation reduction during policy
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.

bridgeQuestions.q: Expected inflation falls faster after a credible announcement. How can that connect to the sacrifice ratio?
options: A lower final inflation rate automatically raises the ratio even with unchanged loss
Credibility changes the denominator from inflation reduction to unemployment
The ratio must become zero in every credible disinflation plan
A smaller cumulative output loss can lower the measured ratio
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Two disinflation paths reach the same inflation target. Which family destination uses their sacrifice ratios to compare costs?
options: GDP component classification
Bank reserve accounting
Disinflation and policy
Short-run curve axis reading
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.

short-run-phillips-curve.title: Short-Run Phillips Curve
short-run-phillips-curve.description: Interpret movements along the short-run inflation–unemployment tradeoff.

easy.q: The Phillips curve shows a short-run trade-off between:
options: Inflation and unemployment
Taxes and spending
Money supply and money demand
Imports and exports
easy.commonError: Confusing the Phillips curve with the money market.
easy.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows a trade-off between inflation and unemployment.

easy.q: In the standard Phillips-curve convention, the vertical axis measures:
options: Unemployment rate
Inflation rate
Real GDP
Money supply
easy.commonError: Reversing the Phillips curve axes.
easy.feedback: The vertical axis measures the inflation rate.

easy.q: In the standard Phillips-curve convention, the horizontal axis measures:
options: Inflation rate
Price level
Unemployment rate
Money demand
easy.commonError: Reversing the Phillips curve axes.
easy.feedback: The horizontal axis measures the unemployment rate.

easy.q: In the short run, expansionary policy usually moves the economy toward:
options: Higher inflation and lower unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment
Higher unemployment and lower inflation
No change in either variable
easy.commonError: Missing the short-run tradeoff.
easy.feedback: Expansionary policy raises inflation pressure and lowers unemployment in the short run.

easy.q: In the short run, contractionary policy usually moves the economy toward:
options: Higher inflation and lower unemployment
Lower inflation and higher unemployment
Higher inflation and higher unemployment
Lower unemployment and higher output
easy.commonError: Reversing contractionary policy effects.
easy.feedback: Contractionary policy lowers inflation but raises unemployment in the short run.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Point a has:
options: Lower unemployment and higher inflation than point c
Higher unemployment and lower inflation than point c
The same unemployment and lower inflation than point c
No inflation
easy.commonError: Reading the Phillips curve axes backward.
easy.feedback: Point a is at U1 and I2, while point c is at U2 and I1.
easy.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from point c to point a shows:
options: Lower inflation and higher unemployment
Higher inflation and lower unemployment
Higher inflation and higher unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment
easy.commonError: Reversing movement along SRPC.
easy.feedback: Moving from c to a raises inflation and lowers unemployment in the short run.
easy.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

easy.q: In the long run, unemployment returns to:
options: The natural rate
Zero
The inflation rate
The money multiplier
easy.commonError: Thinking policymakers can permanently hold unemployment below natural.
easy.feedback: The natural-rate hypothesis says unemployment returns to its natural rate in the long run.

easy.q: At point A, what is the unemployment rate?
options: 2.5 percent
8 percent
5 percent
10 percent
easy.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
easy.feedback: Point A lies directly above 5 on the unemployment axis.
easy.imageAlt: Phillips graph with downward SRPC0, vertical LRPC, and their intersection A.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from −2.5 to 10. Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6.5), A at (5,2.5), and (10,−1.5). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5. Dashed guides from A mark 5 on the horizontal axis and 2.5 on the vertical axis.

easy.q: Relative to point A, what does point B show on SRPC0?
options: Lower unemployment and higher inflation
Higher unemployment and lower inflation
Lower unemployment and lower inflation
Higher unemployment and higher inflation
easy.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
easy.feedback: Point B is left of A on the unemployment axis and above A on the inflation axis.
easy.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through B at (3,3.5) and A at (5,2.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies above and left of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

easy.q: How does point B compare with the natural-rate point A in the displayed Phillips-curve graph?
options: Lower unemployment and higher inflation
Higher unemployment and higher inflation
Higher unemployment and lower inflation
Lower unemployment and lower inflation
easy.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
easy.feedback: Point B is to the right of A on the unemployment axis and below A on the inflation axis.
easy.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through A at (5,2.5) and B at (7,1.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies below and right of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

medium.q: The short-run Phillips curve slopes downward because higher AD tends to:
options: Raise output, lower unemployment, and raise inflation
Lower output, lower unemployment, and lower inflation
Raise unemployment while lowering inflation forever
Shift LRPC left immediately
medium.commonError: Missing the AD-to-unemployment channel.
medium.feedback: Higher AD raises output and prices, which maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation.

medium.q: Why is there no permanent Phillips-curve tradeoff?
options: Expectations adjust; unemployment returns to normal
Money demand becomes zero
AD stops affecting the short run
Inflation cannot change wages
medium.commonError: Treating the short-run tradeoff as permanent.
medium.feedback: Once expectations adjust, unemployment returns to the natural rate.

medium.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point c, expansionary policy that raises inflation above expectations moves the economy to:
options: a
b
c
d
medium.commonError: Moving to the long-run point immediately.
medium.feedback: Expansionary policy moves the economy along SRPC1 from c to a: higher inflation and lower unemployment.
medium.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Policy shifts LRPC whenever actual inflation changes

legendary.q: Two episodes produce the same increase in inflation. In one, unemployment falls after aggregate demand expands; in the other, unemployment rises after an adverse supply shock. What explains the difference?

Both episodes shift the LRPC because inflation changes the natural rate in opposite directions.
The supply shock lowers expected inflation and moves the economy down an unchanged SRPC.
The demand expansion moves along an SRPC, while the supply shock shifts the curve.
legendary.commonError: Assuming every inflation change is a movement along one fixed Phillips curve.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph with A on SRPC0 and LRPC. Later observations show unemployment at A’s rate but persistently higher inflation. One analyst says the SRPC must have become vertical; another says the same vertical LRPC can coexist with a higher SRPC after contracts adjust. Which additional evidence would support the second interpretation?
options: Inflation rose once, which by itself proves that expectations already adjusted fully.
Current unemployment equals the natural rate, which requires every SRPC to be vertical.
The price level is higher, which proves that the natural unemployment rate permanently fell.
Wage-setting expectations have risen to match the sustained inflation while labor-market structure and supply conditions are unchanged.

legendary.q: A demand expansion moves the economy to lower unemployment and higher inflation. A year later unemployment returns to its original rate while inflation remains higher. Which sequence fits?

Movement along an SRPC followed by an upward SRPC shift
Two movements along one permanently fixed SRPC
An LRPC shift left followed by falling expectations

legendary.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

legendary.q: An adverse supply shock raises inflation while output falls. How should the AD-AS result transfer to the Phillips model?
options: Higher inflation and unemployment indicate an upward SRPC shift
Higher inflation and lower unemployment indicate movement along SRPC
Lower inflation and unemployment indicate a downward SRPC shift
Unchanged inflation with lower unemployment indicates an LRPC shift
legendary.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
legendary.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

legendary.q: A policymaker cites the downward-sloping SRPC as proof that permanently higher inflation will secure permanently lower unemployment. What is the decisive flaw?
options: The SRPC actually slopes upward for every demand change
Inflation cannot respond to aggregate demand in the short run
The natural rate is always zero after an expansion
Expected inflation adjusts, so the short-run unemployment gain is not permanent
legendary.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
legendary.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

boss.q: What does the short-run Phillips curve show?
options: A short-run tradeoff between inflation and unemployment
A long-run tradeoff between inflation and output
A fixed relationship between money supply and GDP
A direct measure of government spending
boss.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows that lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation, and higher unemployment is associated with lower inflation.

boss.commonError: Reversing the short-run inflation-unemployment tradeoff.
boss.q: Expansionary policy raises aggregate demand. In the short run, what Phillips curve movement should follow?

Higher inflation and lower unemployment
Higher inflation and higher unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment
boss.feedback: Expansionary policy raises AD, which can lower unemployment but raises inflation in the short run.

boss.q: Aggregate demand contracts unexpectedly while expected inflation is initially fixed. What short-run Phillips-curve movement is most likely?
options: Toward lower inflation and higher unemployment.
Toward higher inflation and lower unemployment.
The entire SRPC shifts up-right immediately.
Unemployment stays fixed at the natural rate in the short run.
boss.commonError: Confusing a demand-driven movement along the SRPC with a shift of the curve.
boss.feedback: An unexpected demand contraction moves the economy down and right along the current SRPC.

boss.q: On a given SRPC, which combination lies farther up and left?
options: Higher inflation and higher unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment
Higher inflation and lower unemployment
Lower inflation and higher unemployment
boss.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
boss.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

The economy moves down and right along its SRPC
The SRPC shifts upward at every unemployment rate
The LRPC shifts left of the natural rate

boss.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.

boss.q: Which event most directly shifts rather than moves along the SRPC?
options: A change in expected inflation
An unexpected change in aggregate demand
A temporary change in real spending
A movement between two points on one curve

boss.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

Shift SRPC downward, then keep unemployment permanently below natural
Move down-right along SRPC, then shift LRPC right after wages adjust
Move up-left along SRPC, then shift SRPC upward toward the natural rate

boss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

boss.q: A supply disruption raises inflation and unemployment together. Which interpretation survives both the graph and mechanism tests?

The SRPC shifts downward because output fell
The SRPC shifts upward because the tradeoff worsens

boss.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
boss.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

boss.q: A central bank unexpectedly expands demand. Which claim correctly separates the short run from the long run?
options: Inflation falls temporarily and remains lower after all contracts adjust
Unemployment may fall temporarily, but expectations adjustment removes the permanent tradeoff
Unemployment falls permanently because the SRPC stays downward sloping after expectations adjust
The SRPC immediately becomes vertical before output or nominal wages can change
boss.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
boss.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

legendaryBoss.q: A demand expansion moves unemployment below natural. Wage contracts later incorporate the higher inflation. What is the next Phillips-curve development?
options: The SRPC shifts upward and unemployment moves back toward natural
The economy stays on the original SRPC at permanently lower unemployment
The LRPC shifts left because nominal wages increased
The SRPC shifts downward as expected inflation rises
legendaryBoss.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

legendaryBoss.q: One episode has rising inflation with falling unemployment; another has rising inflation with rising unemployment. What distinguishes them?
options: Both are identical movements along one unchanged SRPC despite their opposite unemployment changes in the two episodes
The first shifts LRPC left while the second shifts aggregate demand right
Both establish a permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff without expectations adjustment
The first can be demand movement along SRPC; the second can be an adverse supply shift
legendaryBoss.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
legendaryBoss.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

legendaryBoss.q: A government maintains a fixed unemployment gap below the natural rate through successive demand expansions. Expectations adapt to observed inflation, the Phillips slope is unchanged, and no supply or structural shock occurs. Which distinction explains why a permanently higher but stable inflation rate is insufficient?
options: Maintaining the gap requires only a one-time increase in inflation; expectations adjustment then preserves the lower unemployment.
Maintaining the gap shifts LRPC left even though the prompt holds labor-market structure fixed.
Maintaining the gap requires continuing positive inflation surprises; once inflation stabilizes and expectations catch up, unemployment returns toward natural.
Maintaining the gap requires falling actual inflation while expected inflation rises.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
legendaryBoss.feedback: A fixed below-natural unemployment gap requires a positive actual-minus-expected inflation gap. Adaptive expectations catch up to a stable inflation rate, eliminating that gap. Continued surprises and a return to natural are alternative policy paths, not simultaneous endpoints.

repairQuestions.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.

repairQuestions.q: Can a downward-sloping SRPC guarantee permanently lower unemployment from higher inflation?
options: No, because demand never affects unemployment
No, because expected inflation adjusts
Yes, because the same SRPC is permanent
Yes, because natural unemployment becomes zero
repairQuestions.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.

repairQuestions.q: An adverse supply shock raises inflation and unemployment together. What curve change is indicated?
options: An upward shift of the SRPC
Movement up-left along the same SRPC
A downward shift of the SRPC
A vertical movement along the LRPC
repairQuestions.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.
repairQuestions.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.

bridgeQuestions.q: Aggregate demand expands unexpectedly, raising output and the price level. What linked Phillips result follows first?
options: Lower unemployment and higher inflation along the current SRPC
Higher unemployment and higher inflation from an SRPC shift
Lower unemployment and lower inflation from an LRPC shift
Unchanged unemployment with a downward SRPC shift
bridgeQuestions.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.

bridgeQuestions.q: After a move to lower unemployment and higher inflation, wage setters revise inflation forecasts upward. What happens to the short-run Phillips curve?
options: Aggregate demand shifts the LRPC left
Productivity makes the SRPC vertical
Money demand shifts the SRPC downward
Expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward
bridgeQuestions.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.

bridgeQuestions.q: A short-run unemployment gain disappears as expectations adjust. Which family destination explains the long-run endpoint?
options: A horizontal LRPC at zero inflation
A sacrifice ratio equal to unemployment
The vertical LRPC at the natural rate
A permanently flatter SRPC
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.

bridgeQuestions.q: A contraction moves the economy down the SRPC toward lower inflation and higher unemployment. Which applied destination studies that policy path?
options: Bank reserve creation through repeated lending and redepositing
Disinflation and its short-run costs
GDP accounting identities for measuring current national output
Comparative advantage from differences in opportunity cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.

long-run-phillips-curve.title: Long-Run Phillips Curve
long-run-phillips-curve.description: Apply the natural-rate hypothesis and vertical long-run Phillips curve.

easy.q: The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at:
options: The natural rate of unemployment
Zero inflation
The money supply
The highest price level
easy.commonError: Confusing SRPC with LRPC.
easy.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Which unemployment rate is the natural rate?
options: U1
U2
U3
I1
easy.commonError: Ignoring the vertical LRPC.
easy.feedback: The LRPC is drawn at U2, so U2 is the natural rate of unemployment.

I2
I3
I4

easy.feedback: At U3, the upper curve SRPC2 is at I4.

options: I1
I2
I3
I4
easy.commonError: Reading the upper curve instead of SRPC1.
easy.feedback: The lower point at U4 on SRPC1 is at I1.

On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

easy.q: Where is the long-run Phillips curve drawn?
options: Vertically at the natural rate of unemployment
Horizontally at the current inflation rate
Downward sloping through every short-run point
Vertically at zero unemployment
easy.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
easy.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

easy.q: What does a vertical LRPC imply?
options: Higher inflation permanently lowers unemployment
Inflation is fixed in the long run
The natural rate always equals zero
There is no permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff
easy.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
easy.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

medium.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which pair of points are long-run equilibria?
options: a and d
b and c
a and b
c and d
medium.commonError: Treating all SRPC points as long-run equilibria.
medium.feedback: Points b and c lie on the vertical LRPC at U2.
medium.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.

Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

medium.q: Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 5 percent while unemployment remains at its natural rate. Which long-run outcome fits the vertical Phillips curve?
options: Inflation is higher, but unemployment is unchanged at the natural rate.
Inflation is higher and unemployment is permanently lower.
Inflation is unchanged and unemployment falls to zero.
Both inflation and unemployment are permanently higher.
medium.commonError: Treating a higher expected inflation rate as a permanent way to lower unemployment.
medium.feedback: Along the long-run Phillips curve, different inflation rates can coexist with the same natural rate of unemployment.

medium.q: What natural rate of unemployment is shown by the LRPC?
options: 3 percent
6 percent
5 percent
10 percent
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: The vertical LRPC is drawn at 5 percent unemployment, so that is the natural rate.

medium.q: If inflation rises while the economy remains on the LRPC, what happens to unemployment in this graph?
options: It remains at 5 percent
It falls below 5 percent
It rises above 5 percent
It becomes equal to the inflation rate
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: A vertical long-run Phillips curve means the long-run unemployment rate is pinned at the natural rate.

medium.q: Demand expansion temporarily pushes unemployment below natural. After expected inflation adjusts, where does unemployment tend to go?
options: To zero regardless of labor institutions
Above natural forever with no inflation change
Back toward the natural rate
Permanently farther below the natural rate
medium.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
medium.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

medium.q: Job-matching technology improves and lowers structural unemployment. What Phillips-curve change can follow?
options: The LRPC becomes downward sloping
The LRPC shifts left to a lower natural rate
The economy moves left along the same LRPC
The SRPC must shift upward at every point
medium.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
medium.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

medium.q: A rise in long-term mismatch raises the natural rate. What happens to the LRPC?
options: It shifts right
It shifts left
It rotates to horizontal
It stays fixed at the old natural rate
medium.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
medium.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

medium.q: Why can many inflation rates appear on the same vertical LRPC?
options: Inflation is unable to change nominal wages
Every point has zero expected inflation
Aggregate demand fixes the natural rate
Long-run unemployment equals natural after expectations adjust
medium.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
medium.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

hard.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which point reflects high inflation with unemployment at the natural rate?
options: a
b
c
d
hard.commonError: Confusing short-run and long-run points.
hard.feedback: Point b lies on the LRPC at U2 and inflation I2.
hard.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
hard.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

hard.q: In the standard expectations-augmented Phillips model with no supply-shock offset, actual inflation equals expected inflation. What does the equation imply about unemployment?
options: At the natural rate
Below the natural rate
Above the natural rate
Equal to zero
hard.commonError: Missing the role of inflation surprises.
hard.feedback: With no inflation surprise, unemployment equals the natural rate. The no-offset assumption matters: an independent supply shock can also affect the relationship.

hard.q: Which event is most likely to shift the LRPC right?
options: Higher natural unemployment
Lower actual inflation
Temporary AD expansion
Unexpected money growth
hard.commonError: Confusing inflation changes with natural-rate changes.
hard.feedback: The LRPC shifts when the natural rate of unemployment changes.

hard.q: Which event is most likely to shift the LRPC left?
options: Better labor-market matching
Higher expected inflation
Unexpected AD expansion
Higher oil prices only
hard.commonError: Treating expected inflation as a natural-rate change.
hard.feedback: Better labor-market matching can lower the natural rate and shift the LRPC left.

hard.q: Inflation rises permanently after repeated demand expansion, but labor-market structure is unchanged. Which long-run statement is strongest?
options: Unemployment remains permanently below natural after expectations fully adjust
The LRPC shifts right because the price level rose over time
Unemployment returns toward the same natural rate on an unchanged LRPC
The LRPC shifts left because higher inflation permanently improves job matching
hard.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
hard.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

hard.q: The natural rate falls because job search becomes faster. How should SRPC and LRPC reasoning be separated?
options: LRPC stays fixed while unemployment permanently departs from its vertical location
LRPC shifts left; short-run curves may also reposition around the new natural rate
The economy merely moves upward along the old LRPC as inflation changes
Only inflation expectations can shift LRPC in the long-run model
hard.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
hard.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which comparison best captures the long-run result of higher expected inflation?
options: b and c have same unemployment but different inflation
a and b have same unemployment but different inflation
c and d have same inflation but different unemployment
a and d have same inflation but different unemployment
elite.commonError: Missing vertical long-run logic.
elite.feedback: Both b and c lie on the LRPC at U2, but b has higher inflation.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

elite.q: Assume a fixed natural rate, no supply shocks, and an unchanged Phillips slope. Each year expected inflation equals the previous year’s actual inflation. Policy keeps unemployment the same fixed distance below natural. What must happen to actual inflation and the inflation surprise?
options: Both actual inflation and the size of the positive surprise must rise each year.
Actual inflation rises each year, but the required positive surprise can remain constant.
Actual inflation stays fixed while expected inflation falls each year.
Actual and expected inflation can remain equal while unemployment stays below natural.
elite.commonError: Assuming one expansion can hold unemployment below the natural rate forever.
elite.feedback: With an unchanged slope and unemployment gap, the required actual-minus-expected inflation gap is constant. Because expectations catch up to the previous actual rate, actual inflation must rise again by that same amount. Ever-higher inflation does not require ever-larger forecast errors.

elite.q: Which feature of the graph shows that the natural rate is unchanged after the SRPC shift?
options: LRPC stays vertical at 5 percent unemployment
LRPC shifts left to 3 percent unemployment
SRPC1 becomes vertical at 6 percent unemployment
Point B moves to the right of point A
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: The LRPC staying fixed at 5 percent says the natural rate is unchanged, so inflation changes do not permanently buy lower unemployment.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips graph with two downward-sloping SRPCs, vertical LRPC, and points A and B.

Solid blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6), A at (5,3), and (10,0). Dashed purple SRPC1 is parallel above it, running through (0,9.6), B at (6,6), and (10,3.6). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and intersects SRPC0 at A and SRPC1 at inflation 6.6. Dashed guides mark A at (5,3) and B at (6,6).

elite.q: Which description of point A is correct?
options: A is only on SRPC0 and remains below the natural unemployment rate.
A is only on LRPC and remains above the natural unemployment rate.
A is on both SRPC0 and LRPC at the natural rate
A is the location where SRPC0 turns into a vertical Phillips curve.
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: Point A is where the short-run curve crosses the long-run curve, so unemployment equals the natural rate there.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips graph with downward SRPC0, vertical LRPC, and their intersection A.

Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6.5), A at (5,2.5), and (10,−1.5). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5. Dashed guides from A mark 5 on the horizontal axis and 2.5 on the vertical axis.

elite.q: If point B persists and expectations adjust, what long-run change is predicted?
options: SRPC shifts upward; unemployment returns to 5 percent
LRPC shifts left; unemployment stays at 3 percent
SRPC shifts downward; unemployment stays at 3 percent
LRPC shifts right; unemployment rises above 5 percent
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: With unemployment below the natural rate, expectations eventually adjust, shifting the SRPC and bringing unemployment back to the natural rate.
elite.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.

Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through B at (3,3.5) and A at (5,2.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies above and left of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

elite.q: With unemployment above the natural rate at B, what long-run Phillips-curve adjustment should follow?
options: LRPC shifts right; unemployment stays at 7 percent
SRPC shifts up; unemployment stays at 7 percent
SRPC shifts down; unemployment returns to 5 percent
LRPC shifts left; unemployment falls below 5 percent
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: With unemployment above the natural rate, inflation expectations tend to fall, shifting the SRPC downward and returning unemployment to the natural rate.

elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through A at (5,2.5) and B at (7,1.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies below and right of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

legendary.q: Two economies have the same natural unemployment rate but very different average inflation rates over many years. Which observation is most consistent with a vertical long-run Phillips curve?
options: The higher-inflation economy must have permanently lower unemployment because inflation buys a lasting tradeoff.
The lower-inflation economy must have permanently higher unemployment because prices grow more slowly.
Both can remain at the same long-run unemployment rate despite different inflation rates.
Different inflation rates require different natural unemployment rates even when labor markets are otherwise alike.
legendary.commonError: Inferring a permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff from cross-country inflation differences.
legendary.feedback: The vertical LRPC allows different steady inflation rates at the same natural unemployment rate.

legendary.q: A matching reform lowers the natural unemployment rate from 6.4 percent to 5.6 percent. At the same time, an unexpected demand expansion lowers actual unemployment to 4.9 percent. Later inflation expectations fully adjust while the reform remains in place and no new surprises occur. Which decomposition separates the durable change from the initial cyclical change?
options: LRPC shifts left by 1.5 percentage points; actual unemployment at 4.9 percent is the new permanent natural rate.
LRPC stays at 6.4 percent; both the reform and demand expansion are temporary movements along SRPC.
LRPC shifts to 5.6 percent, but expectations adjustment permanently fixes unemployment at 4.9 percent.
LRPC shifts left by 0.8 percentage point; the initial gap is 0.7 point below the new natural rate, and long-run unemployment returns to 5.6 percent.
legendary.commonError: Confusing a change in the natural rate with a movement caused by inflation.
legendary.feedback: The structural shift is 6.4 − 5.6 = 0.8 percentage point. Actual unemployment is temporarily 5.6 − 4.9 = 0.7 point below the new natural rate. Once the demand surprise disappears, the long-run anchor is 5.6, not the old 6.4 or temporary 4.9.

legendary.q: An unexpected monetary expansion temporarily lowers unemployment. Inflation expectations then fully adjust while the higher inflation rate persists. What is the long-run result?
options: Unemployment returns to the natural rate at a higher inflation rate.
Unemployment remains permanently below the natural rate.
Unemployment rises permanently above the natural rate.
Inflation returns automatically to its original rate while unemployment stays low.
legendary.commonError: Stopping the analysis before expectations adjust.
legendary.feedback: The short-run unemployment effect disappears when expectations adjust, leaving higher inflation and natural-rate unemployment.

legendary.q: Policy holds unemployment below natural with successive demand expansions. Expected inflation rises each round. The repeated expansions then stop and actual inflation stabilizes at its higher rate. Which subsequent path is consistent with the natural-rate model?
options: A sequence of upward-shifting SRPCs ending back at natural unemployment with higher inflation
One unchanged SRPC delivering permanently lower unemployment after every contract renewal
A leftward LRPC shift caused solely by faster inflation with unchanged labor structure
A downward SRPC shift ending in deflation and a lower natural unemployment rate
legendary.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
legendary.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate. Return to natural is conditional on ending the repeated effort to maintain a surprise.

legendary.q: Economy A lowers its natural rate through better job matching; Economy B only creates an unexpected demand boom. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both economies permanently shift LRPC left because unemployment initially declines
Only Economy B changes long-run unemployment by raising aggregate demand
Neither economy can affect unemployment at either a short or long horizon
A can shift LRPC left; B can only move unemployment below natural temporarily
legendary.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
legendary.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

legendary.q: Inflation expectations instantly match a fully anticipated monetary expansion in the model. What Phillips prediction is most consistent?
options: A rightward LRPC shift from higher money growth and unchanged labor institutions
A guaranteed fall in both inflation and unemployment after expectations adjust
Little or no temporary unemployment movement away from the natural rate
A permanent unemployment decline along the SRPC once nominal spending increases
legendary.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
legendary.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

boss.commonError: Confusing the short-run and long-run Phillips curves.
boss.q: What does the vertical long-run Phillips curve represent?
options: The natural rate of unemployment
The current inflation rate
The money supply target
The sacrifice ratio
boss.feedback: The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

boss.commonError: Reading the natural rate from the wrong point.
boss.q: On the graph, where does the LRPC identify the natural rate of unemployment?
options: U1
U2
U3
I2
boss.feedback: The LRPC is drawn at U2, so U2 is the natural rate of unemployment.
boss.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
boss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

boss.q: A government insists on holding unemployment below the natural rate after inflation expectations have adjusted. What does the long-run Phillips-curve model predict?
options: A stable inflation rate will permanently sustain lower unemployment.
The policy requires continuously accelerating inflation.
Unemployment will fall to zero without further inflation.
The natural rate automatically falls whenever aggregate demand rises.
boss.commonError: Believing a stable higher inflation rate buys a permanent unemployment reduction.
boss.feedback: Once expected inflation catches up, maintaining below-natural unemployment requires repeated new inflation surprises.

boss.q: At what unemployment rate is the LRPC located?
options: The cyclical unemployment rate alone
The natural rate
Zero unemployment
The current inflation rate
boss.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
boss.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

boss.q: What makes the LRPC vertical?
options: Expected inflation adjusts in the long run
Aggregate demand never changes output even temporarily
Inflation must remain constant at every natural-rate point
Unemployment cannot change during a short-run demand surprise
boss.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
boss.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

boss.q: Which event can shift the LRPC?
options: A one-time surprise demand expansion with fixed expectations
A movement along the current SRPC after demand changes
A temporary inflation forecast error in wage contracts
A structural change in the natural rate
boss.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
boss.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

boss.q: A policy claim says 6% inflation can permanently hold unemployment below natural. Which model result rejects it?
options: The natural rate falls whenever inflation rises
Expectations adjustment returns unemployment toward the vertical LRPC
The SRPC is always vertical even in the short run
Inflation cannot influence nominal demand
boss.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
boss.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

boss.q: Job-search reform lowers mismatch while inflation expectations are unchanged. Which graph change captures the durable labor effect?
options: The LRPC shifts left to the new natural rate
Movement up the existing LRPC
An upward SRPC shift from higher expected inflation
A permanent move left along one SRPC
boss.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
boss.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

boss.q: Unemployment is below natural and actual inflation exceeds expected inflation. What long-run adjustment follows?
options: Expected inflation falls and SRPC shifts downward
Natural unemployment disappears as inflation continues
Expected inflation rises and unemployment returns toward natural
LRPC shifts left and locks in the lower unemployment
boss.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
boss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

legendaryBoss.q: A surprise expansion moves unemployment below natural; later contracts incorporate the higher inflation. What identifies the long-run endpoint?
options: A permanently lower natural rate caused by nominal demand after contracts renew
A horizontal LRPC at the new inflation rate with lower permanent unemployment
Lower inflation with unemployment still below natural after expectations fully adjust
The same natural unemployment rate with higher expected and actual inflation
legendaryBoss.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

legendaryBoss.q: A labor-market reform lowers the natural rate while a demand expansion temporarily lowers unemployment even further. Which distinction is essential?
options: Demand shifts LRPC permanently while reform only changes the current inflation rate
Neither change can alter a Phillips curve once expectations are specified
The reform shifts LRPC; the demand expansion creates temporary movement relative to it
Both changes are movements along one unchanged SRPC despite different mechanisms
legendaryBoss.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
legendaryBoss.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

legendaryBoss.q: Two economies have different steady unemployment rates but the same long-run inflation. What can explain the difference without restoring a long-run tradeoff?
options: A common SRPC that never shifts
Different natural rates locate their vertical LRPCs differently
Different inflation rates along the same downward LRPC
Permanent forecast errors in both economies
legendaryBoss.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
legendaryBoss.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

repairQuestions.q: Why does higher inflation not permanently lower unemployment in the natural-rate model?
options: Expected inflation adjusts and unemployment returns toward natural
Aggregate demand has no short-run effect
The natural rate always falls with inflation
Nominal wages never respond to prices
repairQuestions.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
repairQuestions.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.

repairQuestions.q: Structural unemployment falls because matching improves. Is that movement along or a shift of LRPC?
options: Movement upward along the LRPC
Movement left along a fixed LRPC
An upward shift of SRPC only
A leftward shift of the LRPC
repairQuestions.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.
repairQuestions.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.

bridgeQuestions.q: Expected inflation has fully adjusted after an expansion. Which prior family idea now leads to the LRPC conclusion?
options: The temporary SRPC movement ends at natural unemployment
The SRPC remains a permanent menu of choices
The sacrifice ratio becomes the natural rate
Deflation moves LRPC to zero unemployment
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.

bridgeQuestions.q: The LRPC places unemployment at its natural rate. Which labor-family concept supplies that location?
options: Natural-rate unemployment from frictional and structural forces
Cyclical unemployment at every inflation rate
Zero unemployment after demand expansion
Labor-force participation alone
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

bridgeQuestions.q: A central bank begins disinflation from the natural rate. Which next family concept measures the possible output cost of the temporary adjustment?
options: The GDP deflator base year
The money multiplier
Comparative advantage
The sacrifice ratio
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
